articles.title: EXPLAINER - Anthropic threat intelligence report: What to know
articles.body:
US artificial intelligence firm Anthropic released a threat intelligence report detailing dozens of state-linked cyber intrusions, automated weapons design efforts, and covert influence operations that used its flagship model, Claude.
"Over the past eight months, our Threat Intelligence team identified and disrupted operations in which threat actors tried to use Claude for malicious activity," the San Francisco-based company said Thursday, asserting that it intervened against unauthorized actors between December and August.
The document outlines activity across seven primary harm categories: cyber operations, foreign influence campaigns, surveillance architectures, fraud, biological misuse, conventional arms development, and model distillation, the unauthorized extraction of an AI system's underlying reasoning by rival developers.
The company said that it dismantled the offending accounts, upgraded internal safety filters, and shared intelligence with government authorities and industry peers where appropriate.
Anthropic claimed foreign intelligence services used multi-agent frameworks to orchestrate cyber espionage and automate offensive operations. A Russian state-linked actor, identified in the report as consistent with the espionage group Midnight Blizzard, allegedly used Claude to target military and diplomatic networks across Ukraine, Europe, and the US.
According to the report, the Russian group deployed automated agents that reverse-engineered proprietary software development kits for military drone vision systems and extracted entire mailboxes from two drone component manufacturers. The company asserted that the operators built autonomous feedback loops.
"If their monitoring AI agents identified that any of their deployed malware was detected by a security product, agents would then set about the process of autonomously modifying and rebuilding the malware to evade the existing detections," it said.
The same actor reportedly breached a North African government technology authority, stealing credentials that compromised more than 300,000 national identity records and corporate registry files for more than half a million businesses.
In another case, Anthropic alleged that Chinese-speaking operators linked to regional security research firms and computer engineering students in Hunan province established an autonomous "exploit foundry".
The group reportedly utilized parallel AI swarms to disassemble firmware from commercial network appliances without human intervention, identifying more than a dozen potential zero-day vulnerabilities, undisclosed software security flaws, in a single month.
The firm claimed the cluster also maintained a fleet of 13 automated collection agents to ingest content from target websites, including publicly accessible US military and government contract postings.
Anthropic documented several instances where threat actors allegedly applied its coding and reasoning tools to kinetic weapons programs. In northern Yemen, the company claimed to have disrupted a technical cell that used Claude Code to design guidance, navigation, and control software across three missile initiatives.
The Yemeni projects reportedly included a tactical guided rocket powered by a smartphone-grade flight computer, a multi-stage ballistic missile with an intended range exceeding 2,000 kilometers (1,242 miles), and an advanced variant known as the "R2000" designed to carry a hypersonic glide vehicle.
Anthropic did not publicly identify the group behind the activities. However, media reports have linked them to Yemen’s Houthis, which controls large parts of northern Yemen.
The company noted that after a test-fire of the tactical guided rocket failed, the operators returned to the model within hours to analyze and diagnose the malfunction. The company acknowledged that the cell had already constructed an offline simulation toolkit that functioned independently of the Claude environment. It did not specify which actor in the country was responsible for this usage.
In Russia, Anthropic uncovered an effort by freelance developers linked to a regional university and a federal research center associated with the Russian Academy of Sciences to engineer Serafim, also tracked as DronDoc, a full-stack autonomous first-person-view (FPV) kamikaze drone swarm.
The actors used Claude Code to build coordination logic and onboard small language models designed for autonomous lethal engagement, enabling the drones to identify an explicit "person" target class and issue detonation commands without human intervention. The system's computer vision was trained on scraped Ukrainian combat footage and validated in simulation using strike coordinates in the eastern Donetsk region.
The report also pointed to military applications in Asia, claiming a Chinese researcher linked to the People's Liberation Army (PLA) Academy of Military Sciences built a 16-module electronic warfare suite. The software allegedly calculated radar jamming allocations and modeled engagement envelopes for US-made Patriot and THAAD air defense batteries, eventually configuring a simulation scenario targeting 12 command bunkers, radar sites, and air bases in Taiwan. A separate Chinese defense researcher reportedly used the tool to benchmark domestic anti-torpedo systems against active US Navy undersea warfare programs.
In the Middle East, Anthropic claimed an Iranian threat actor aggregated open-source intelligence to compile targeting handbooks and recommendations against US naval forces. The actor reportedly processed ship transponder signals, commercial satellite imagery, and personnel rosters scraped from public military photographs, while cataloging vulnerabilities in shipboard systems.
The report claimed that state-backed influence networks in Russia, Iran, and the United Arab Emirates integrated Claude into foreign propaganda pipelines. In the Central African Republic, an operative allegedly tied to the Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) and the Africa Corps network used the model to script pro-Kremlin radio broadcasts for Radio Lengo Songo in Bangui and forge local Defense Ministry documents.
Anthropic further alleged that Russian state-run news organizations, including RT, Sputnik, and RIA Novosti, utilized Claude as an automated sub-editor. These editorial pipelines produced localized propaganda targeting domestic political discourse across Moldova, Latin America, Africa, and global English broadcasts. The pipelines reportedly generated localized news copy, broadcast captions, and defamatory material targeting Moldovan President Maia Sandu ahead of national parliamentary elections in September 2025.
In Iran, state propaganda bodies, including the Islamic Culture and Communications Organization and organs tied to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), allegedly weaponized the model under Tehran's doctrine of "Jihad al-Tabyin," or explanatory jihad. 
 
Anthropic claimed these actors generated statements impersonating IRGC spokespersons and independent voices, compiled profiling databases against political dissidents, drafted contingency funeral plans for the country's Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei — who was killed at the beginning of the US-Israeli war against the country — and fabricated false policy statements attributed to US think tanks such as CSIS, Brookings, and RAND during the ongoing Iran war.
In Africa, Anthropic claimed that an independent technical contractor working for Mali's state intelligence service, the Agence Nationale de la Securite d'Etat, used the model to design "Lakana 360," a nationwide surveillance platform.
The architecture was built to conduct bulk monitoring across 25 million mobile subscribers, capturing voice communications, text messages, and location metadata. Anthropic noted that the developer specifically eliminated court warrant checkpoints from the system module that generated automated intelligence profiles on targeted phone numbers.
The report also uncovered commercial surveillance operations, revealing that Israeli-Singaporean vendor S2T Unlocking Cyberspace used the model to profile social media users across Iran and the Gulf. The platform mapped user locations, classified populations into six demographic categories, generated formal Arabic-language intelligence briefings styled as government reports, and maintained a reserve of more than 255 synthetic personas to infiltrate online communities.
The report highlighted attempts by researchers to exploit the system for dual-use biological work.
Virologists allegedly used commercial intermediaries to conduct gain-of-function research on the chikungunya virus for an overseas military institute, seeking to increase its transmissibility or virulence. Separately, another user explored genetic mutations that could help highly pathogenic avian influenza adapt to mammals and spread through the air.
Furthermore, the company accused Chinese artificial intelligence laboratories, including Moonshot AI and DeepSeek, of executing industrial-scale distillation attacks. These firms allegedly rerouted inbound user prompts to Claude to harvest its chain-of-thought reasoning and train their own architectures.
Anthropic noted that these unauthorized pass-throughs inadvertently exposed sensitive third-party data, including internal closed-circuit television surveillance footage from Chengdu and active database credentials belonging to the Russian Defense Ministry.
While the report detailed extensive foreign exploitation, it omitted any examination of the US military's own integration of Claude onto classified defense networks during recent military engagements.
In July 2025, Anthropic signed a $200 million contract with the Pentagon, making Claude a frontier artificial intelligence model authorized for use on US classified networks through partnerships with data analytics firms such as Palantir. Defense agencies utilized the system to process intelligence data, evaluate logistics, and support operational decision-making.
However, the military partnership collapsed into a public legal clash in early 2026. The original contract barred the Pentagon from utilizing Claude for mass domestic surveillance of American citizens or within fully autonomous weapons systems that select and engage targets without human intervention. In February 2026, the Pentagon demanded that Anthropic lift these restrictions to permit deployment "for all lawful purposes."
Following Anthropic's refusal, US President Donald Trump ordered all federal agencies to phase out the company and US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth designated Anthropic a "supply chain risk." The designation effectively excluded the company from new defense contracting until a US federal judge struck down the measure.
Despite replacing Claude on classified networks with tools from other technology firms, the Pentagon reportedly continues to employ artificial intelligence across combat commands, including operations connected to the Iran war, which is now in its seventh month.
Anthropic's threat report provided no data regarding whether its models or competing commercial systems were utilized in support of US strikes or naval operations across the Gulf, leaving the full scope of military AI deployment undisclosed.

articles.title: Iran Is Rebuilding Its Missile Arsenal Underground After US and Israeli Strikes Cripple Production
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Iran Is Rebuilding Its Missile Arsenal Underground After US and Israeli Strikes Cripple Production
Iran has resumed producing ballistic missiles inside underground facilities, assembling stockpiled components despite US and Israeli strikes meant to cripple the program, according to intelligence findings reported by the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) on September 10.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
US and Middle Eastern officials familiar with the matter described activity to the oulet at several buried sites, including the Khojir missile complex in southeastern Iran. The officials indicated that Tehran is assembling both liquid-propellant missiles, fueled just before launch, and solid-propellant types that can be stored ready to fire.
Iran is also attempting to build new underground assembly points to avoid being struck again, they noted. For now, the missiles are being pieced together from existing components in smaller quantities than before the war, the officials added. US and Israeli strikes damaged industrial facilities, while a naval blockade has complicated imports of parts and solid-fuel ingredients.
Tal Inbar, a senior analyst at the US-based Missile Defense Advocacy Alliance, argued that the pattern was predictable once the bombing stopped. "When there are no bombings of the facilities, you can replace damaged infrastructure, and you can buy new components from other countries and store them in the facilities," he explained.
Analysts assessed that Iran retains thousands of ballistic missiles and could assemble at least a couple hundred more from components already on hand. One former CIA analyst now at King's College London noted that Tehran had stockpiled finished warheads, airframes, and guidance systems before the fighting began.
US officials have maintained that the program lies in ruins. Sean Parnell, the Pentagon's chief spokesman, stated that American forces had destroyed up to 90% of Iran's drone, ballistic missile, and naval industrial base. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had gone further in April, declaring the missile effort "functionally destroyed" and beyond repair.
"You have no defense industry, no ability to replenish your offensive or defense capabilities," Hegseth declared. The fresh intelligence undercuts that assessment, suggesting the pause in fighting has given Tehran room to recover.
Among the weapons Iran keeps firing is the Kheibar Shekan, described as mobile, accurate, and relatively cheap to produce. Those qualities make it well-suited to sustained, high-volume attacks that strain enemy air defenses.
On Wednesday, Iran launched a heavy salvo at an air base in Jordan that houses US troops. Footage showed projectiles fitted with cluster warheads, a type used earlier in the war to overwhelm Israeli air defenses.
Satellite imagery has shown Iran repairing roads, bridges, and production sites, and reopening tunnel entrances collapsed by earlier airstrikes. Weapons stored inside those underground sites are likely well preserved, according to Israeli military assessments.
Iran built its missile program in the 1980s during the war with Iraq and rebuilt quickly after last year's 12-day conflict with Israel. Nicole Grajewski, an Iranian-strategy expert at Sciences Po, noted that the missile network regenerates faster than the nuclear program and is heavily dispersed by design.
The rebuilding effort has extended well beyond missile assembly during the current lull in fighting. Since a 60-day ceasefire took hold in mid-June, later extended by two months in August, Tehran has worked to replenish its arsenal from outside sources as well. Russia began shipping explosives, ammunition, and drone parts to Iran across the Caspian Sea, a route Western navies cannot interdict. That maritime corridor has helped Iran restock weapons depleted by earlier US and Israeli strikes.

articles.title: Iran bags US hardware, German voters revolt, and Zelensky survives a 160km ‘near-miss’: RT stories that shaped the week
articles.body:
Iran bags US hardware, German voters revolt, and Zelensky survives a 160km ‘near-miss’: RT stories that shaped the week
Gulf turns into a shooting gallery
The US-Iran conflict moved increasingly onto the water this week, with oil tankers, warships, and drones all getting involved around one of the world’s most important shipping routes.
Washington struck five Iranian crude carriers on Tuesday after previously attacking three other commercial vessels. Tehran retaliated, claiming strikes on eight tankers and two US Navy vessels, while an Iranian attack reportedly damaged several US warplanes at an airbase in Jordan.
Iran also captured an American underwater drone and, two days later, released footage of a US Saildrone surveillance vessel burning in the water.
Tehran says the Strait of Hormuz remains under its control and has announced plans for another restricted shipping zone nearby.
Oil markets react
The escalating hostilities saw Brent crude surge back above $100 a barrel this week, breaking the threshold for the first time in months.
Meanwhile, Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure have added to fears of further disruption as the kingdom’s oil production in August reportedly fell to its lowest level since 1990 amid growing pressure on its usual export routes.
Trump dividend
As oil prices continue to destabilize the global energy markets, the fallout is expected to become a major issue in the upcoming US November mid-term election. The US president, however, has refused to back down, promising “a lot more” strikes on Iranian tankers.
As for concerned voters, Trump promised to pay every American adult a $5,000 “Trump Dividend” if Republicans keep control of Congress. He did not explain exactly how the payouts potentially costing well over $1 trillion would be funded.
Speaking of enormous piles of money...
An RT investigation looked at Ukraine’s industrial-scale scam-call business, which is estimated to generate around $1 billion every month and employs some 60,000 people.
The business has also become entangled with allegations that corrupt Ukrainian officials have been taking protection money from the very fraudsters they were supposed to go after, leading to the resignation of Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko.
By Friday, Zelensky’s chief of staff Kirill Budanov was also reportedly under investigation over possible financial crimes.
Separately, the New York Times reported that Ukraine lost around $1.2 billion to fraud, waste and mismanagement in military procurement in 2024 alone.
Washington keeps trying diplomacy
While investigators searched for Ukraine’s missing money, Washington continued looking for a peace deal. After Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow and Kiev last weekend, Trump spoke with Putin by phone on Tuesday.
Moscow said it hopes Russia-US-Ukraine talks can resume, while Zelensky floated the UAE, Türkiye and Switzerland as possible venues.
Talking to Russia may be catching on
While Washington has reopened direct channels with Moscow, some European governments that have spent years doing the opposite have increasingly felt the political cost at home.
The clearest example came in Germany, where the Alternative for Germany (AfD) won 43.8% in Saxony-Anhalt last weekend, crushing Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s CDU. Migration was a major issue, but the AfD has also campaigned against sanctions on Russia, Germany’s massive support for Kiev and the abandonment of cheap Russian energy.
Merz said he was “deeply shocked” by the result. He then announced that he would change virtually nothing.
Brussels’ response was hardly more conciliatory, with German media reporting this week that Saxony-Anhalt could lose hundreds of millions of euros in EU funding if the AfD manages to form a government and clashes with Brussels.
Similar frustration was visible in neighboring Poland, where protesters marched under a “Poland for Peace” banner and accused Warsaw of “trying to turn Russophobia into our national sport” and pushing the country toward confrontation with Moscow.
Public dissent grows, governments double down
None of this appears to have slowed Europe’s confrontation with Russia. Moscow this week ordered Germany’s consulate in St. Petersburg and Goethe-Institut cultural centers in Russia to close in retaliation for similar measures taken by Berlin.
Hungary’s new government, which has reversed the comparatively pragmatic Russia policy of former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, expelled ten Russian diplomats. Moscow promised a “harsh and painful” response.
Lithuania, meanwhile, moved closer to scrapping its constitutional ban on hosting weapons of mass destruction, potentially opening the door to nuclear weapons being stationed in the NATO country. Moscow warned that any such weapons would become Russian targets.
160km ‘near miss’
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store continued the Western ‘Russian drone’ hysteria by claiming that Vladimir Zelensky’s plane had been “almost hit by a drone” while leaving Moldova. Western media duly ran with the story.
However, soon after, Moldova itself pointed out that Zelensky’s aircraft had been sitting safely on the ground, faced “no direct threat,” and that the drone eventually crashed around 160km from Chisinau airport.
Europe counts the bill
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov summed up Europe’s current approach rather dramatically, accusing the EU of committing economic “harakiri” by cutting itself off from Russian energy while its own citizens and industry bear the cost.
The assessment was only further proved accurate after Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, one of Kiev’s strongest supporters, similarly warned on Thursday that the EU can forget about competing with China or the US after cutting itself off from cheap Russian energy.
Russia and India are doing business
While much of Europe remains focused on sanctions, diplomatic expulsions and military confrontation, Moscow and New Delhi spent the week discussing planes, trade, energy, space and investment.
The first INNOPROM. India industrial fair opened in New Delhi, bringing together more than 120 Russian and Indian companies, with agreements covering 105 Russian Il-114-300 regional passenger aircraft and plans for local production of the SJ-100 jet in India.
Russian President Vladimir Putin visited India for talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the BRICS summit, as the two countries work toward $100 billion in bilateral trade and closer economic ties.
In other news
Artificial intelligence had another reassuring week as Anthropic revealed five cases in which scientists used its Claude models to help research dangerous pathogens and increase transmission of deadly viruses, which could be used to develop lethal biological weapons.
The report came days after Anthropic researcher Evan Hubinger said he believes there is a greater than 10% chance AI could “kill all humans” within the next decade, while his colleague Jacob Coxon quit the company, warning that sufficiently advanced AI could one day help create “extinction-level bioweapons.”
OpenAI, meanwhile, faced fresh reports that its autonomous agents had once again bypassed restrictions and used outside websites to communicate with one another.
The UN, meanwhile, redrew the world this week and officially endorsed a new map that shows Africa closer to its true relative size instead of the heavily distorted Mercator projection. The General Assembly vote was 164-1, with the US casting the only opposing vote.
Friday also marked 25 years since the September 11 attacks on the US. Fyodor Lukyanov argued for RT that the attacks ended America’s post-Cold War sense of security, while Washington’s response accelerated the decline of the unipolar order it had dominated.

articles.title: Russian Lawmaker Threatens New Oreshnik Strike on Ukraine
articles.body:
A Russian lawmaker threatened Ukraine with another Oreshnik ballistic missile strike on Friday, Sept. 11, claiming Kyiv’s actions were already “close” to triggering the use of the weapon.
According to Russian propaganda reports, Russian State Duma Defense Committee member Andrey Kolesnik issued the threat during a recent interview.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We could use Oreshnik if terrorist attacks against civilians become more frequent. I think Ukraine is already close to being struck with Oreshnik,” Kolesnik said.
The lawmaker cited recent Ukrainian attacks on the Russian cities of Novorossiysk and Sochi, describing them as “terrorist” operations and claiming they targeted areas where no military facilities were sited.
However, he provided no evidence to support the allegation.
A major Russian naval base used by Moscow’s Black Sea Fleet is located in Novorossiysk along with oil infrastructure that generates revenue for Russia’s war against Ukraine. Ukrainian forces recently reported strikes against Russian naval and military infrastructure in the area.
Kolesnik also referred to the use of Ukrainian uncrewed surface vessels, rejecting the possibility that electronic warfare had diverted the weapons from their intended targets.
“These were uncrewed boats clearly following their course,” he said, claiming that Ukraine would soon “feel what Oreshnik is.”
EU Fails to Extend Russia Sanctions For Second Time
Russia used Oreshnik twice
Oreshnik is a Russian nuclear-capable intermediate-range ballistic missile reportedly capable of traveling at hypersonic speeds and carrying multiple warheads.
Russia first used the missile against the Ukrainian city of Dnipro on Nov. 21, 2024. Russian leader Vladimir Putin presented the launch as a warning to Ukraine and its Western partners.
Moscow used Oreshnik for a second time on Jan. 9, 2026, striking near Lviv, close to Ukraine’s border with Poland. Ukrainian officials said the missile carried inert warheads that rely on kinetic energy that caused limited damage to a state-owned facility.
The latter launch was part of a wide-ranging Russian attack involving 242 drones and 36 missiles. Four people were killed in Kyiv during the barrage, while more than 500,000 households temporarily lost electricity.
European and Ukrainian officials condemned the second Oreshnik launch as a dangerous escalation involving a weapon capable of carrying a nuclear payload.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Russia targets Kyiv gas stations for second day
articles.body:
Key developments on Sept. 11:
- 'There might be nothing left tomorrow' — Russia ramps up attacks on Kyiv's gas stations
- Canada sanctions 8 individuals over deportation, militarization of Ukrainian children
- Ukrainian Flamingo missiles strike chemical plant in Russia's Volgograd, Fire Point says
- Russian forces executed 2 Ukrainian POWs near Dobropillia, prosecutors say
- 'The time has come' — Belarus's Lukashenko inspects troops, says army 'needs shaking up'
- Ukrainian drones hit oil refinery, Ozon warehouse as Russia's Saratov comes under attack
Russian drones struck two gas stations in Kyiv on Sept. 11, killing two people and injuring 12 others, including a child, local authorities said.
An air raid siren sounded in the capital at around 9:10 a.m. local time. About half an hour later, explosions were heard across the city, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground.
Five people were hospitalized, while one was treated at the scene, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko. At 11:45 a.m. local time, Klitschko said two of the injured had died in the hospital.
The number of people injured rose to 12 by around 3 p.m. local time, including a 12-year-old boy, the Kyiv City Military Administration (KMVA) said.
As of 3 p.m. local time, seven people remained hospitalized, according to the mayor.
One emergency responder was among the injured in the Russian attacks on the gas stations, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said.
Artem, 25, a refueling technician who asked to be identified by his first name only, said the station previously closed only during "red-level" air raid alerts, which signal a potential missile attack. Following a series of strikes on the city, the station also began closing during "yellow-level" alerts on Sept. 11, which indicate a drone attack, he added.
Artem added that amid the recent attacks, customers have also started buying more fuel, filling their car tanks and storing additional gasoline in personal jerry cans.
"It's scary that there might be nothing left tomorrow," the refueling technician said.
A Russian drone hit an office building in the Podilskyi district, damaging the building and starting a fire on the fourth floor, while a neighboring one-story non-residential building also caught fire, Klitschko said.
Another Russian drone struck the same office building again in a seperate attack hours later at around 6:50 p.m., according to Klitschko. As a result of this strike, a nearby warehouse caught fire, Klitschko said.
The Sept. 11 attacks came as Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski arrived at Kyiv's main train station. The exact agenda of his visit is not known, but it comes amid growing tensions between Poland and Ukraine.

Canada sanctions 8 individuals over deportation, militarization of Ukrainian children
Canada has sanctioned eight individuals involved in Russia's unlawful deportation, indoctrination and militarization of Ukrainian children, the Ukrainian Bring Kids Back UA initiative told the Kyiv Independent on Sept. 11.
The sanctions entered into force on Sept. 4 and were announced during President Volodymyr Zelensky's visit to Canada.
The sanctioned individuals include Russian officials, youth movement leaders, and occupation officials accused of facilitating the abduction of Ukrainian children from Russian-occupied territories and their integration into Russia's education system.
Crucially, the list of sanctioned individuals goes beyond deportation and targets those who abducted Ukrainian children, but also those who run the system of their re-education, Maksym Maksymov, head of Bring Kids Back UA, told the Kyiv Independent.
The list included Grigory Gurov, head of Russia's Federal Agency for Youth Affairs and former chairman of the board of the Movement of the First, a Russian state-led youth organization, Artur Orlov, chairman of the board of the Movement of the First, and Denis Chornobay, head of the movement's regional branch in occupied Donetsk.
"These are the people responsible for programs of indoctrination and militarisation — for ensuring that Ukrainian children cease to identify as Ukrainians and ultimately end up in the Russian army," Maksymov said.
read also
Ukrainian Flamingo missiles strike chemical plant in Russia's Volgograd, Fire Point says
Ukraine carried out an FP-5 "Flamingo" missile strike on Russian military-industrial facilities in Volgograd overnight on Sept. 11, according to Ukrainian missile manufacturer Fire Point.
"Flamingos paid a little visit to Volgograd last night," Fire Point said in a social media statement. "Ukrainian sanctions, as always, proved to be the most effective."
The company said direct hits on the facilities sparked a "massive fire."
The FP-5 Flamingo is a Ukrainian heavy cruise missile manufactured by Fire Point that first entered service in August 2025. While early versions were relatively inaccurate, the missile has since undergone modifications and upgrades and has been used in several attacks on Russian military-industrial facilities.
"The Flamingo was fairly inaccurate in the beginning," Fabian Hoffmann, a senior research fellow at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, told the Kyiv Independent, explaining that Fire Point has since modified and upgraded the missile. "The missile is now operationally more useful," he said.
Footage posted by monitoring channels on social media showed fires apparently coming from the facility, although the extent of the damage remained unclear.
Volgograd Region Governor Andrey Bocharov acknowledged that a Ukrainian missile strike had taken place in the city, claiming that "an industrial facility in southern Volgograd" was damaged by "falling debris."
read also
Russian forces executed 2 Ukrainian POWs near Dobropillia, prosecutors say
Russian troops shot dead two Ukrainian prisoners of war (POWs) in an execution near the eastern city of Dobropillia on Sept. 2, the Donetsk Oblast Prosecutor's Office said on Sept. 11.
According to the pretrial investigation, the two National Guard soldiers were carrying out a combat mission at a position in a forest belt near Dobropillia, Donetsk Oblast, when Russian soldiers captured them.
The Russian troops then allegedly shot the Ukrainian servicemen with automatic weapons, prosecutors said.
The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) is investigating the case under Article 438 of Ukraine's Criminal Code, which covers war crimes resulting in death.
Investigators are carrying out urgent investigative measures to establish the circumstances of the incident and identify the Russian servicemen allegedly involved, the prosecutor's office said.
The execution of prisoners of war is prohibited under the Geneva Conventions and constitutes a war crime.
read also
'The time has come' — Belarus's Lukashenko inspects troops, says army 'needs shaking up'
Belarusian dictator Alexander Lukashenko announced the continued inspection of Belarus' armed forces for readiness, the state-owned Belarusian news agency BelTA said on Sept. 11.
"I've already said it in plain terms: the army needs shaking up, the time has come. The whole army. We'll check everyone. Up to mobilization," Lukashenko said.
Currently, an artillery brigade and communications units are being checked for readiness, after tank and motor rifle units had already been inspected, according to Lukashenko.
"We are preparing for war so that there won't be one," he said.
The tests should resemble actual battles to prepare the Belarusian troops properly, according to the dictator.
"These are the lessons of the special military operation," Lukashenko added, referring to Russia's full-scale invasion.
Lukashenko also said that his youngest son, Nikolai Lukashenko, was currently serving in the army as a lieutenant after being drafted, without revealing the unit where he serves.
read also
Ukrainian drones hit oil refinery, Ozon warehouse as Russia's Saratov comes under attack
Ukrainian drones struck the Russian city of Saratov overnight on Sept. 11, hitting a local oil refinery and a logistics hub operated by e-commerce giant Ozon, according to Ukraine's General Staff and satellite imagery published by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL).
Videos circulating on social media appeared to show drones and Russian air defenses in operation in the region.
The attack on an oil refinery owned by Russian energy giant Rosneft sparked a fire at the facility, Ukraine's General Staff said, adding that the extent of the damage was still being assessed.
Saratov Oblast Governor Roman Busargin posted on Telegram around 2 a.m. local time about a threat from unmanned aerial vehicles, claiming that emergency services had been placed on full alert.
Soon after the strike on the refinery, a logistics hub belonging to Russian e-commerce giant Ozon was also reported to be set ablaze in Saratov. Video published by Exilenova+ appeared to show a major fire emanating from the facility shortly after explosions were heard.
Satellite imagery published later in the day by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL) showed the Ozon warehouse had been completely gutted by fire following the Ukrainian attack. The logistics center covers 100,000 square meters.
"Good results from our long-range strikes aimed at reducing Russia’s capacity to wage war. An enterprise and an oil industry facility were hit in the Saratov and Volgograd regions…Thank you to everyone who is developing Ukraine’s strength so that there will be no safe havens left in Russia for anything that supports the war," President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sept. 11.

articles.title: Why North Korea's Kim Jong Un doesn't need a US deal
articles.body:
Why North Korea's Kim Jong Un doesn't need a US deal
September 11, 2026
In August, US President Donald Trump revived a charm offensive aimed at Pyongyang by drastically scaling back joint US military exercises with South Korea and heaping praise on North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.The US president said the North Korean dictator "has always treated me with great respect."
North Korea's response to Trump's overtures has been markedly less enthusiastic, ranging from firing a barrage of missiles to publicly denying Trump's claims that Kim has responded "very positively" to a request for talks.
This week, as the US and South Korea, along with Japan, kicked off a five-day military drill, there was no mention of any pullback from Washington, nor any sign of diplomatic progress with Pyongyang.
Instead, Kim on Monday commissioned a naval destroyer, while again emphasizing North Korea must establish a "powerful and reliable nuclear war deterrent" and strengthen "maritime defense." Kim also said North Korea would soon unveil a "significant" naval advancement.
No urgency for deal with US
Unlike the summit diplomacy of Trump's first term, Kim's dismissive stance comes at a time when North Korea has alternatives to a grand bargain with the United States.
"For Kim, the stakes are simply lower than they were in 2019. There is no longer the same sense of urgency in Pyongyang to get back to the negotiating table with Washington," Joon Ha Park, a correspondent at Korea Risk Group in Seoul, told DW.
"North Korea now has a treaty-based alliance with Moscow and is drawing closer to Beijing, while its military capabilities have expanded significantly. That's why a single reduction in ROK-US military exercises is not enough for Pyongyang to be swayed," he added, referring to military ties between South Korea and the US.
Kim rides high
Park agrees that Kim is arguably in his strongest position since taking power in 2011.
Just six years ago, amid crippling sanctions and the coronavirus pandemic, an emotional Kim stood at the lectern marking the 75th anniversary of the Korean Workers' Party and expressed regret for having failed the North Korean people.
Fast forward to today, and North Korea's economy appears to be on a stronger footing. Estimates released last year by South Korea's central bank showed the economy expanded by 3.7% in 2024, its fastest rate of growth in eight years.
Kim has brought North Korea closer to Russia and China than the traditionally isolated country has been in decades. This week, both Moscow and Beijing sent messages marking North Korea's 78th founding anniversary and praising the strategic importance of their deepening partnerships with Pyongyang.
Kim's recent spate of good fortune began in 2023, after a summit with Vladimir Putin in Russia's far east. The meeting opened the door for North Korea delivering arms to help Russia fight the Ukraine war, with Moscow sending back aid.
Since then, Pyongyang has heavily ramped up industrial military production, buoyed by fresh financing that skirts international sanctions.
Beijing responds to the Russia-North Korea alliance
China, North Korea's traditional benefactor, quickly took notice of the growing alignment between Moscow and Pyongyang, but initially kept its distance.
"The war in Ukraine has opened up a crucial lifeline for the [North Korean] regime, delivering weapons, ammunitions and soldiers to Russia in return for cash, foodstuff and ostensibly advanced military technology," Alexander Lipke, policy fellow with the Asia Program at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), told DW.
"These warming ties with Russia have also alarmed China, which is also actively attempting to cement its position as Pyongyang's preeminent partner," he added.
By 2025, Russia and North Korea's ever closer ties forced Beijing to pivot and showcase its leading role among the three countries. In September that year, Kim was invited to the "Victory Day" celebrations in Beijing, and for the first time, stood publicly on stage alongside Xi and Putin.
For a regime known for its international isolation, Kim standing shoulder to shoulder with the leaders of Russia and China was a major milestone. This was again the case when in June 2026, Xi's first foreign trip of the year took him to Pyongyang.
Denuclearization off the table?
Notably, any mention of "denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula" was omitted from communiques following these high-level meetings, despite the phrase previously being part of boilerplate diplomatic language from Beijing and Moscow.
This diplomatic softening comes as North Korea aggressively takes steps to ramp up its nuclear program. In February 2026, Kim said North Korea's status as a nuclear weapons state was "irreversible," while calling for the country's nuclear force to be expanded. Recent analysis of satellite imagery suggests increased activity at known North Korean nuclear sites.
Pyongyang has also insisted on US recognition as a nuclear weapons state as a precondition for any talks with Washington, while emphasizing that any future summits must omit language on "denuclearization."
North Korea is estimated to have nearly 60 nuclear warheads, which is double the 20-30 warheads Pyongyang is thought to have possessed during Trump's last diplomatic episode with Kim in 2018 and 2019.
"North Korea is no longer looking for talks centered on denuclearization or even traditional arms control. It increasingly wants recognition, implicitly or otherwise, as a nuclear weapons state," said Park from the Korea Risk Group.
He added that any Trump summit without denuclearization included as part of the official agenda "could be portrayed by Pyongyang both domestically and internationally as implicit US acceptance of North Korea's nuclear status."
Sanctions don't matter anymore?
Since its first nuclear test in 2006, North Korea has been subject to a strict sanctions regime, with the UN Security Council having passed nine sanctions resolutions aimed at restricting exports, along with asset freezes.
The last package was passed in 2017. At that point, it was combined with pressure and fiery rhetoric from the first Trump administration, raising tensions on the Korean Peninsula. Kim was under heavy economic pressure and seeking sanctions relief in return for concessions on his nuclear program. But that moment has now long passed.
"North Korea's diplomatic situation has vastly improved, reducing the pressure to come to the table to cut a deal with the US," said Lipke, adding that "independent sanctions enforcement has widely collapsed," with Russia and China no longer actively pursuing their non-proliferation stance of previous decades.
Lipke said North Korea no longer needs a bargain with the US regarding sanctions relief in return for partial denuclearization.
"But the bargain now on the table could potentially be much larger for North Korea, a freeze in nuclear development in exchange for the recognition by the US as a de-facto nuclear state in front of the whole world."
Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

articles.title: 9/11 – spies, strategy, missed opportunities and lessons learned
articles.body:
For decades, countless leaders have stated that a government’s primary duty is to protect its citizens, yet the 11th of September, 2001, demonstrated that this can fail: intelligence was available, but no one pieced the connections together, reports the BBC.
The attack on the Twin Towers shaped security, intelligence, and foreign policy for decades to come. On the 11th of September, 2001, as Al-Qaeda suicide pilots crashed into the World Trade Center skyscrapers, BBC journalist Frank Gardner had just finished a stint at the broadcaster’s Middle East bureau. While driving the journalist to Tel Aviv airport, a Palestinian taxi driver suddenly turned up the radio volume and said that something massive had happened in the US. The driver was not exaggerating—2,977 people lost their lives that day.
The attacks did not come out of the blue. The US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) had known for years about Al-Qaeda and the activities of its leader, Osama bin Laden. The CIA had even established a task force to capture bin Laden. Nine days after the attacks, then-US President George Bush declared a war on terror. The subsequent 25 years brought both significant successes and major failures in the field of intelligence on both sides of the Atlantic. Successes included the thwarting of terrorist plots and the arrest of criminals. What was the broader picture? How have intelligence, counter-terrorism operations, and strategic planning evolved over these 25 years?
No one disputes that the 9/11 attacks represented a serious intelligence failure.
At the time, both the CIA and the Federal Bureau of Investigation possessed information that—had it been properly shared between the agencies—could have prevented the terrorist attack. The subsequent report attributed the failure to shortcomings in imagination, policy, capabilities, and management within the US government. It concluded that the CIA and FBI failed to adequately assess and share intelligence, and to take the necessary steps to thwart the attack.
The major lessons have been learned—albeit not entirely—and information sharing among Western intelligence agencies has become far more comprehensive than it was in 2001. Since the 9/11 attacks, a comprehensive reorganization of US intelligence agencies has taken place, and the National Counterterrorism Center and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence have been established near Washington to facilitate the flow of necessary information among the 18 American intelligence agencies. The relationship between the CIA and Britain’s MI6 is arguably the closest of its kind in the world. This is complemented by the Five Eyes alliance, which coordinates the exchange of intelligence information among the US, Canada, the UK, Australia, and New Zealand.
However, catastrophic failures have occurred even after the Twin Towers terrorist attack. Prior to the US-led invasion of Iraq, MI6 allowed the intelligence in its possession to become politicized; this dealt the greatest blow to the British service’s reputation since the exposure of Soviet double agents in the 1950s and 1960s.
Facing immense political pressure to find evidence that Iraq—under Saddam Hussein—still possessed weapons of mass destruction,
MI6 passed flawed intelligence to the government of then-Prime Minister Tony Blair.
Iraq had previously possessed weapons of mass destruction, but these had been eliminated following the 1991 Persian Gulf War. After the 2003 invasion of Iraq, MI6 completely overhauled its procedures for evaluating intelligence obtained from field agents. There is now a clear separation between the work of active field agents (who gather information in places like North Korea or Iran, or from within terrorist groups) and the intelligence assessment team. The assessment team verifies the data and often requests additional information before drawing conclusions. General Richard Shirreff, who commanded a division in Iraq, stated that the 2003 invasion was based on flawed intelligence. He asked whether lessons had been learned from this, answered “no” himself, and remarked that “learning is not our strong suit.”
The invasion of Iraq prompted further inquiries, which eventually resulted in the Butler Report. It concluded that British intelligence regarding Iraq’s alleged weapons of mass destruction was deeply flawed and relied on unverified sources.
MI5, too, has made mistakes amidst its numerous successes.
Lord Jonathan Evans, who led the service from 2007 to 2013, noted that following the 9/11 terrorist attacks, the assessment was that Al-Qaeda—along with associated individuals and groups—posed the greatest security threat to Britain. However, with a database of 20,000 subjects of interest and numerous simultaneous investigations, MI5 did not always set its priorities correctly. In 2005, the service failed to prevent the terrorist attack carried out by suicide bombers in London, which claimed 52 lives. MI5 was aware of Mohammad Sidique Khan, the group’s leader, but did not know what he was planning to do. A similar error led to the Manchester Arena bombings in 2017.
Lord Evans noted that while the terrorist threat has not disappeared, the landscape has changed. Threats to national security—in various forms—emanate from Russia, Iran and its allied groups, and China.
One could argue that US President Donald Trump’s decision to launch attacks on Iran alongside Israel was also an intelligence failure. All US allies in the Persian Gulf region were aware of the possibility that Iran might close the Strait of Hormuz. The warning signs were clearly visible, yet Trump lacked a contingency plan when Tehran did exactly what had been predicted.
The immediate aftermath of the 9/11 terrorist attacks was marked by the fear that a similar event might occur again.
Al-Qaeda had even threatened a swarm of planes carrying out attacks on buildings. In their haste to prevent a recurrence of such attacks, the US and its allies committed numerous human rights violations. Suspects were captured in Afghanistan and Pakistan, often based on flimsy evidence. Hundreds of individuals were transported to the Guantanamo base, where they were imprisoned without trial and subjected to torture. Human rights groups have described this as a moral stain on the US conscience. Scandals also emerged regarding the cruel treatment of detainees in Iraq and Afghanistan. Although some of the individuals involved were held accountable, critics have pointed out that high-ranking figures escaped punishment. The US continues to practice detention without trial at the Guantanamo base. Human rights violations also occurred in Great Britain following the 9/11 terrorist attacks. MI6 was involved in the 2004 abduction of Libyan Islamist Abdelhakim Belhaj and his wife in Thailand, and their subsequent rendition to Libya. There, they spent years in prison, where they were subjected to torture. The case later came to light, and in 2018, Great Britain issued a public apology.
Sir Alex Younger, who headed MI6 from 2014 to 2020, stated shortly after leaving office that by focusing on counter-terrorism operations, the British had overlooked China’s emergence as a military power and a strategic challenge.
In 2016, General Shirreff published the political thriller War With Russia, in which he predicted a full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine. In the wake of the 9/11 attacks,
Western nations were preoccupied with the War on Terror
—fighting the Taliban and ISIS, and attempting to stabilize the situation in Iraq—while failing to notice Russia and China developing massive armament programs featuring innovations in hypersonic missile technology. The military successes of both superpowers have significantly eroded the military superiority NATO once enjoyed. Like Iran, Russia, and North Korea, China is considered a challenging target for intelligence gathering. While the use of biometric data was still in its infancy in 2001, technological advancements have since made it much harder for agents to infiltrate China.
Alongside Russia, China is one of MI6’s primary targets. Sam Olsen, a senior analyst at the security intelligence firm Sibylline, noted that while Western intelligence agencies possess a great deal of information about China, the threat lies in the fact that they often see only isolated fragments without fully grasping how they fit together. China’s strength no longer resides solely in missiles, ships, and troops; it increasingly lies in semiconductors, critical minerals, batteries, ports, communication systems, and industrial capacity. Olsen emphasized that the challenge often lies not in gathering intelligence, but in interpreting it strategically.
Twenty-five years ago, US intelligence personnel held the pieces of the puzzle but failed to assemble them and clearly see what lay ahead. Ultimately, intelligence gathering is pointless if the information cannot be utilized for strategic purposes.

articles.title: India and Russia are building something big in space
articles.body:
India and Russia are building something big in space
Space exploration and satellite navigation are fragile, failure-prone and enormously expensive. Yet they offer something few other fields can match: technological superiority and strategic prestige.
The main players in space remain Russia, the United States, and China, followed by India, the European Union, and Japan. Newer entrants include the United Arab Emirates, Iran, and a range of states in South America and West Asia. Because the sector is so costly and high-risk, cooperation is highly valued – it brings redundancy, speeds up technological progress, and cuts the price of getting there.
Russian First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov earlier this week, in the runup to Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to New Delhi, noted that Russia and India are considering the possibility of cross-flights involving mixed crews to their future national orbital stations. He said that this cooperation could eventually extend to joint scientific experiments and research.
In May this year, Indian National Security Adviser Ajit Doval visited the Roscosmos Joint Industry Information Center, while in August, Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar traveled to Moscow to co-chair the 27th session of the India-Russia Inter-Governmental Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific, Technological and Cultural Cooperation (IRIGC-TEC).
Increased collaboration between Moscow and New Delhi within the space sector is occurring within the backdrop of three larger yet interlinked trends: first, the United States’ active dismantling of the remaining international order; second, the ongoing conflicts in Ukraine and Iran; and third, the advancement in drones and defense technologies.
The current US administration has upended the established decades-long US foreign policy by targeting longstanding allies with tariffs and sanctions in the attainment of its goals. India has become a target more than once of American tariffs and economic pressure. Attempts to reach a deal with the Trump administration have failed to produce long-term tangible gains.
This, however, has had a deep impact on the Indian populace. Since the normalization of Indo-US ties, the Indian public had forgotten that historically, American interests had been antagonistic to India during the entire Cold War period. These buried emotions have been surfacing lately with public skepticism regarding American intentions. Deepening cooperation with Russia and attempts to normalize ties with China are New Delhi’s way of signaling its displeasure toward American actions.
Recent developments in Indo-Russian cooperation have involved mutual deployment of ground stations, co-production of engines, and development of national orbital stations. These will allow Russia to offset vulnerabilities by outsourcing joint-production capabilities of critical components to India out of Ukraine’s reach.
The astronomical advancements in drone and smart defense technologies have underscored the significance of satellite-based constellations in warfare. A variety of Russian munitions and weapon systems employ GPS/GLONASS and the upcoming Rassvet system in precision guidance and control. UMPK-equipped glide-bombs, cruise missiles such as the Kh-101, drones like the Shahed-136, Geran-3 & -4, and Orlan-10, along with ballistic missiles such as the Iskander-K, witness a significant increase in accuracy and precision with minimal falloff over large distances.
Furthermore, despite the destruction of existing Viasat infrastructure in Ukraine during the conflict’s opening days, the rapid deployment of Starlink prevented the complete collapse of Ukrainian command and control structures. These attributes make the systems vital to any future operational requirements against adversaries with both limited and significant electronic warfare capabilities.
India’s worst-case military scenarios stipulate for a two-front war. The ability to deploy these munitions and weapon systems may provide its forces with definite tactical and strategic advantages in critical sectors along and beyond the lines of engagement. However, all these require the backbone of GPS/GLONASS capabilities and/or the Rassvet/Starlink low-orbit constellations on which these systems rely. Russia is currently in the process of operationalizing its Rassvet constellation to full functionality.
India’s own NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation) is in dire straits. The indigenous satellite navigation system has dropped below the critical threshold of satellites required for accurate geolocation. Simultaneously, the quest for a reliable low-orbit satellite navigation system over the Indian subcontinent has led to multiple contenders, including the French-TATA venture Eutelsat, the American Starlink and Viasat systems, Reliance’s own planned constellation, and possibly the Russian Rassvet system in the near future.
Space-based cooperation need not be limited to the bilateral level. In August 2021, BRICS space agencies signed an agreement for cooperation in remote sensing satellite data sharing. In May of the following year, the BRICS Joint Committee on Space Cooperation was officially launched. This year, BRICS+ engaged in advanced discussions of cooperation with calls for a BRICS Space Economy being made. Whether civilian cooperation in satellite data constellation ultimately advances to include sensitive military collaboration remains to be seen. What is already clear, however, is that low-orbit constellations are set to become a major disruptor in both civilian and military technology, and this is one area in which the Russia-India partnership could deepen further.

articles.title: UAE revises AI data centre plan after Iranian attacks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UAE revises AI data centre plan after Iranian attacks
The United Arab Emirates is quietly revising plans for a 5-gigawatt AI data centre project - one of the biggest outside the US - after the Iran war prompted a rethink of how and where critical infrastructure should be built, six people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
Originally envisaged as a 10-square-mile (26-square-kilometer) campus in Abu Dhabi, the project will now likely comprise a network of data centres spread across the UAE, according to four of the sources, who all spoke on condition of anonymity.
Authorities are also considering ways to better protect the facilities from drone and missile attacks, including with air defenses and by building some underground, they said. The likely modifications to the project’s blueprint have not previously been reported.
Data centre project is central to UAE's global AI ambitions
Plans for the UAE-US AI Campus, which is being built in partnership with American tech companies, were announced during President Donald Trump's visit last year to the wealthy Gulf state.
The project is central to the UAE's ambitions to become a global AI powerhouse as it shifts its economy away from oil. It is led by G42, an AI firm controlled by Sheikh Tahnoun bin Zayed al Nahyan, the UAE national security adviser and brother of its president.
In return for access to Nvidia AI chips and other advanced US technology, the UAE agreed to cut AI ties with China and invest in the Stargate initiative’s American data centres. Stargate is a joint venture between OpenAI, Oracle and SoftBank to build AI infrastructure.
The people who spoke to Reuters included a US official, a Western diplomat and industry executives briefed on the deliberations. The news agency could not determine how close Emirati authorities are to finalizing a new masterplan or the extent to which the proposed changes might affect construction costs and timelines.
Construction on the first phase of the project, a $30-billion, 1-gigawatt compute cluster known as Stargate UAE, began last year with the first 200 megawatts of capacity due to come online this year. When completed, it will have enough capacity to connect every UAE government agency and commercial institution to the world's most advanced AI models, according to Larry Ellison, chairman and chief technology officer at Oracle, which is partnering with G42 on the project.
Responding to Reuters questions about potential revisions to the project, G42 said work on the AI campus was progressing as planned.
“The project's specifics are subject to continuous review in line with the security, resilience and operational standards expected of critical infrastructure at this scale,” the company said without elaborating.
OpenAI said it was working with the UAE to achieve its AI vision and making “good progress on the infrastructure and adoption priorities needed to deliver it."
The Emirati advanced technology ministry and the project’s other American partners – Nvidia, Oracle and Cisco – did not respond to comment requests. Japan’s SoftBank declined to comment.
Iran targets US-linked tech infrastructure
Emirati officials began reviewing their AI infrastructure plans soon after Tehran started firing missiles and drones at Gulf neighbors that host American forces in retaliation for US and Israeli airstrikes against Iran, the sources told Reuters.
Two Amazon Web Services data centres in the UAE were damaged in the attacks in March along with one in Bahrain. The company’s cloud computing services in the region are still disrupted, according to the latest updates on its website.
In April, Iran’s armed forces issued a video warning that Stargate UAE was also a potential target. The video included a map purporting to show where the complex is being built, with the caption: “Nothing stays hidden from our sight.”
Two people familiar with the matter confirmed the location at a site near Al Dhafra Air Base, which was not publicly known. The base on the outskirts of Abu Dhabi hosts US troops and has been targeted during the war, which began in February.
Daniel Benaim, who served as US deputy assistant secretary of state for Arabian Peninsula affairs under President Joe Biden, said the conflict has been an "economic earthquake" for Gulf states, which had long marketed themselves as safe havens.
“Changes to harden critical infrastructure are vitally necessary,” said Benaim, a fellow at the Middle East Institute, a Washington think tank. “Every country in the region is going to look at what they can do to reduce the risk” and reassure international partners and investors.
The first phase of construction at the UAE’s AI campus is expected to continue as planned, although with some modifications to protect the site from aerial attacks, according to an industry executive and another person briefed on the matter. The rest of the project will likely be spread across multiple locations, they said.
In addition to building underground, officials are considering putting facilities that host the most sensitive data, such as that used by the military, inside mountains, the two said. In the United States, China and Europe, data centres have been built inside disused mines, Cold-war era bunkers or caves.
The UAE, located on the southeastern Arabian Peninsula, is mostly flat, desert terrain. But there are mountain ranges running through parts of the north and northeast in the Ras Al Khaimah and Fujairah emirates.
Air defense systems are being incorporated into the redesign, including drone and missile interceptors and electronic jamming equipment, three sources said. Other likely measures include the use of blast-resistant concrete and the addition of backup power and cooling systems, another said.
(Reuters)

articles.title: ‘Weeks, Not Months’: Ukraine’s FP-7 Ballistic Missile Could Soon Strike Russia
articles.body:
Ukraine could begin striking Russia with its new FP-7 tactical ballistic missiles within the coming weeks, Iryna Terekh, CEO of Fire Point, said on Thursday.
Fire Point is one of the Ukrainian army’s largest contractors, producing, among other weapons, long-range FP-1 strike drones and FP-5 “Flamingo” cruise missiles, which have repeatedly struck military targets deep inside Russian territory.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to Terekh, the FP-7 can reach targets up to 200 kilometers (124 miles) away and carry a warhead weighing up to 150 kilograms (330 pounds).
The missile has successfully completed two stages of testing and is now preparing for combat deployment.
“We are talking about weeks, not months,” Terekh said during the MSPO 2026 defense exhibition in Poland, as cited by UNIAN.
The FP-7 is a ground-launched system with a maximum projectile speed of 1,500 meters per second (4,921 feet per second). Fire Point founder and chief designer Denys Shtilerman has compared the missile to the US-made ATACMS system.
In June, Shtilerman said the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) could begin launching the first strikes on Moscow with Ukrainian-made ballistic missiles as early as this autumn.
He said the company was conducting the final testing phase for the new long-range missile and that, following the tests, “flights into Russian territory will begin.”
“The military will determine the targets, but I think they will be significant ones right from the start,” h said.
Ukraine Is Losing Its Tech Edge to Russia, Former Google CEO Says
Terekh added that another company project, the long-range FP-9 missile, with a range of up to 850 kilometers (528 miles), is currently undergoing flight tests.
Because of its range, testing the missile within Ukrainian territory is impossible. As a result, the next stage could effectively involve combat strikes against targets inside Russia, the company’s representative said.
Fire Point officially announced the development of the FP-7 and FP-9 ballistic missiles in September 2025. In February 2026, the company demonstrated the first test launch of the FP-7.
Вітаємо FP7) pic.twitter.com/FxgCHVHMET
— Denys Shtilierman (@DenShtilierman) February 27, 2026
Following such developments, Ukraine will begin to launch deeper and more powerful strikes inside Russia if Moscow continues the war, Presidential Office Chief Kyrylo Budanov told Latvian Television.
“If Russia does not stop hostilities against us, it will feel the consequences ever more strongly,” he said.
Budanov’s warning followed a Sept. 9 strike by Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces (SSO) on two Russian gas-condensate plants in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug.
The SSO said its drones traveled more than 3,000 kilometers (1,864 miles) into Russia, hitting the Novy Urengoy and Purovsky facilities.
Budanov said Ukraine would continue fighting as long as necessary but was ready to end hostilities on acceptable terms.
“We are standing on our land, and no one has the right to simply give that land away to someone else,” he said.
Budanov added that the most realistic arrangement would be to halt fighting along the existing front line and provide Ukraine with security guarantees. However, Kyiv will not legally recognize Russia’s occupation of Ukrainian territory.
