articles.title: What Role Does Denuclearization Have in North Korea-US Dialogue Today?
articles.body:
With his surprise decision to scale back the recent Ulchi Freedom Shield military exercise on the Korean Peninsula, U.S. President Donald Trump clearly signaled his intent to rekindle dialogue with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. However, rather than receiving praise for the goodwill measure, the effort drew rebuke from the North Korean government, which reiterated its position that it has no interest in renewing engagement as long as the United States holds onto denuclearization as a policy objective.
This exchange has renewed debates over long-standing denuclearization policies, particularly as Trump continues his overtures toward the Kim regime in hopes of a possible meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit in November. Some have argued it is time to abandon denuclearization as a policy goal and shift to arms control, while others contend that such a concession would undermine the global nonproliferation regime and place further stress on allied relationships.
Rather than a binary “should they, shouldn’t they” approach, the issue requires a more nuanced examination of the constraints and interests at play. For example, what does the Kim regime mean when it demands that foreign governments drop denuclearization as a precondition for talks? What does the Trump administration hope to achieve by renewing engagement? Further, would dropping denuclearization even be politically sustainable for this administration or other governments?
It’s useful to break down the denuclearization debate, examining the knowns and unknowns for the two sides.
Trump’s Overtures and North Korea’s Response
On August 16, Trump announced the shortening of the annual South Korea-U.S. Ulchi Freedom Shield joint military exercise, reiterating his usual claim that the exercises are costly and adding that they “send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile” to North Korea. He claimed that the Kim regime has been “unthreatening and respectful” during his presidency.
North Korea’s response came on August 19 in the form of a statement attributed to Kim Yo Jong, Kim Jong Un’s high-ranking sister. The statement declared that Pyongyang regarded the reduction of exercises as “unworthy of comment” and has “no interest in it at all” due to “the nature of the military drill with a provocative and offensive feature.” North Korea followed that up two weeks later with another statement attributed to an unnamed Foreign Ministry spokesperson, noting “it is pointless to expect any détente in the region” as the “U.S. remains committed to the complete denuclearization of the DPRK” (an abbreviation of North Korea’s formal name, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea).
But this may be changing. In other contexts, the White House has demonstrated a willingness to abandon status quo policies and pursue rapprochement with authoritarian governments. As a result, the administration may consider shifting from denuclearization-first diplomacy to an approach that de-emphasizes denuclearization through arms control and risk reduction measures, or even eliminates it as a policy objective altogether.
The Knowns and Unknowns of North Korean Demands
The Kim regime has clearly set a precondition for renewed engagement with the United States: drop denuclearization from the agenda. What is less clear is what North Korea actually expects with this precondition.
Pyongyang’s rejections of denuclearization evolved following the brief period of diplomacy in 2018-19. After the failure of Kim Jong Un and Trump to reach an agreement at the February 2019 Hanoi Summit, Pyongyang hardened its stance against denuclearization. In December 2019, North Korean Ambassador to the United Nations Kim Song stated that “denuclearization is already gone out of the negotiation table.” Based on numerous statements since, North Korea’s position has become more absolute: denuclearization is not up for negotiation and Pyongyang has no intention to relinquish its nuclear arms.
Despite the hardline position, the Kim regime has not shut the door completely on potential engagement. North Korea has continued to highlight the “excellent” relationship between Kim Jong Un and Trump, referencing Kim’s “good memories and feelings” towards the U.S. president. Although positive inclinations in a personal relationship do not necessarily translate to rapprochement between governments, these are notable signals that may compel Washington to pursue status quo-changing pathways to engagement.
A challenge for Washington is that the scope of the required policy change is not yet clear. What specific actions would Pyongyang expect from Washington to signal the end of denuclearization? Does this mean a policy pronouncement, rescission of United Nations Security Council resolutions, or something else?
It is also unclear whether the Kim regime would be willing to offer concessions in return. There is no indication thus far of what may be negotiable with denuclearization off the agenda, whether it be arms control or other tradeoffs such as reducing North Korea’s military aid to Russia. This creates a risk: if the United States does give ground on denuclearization, Pyongyang could simply walk away from dialogue since it has already met one of its key policy objectives.
The U.S. Debate Over Denuclearization
On the U.S. side, there is a growing recognition that North Korea’s nuclear capability is now an established reality. Three decades of efforts to persuade Pyongyang to relinquish its nuclear weapons have not curbed the Kim regime’s ability to develop a nuclear weapons program of considerable scale and capability. Trump recently said North Korea has 57 warheads, while the South Korean Ministry of National Defense estimated it to be somewhere between 80 and 120.
From the outset, the United States’ goal has been to achieve a nuclear-free peninsula through diplomatic means. This has contributed to a substantial body of policies, sanctions, and international resolutions aimed at constraining and ultimately eliminating the North Korea nuclear program. Thus, there are significant legal and political considerations that affect the extent to which Washington can pursue alternate approaches.
One consideration is the global nonproliferation regime. A shift in U.S. policy would have ripple effects across the framework designed to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons, including the Non-Proliferation Treaty Review Conference and the International Atomic Energy Agency. Experts have pointed out that abandoning denuclearization would signal a de facto acceptance of North Korea as a nuclear-armed state, and that risks not only undermining the Non-Proliferation Treaty but setting a precedent for other rogue states to pursue nuclear armament.
Also, the United States and the U.N. Security Council have imposed numerous rounds of sanctions on North Korea in response to its nuclear development and testing activities, in part to mitigate the increase in nuclear weapons while also deterring others from pursuing similar programs. A formal policy shift that accepted North Korea as a nuclear-armed state would raise questions about the status of existing sanctions and internationally agreed-upon resolutions. At the U.N. level, alterations to the North Korea sanctions program would require Security Council action, potentially requiring the modification or termination of existing resolutions that could easily be blocked by a veto from France, the United Kingdom, or any of the other five permanent members of the Security Council.
A second consideration is the response from U.S. allies. Most American allies and partners have established policies supporting a nuclear-free North Korea, so any unilateral U.S. decision will have cascading effects, forcing other governments either to adapt to a policy shift or oppose the U.S. approach. This will be particularly important for South Korea and Japan.
Although Seoul has already placed denuclearization as the last step of its “END” strategy (“Exchange, Normalization, Denuclearization”) it has not dropped it as a goal altogether. Meanwhile, Japan’s commitment to North Korea’s complete denuclearization remains a pillar of its security designs. A change would push Tokyo to assess how much policy space exists within its current framework to move closer to Washington’s or Seoul’s approach. It may be possible for the three to retain a formal commitment to denuclearization while also pursuing nuclear risk reduction and arms controls, but there will invariably be an impact to trilateral cooperation that requires close coordination.
Further, any pursuit of diplomatic engagement with North Korea without addressing the Kim regime’s ongoing support for Russia’s war effort against Ukraine will invariably face opposition from the United States’ European allies. These partners may withhold support outright unless the White House is willing to leverage issues related to the Russia-Ukraine War in pursuit of engagement with Pyongyang.
The third factor is domestic politics. While the Trump administration was able to move forward on controversial decisions in the first half of his term, the forthcoming midterm election could bring to power a Democratic-controlled Congress, which would attempt more restraint. Additionally, groups across the political spectrum are opposed to altering denuclearization policy, calling into question the sustainability of such a change. Notably, Trump cannot run for re-election; the coming change in presidential administration after 2028 could result in an outright policy reversal.
What This Tells Us About the Denuclearization Debate
These knowns and unknowns reveal a few key considerations for the denuclearization debate.
To start, it would be useful to canvas North Korea about what it actually means by dropping denuclearization as a policy objective. In other words, if the White House is seeking meaningful engagement, a starting point can be inquiring about the Kim regime’s expectations for moving forward past denuclearization. This can be communicated through direct lines of communication or signaled through talking points in the media.
It is also essential to identify the two sides’ goals if preconditions are met and talks happen. Right now, there is no clear indication of what the White House would be seeking to achieve through another summit between Trump and Kim Jong Un. Conversely, after more than 30 years of focusing on denuclearization, it is unclear what the Kim regime would be prepared to discuss in direct dialogue with the United States. Focused examinations and debates on these issues would be helpful in charting a course forward for any potential engagement.
Finally, it is necessary to determine how to translate goals into sustainable policy adjustments. The reality is that the U.S. and North Korea governments are different in nature, and while the Kim regime may be willing and able to institutionalize a permanent change to the status quo, conditions for a democratically-elected government are different. Unilaterally dropping denuclearization as a U.S. policy objective for a photo op will almost inevitably result in significant political pushback and challenges, both domestically and abroad.
Ultimately, the denuclearization debate must be resolved if dialogue with North Korea remains an objective. However, if the goal is to ensure that the dialogue actually produces meaningful outcomes, the debate will require more nuance and structure than currently exist. What would this policy shift mean in practice? Can the White House build an engagement strategy that is realistic enough to produce useful dialogue with North Korea, ambitious enough to reduce nuclear risks, and durable enough to overcome the inevitable obstacles along the way?
A clear understanding of both parties’ expectations and goals will be essential for coordinating with allies and multilateral agencies and institutionalizing any agreements to safeguard against collapse.

articles.title: How 9/11 turned a terrorist attack into a generation of war
articles.body:
How 9/11 turned a terrorist attack into a generation of war
On the morning of September 11, 2001, Americans watched in horror as hijacked planes struck the World Trade Center and the Pentagon and crashed in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Nearly 3,000 people were killed. Less than a month later, the US went to war in Afghanistan. Two years after that, it invaded Iraq.
What began as an attack by Al-Qaeda would come to reshape US foreign policy, the Middle East, and the way Islam was discussed around the world.
A quarter of a century later, September 11 still casts a long shadow over American public life. Al-Qaeda’s responsibility for the attacks has long been established, but the edges of the story remain blurred. Documents remained classified for years and only emerged piece by piece; lawsuits dragged on; questions lingered over who might have known more, who might have helped, and how far the web surrounding the hijackers actually extended. In the gaps between what was proven, what remained secret, and what was merely suspected, conspiracy theories flourished – but so did genuine political and legal questions that America has never quite managed to put to rest.
Nowhere has that shadow fallen more heavily than on Saudi Arabia; 15 of the 19 hijackers were Saudi citizens, and for decades, victims’ families, lawyers, and advocacy groups have pressed for greater disclosure about possible links between people associated with Saudi institutions and some of the attackers. The result is a peculiar political afterlife of 9/11. Even as Washington and Riyadh have remained strategic partners, questions surrounding the attacks have repeatedly resurfaced whenever the relationship with the kingdom comes under scrutiny.
Under former President Joe Biden, the issue returned to public attention when his administration ordered a new review and declassification of government records related to 9/11, following sustained pressure from victims’ families. The Saudi question also became entangled with a broader political reassessment of Washington’s relationship with Riyadh following the murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi.
In that sense, September 11 left behind more than a settled account of a terrorist attack. It left a long political shadow – one that continued to affect how Americans view particular Arab states, their governments, and eventually, the Muslim world.
The architecture of suspicion
The more immediate consequence of September 11, however, was broader than the hunt for those responsible. The attacks changed the conceptual framework through which the US understood Islam itself.
After 9/11, the country needed explanations: Why did it happen, what produced Islamist violence, and how could another attack be prevented? The American system responded in a characteristically American way: It went looking for expertise. Government agencies poured money into universities, professional associations, and think tanks, demanding explanations – and quickly.
But there was an almost paradoxical mismatch between the question and some of the intellectual tools available to answer it. Many of the scholars being asked to make sense of Islam, political Islam, and jihadist violence built their expertise studying religion in a different context: Christianity in the US, including Christian fundamentalism and its relationship with political extremism.
To Grigory Lukyanov, a research fellow at the Institute of Oriental Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences and deputy dean at Russia’s State Academic University for the Humanities, the episode illustrates something larger about the American response to 9/11: Confronted with an unfamiliar threat and under enormous pressure to produce answers quickly, institutions reached for intellectual tools they already possessed.
“You needed ideas, you needed solutions, you needed an understanding of how to solve the problem,” Lukyanov said. “Money was given to scholars of religion, quick results were demanded, and existing analytical frameworks were transferred onto Islam.”
Islam increasingly became something to be categorized in security terms.
A movement classified as ‘moderate’ might be treated as a potential partner; one categorized as ‘radical’ could become a target of surveillance, sanctions, or counterterrorism operations, but the consequences quickly moved beyond policy and into everyday life. In September 2001, 28% of Americans said they had become more suspicious of people of Middle Eastern descent; in March 2002, 25% of Americans said Islam was more likely than other religions to encourage violence (now, 25 years later, it’s 51%).
For Lukyanov, the resulting distortions were almost built into the speed and structure of the response. “It is difficult to search for alternatives in counterfactual history,” he said. “The attack had happened. What could the United States do – simply not conduct a War on Terror? Retreat into something like the Monroe Doctrine, recoil from what had happened and accept defeat? That was almost impossible to imagine.”
The US of 2001 was at the height of its post-Cold War power, the Russian expert said. The Soviet Union disappeared a decade earlier; China had not yet emerged as a peer economic competitor; Washington possessed unmatched military, financial, and political reach. September 11 was therefore interpreted not only as a terrorist atrocity, but as a challenge to American global leadership.
“Not responding was impossible,” Lukyanov said. “The question is that the response was built on the experience, analytical frameworks, decision-making patterns and limitations that American political elites had at that moment.”
America’s road to endless war
If the securitization of Islam was one consequence of September 11, the most visible was measured in soldiers, bases, and wars. Yet here as well, 9/11 was less a beginning than an acceleration.
The US was hardly a newcomer to the Middle East in 2001. Its involvement expanded dramatically after the Cold War and the 1990-91 Gulf War. The US had troops and military facilities across the region, protected the Gulf monarchies, enforced no-fly zones over Iraq, supported Israel, and remained indispensable to Arab-Israeli diplomacy. By the end of the 1990s, American primacy in the region was difficult to contest.
“The United States began sinking into the Middle Eastern swamp long before September 11,” Lukyanov said. “There were essentially no other external players, and almost no major conflict or problem in the region could be resolved without the participation of Washington.”
September 11 was therefore not the moment America entered the Middle East. It was, in Lukyanov’s words, a crescendo – the moment an already extensive political and military commitment became something larger and far more difficult to control.
Less than a month after the attacks, the US invaded Afghanistan to destroy Al-Qaeda and remove the Taliban government that had sheltered it. The initial campaign was remarkably swift. By December, the Taliban regime had collapsed. What followed was not. The US would remain in Afghanistan for nearly 20 years, its longest war, losing more than 2,400 service members as it tried to build a new political order. It ended in August 2021, with the Taliban sweeping back into Kabul.
Five years later, Taliban fighters patrol the capital in American-supplied Humvees, carrying American weapons and wearing American tactical gear. Around $7 billion worth of US-funded military equipment remained in Afghanistan after the collapse of the forces the US spent two decades building.
Destroying one enemy, creating another
Then came Iraq.
Unlike Afghanistan, the 2003 invasion was not presented as war against the organization that carried out the September 11 attacks. The administration of George W. Bush argued that Saddam Hussein’s regime possessed weapons of mass destruction (which were never found) and presented Iraq as part of a broader post-9/11 security threat. But by then, the invasion had already removed the Iraqi state’s leadership, dissolved much of its coercive apparatus, and opened a political vacuum at the center of the Arab world.
One consequence of the US invasion of Iraq can still be felt today, Lukyanov argues, pointing to the ongoing exchange of strikes between Iran and US forces across the region.
“It was the American invasion of Iraq, prompted by the 9/11 policies, that created the conditions for a geopolitical conflict in that country, escalating the geopolitical standoff between the United States and Iran,” Lukyanov adds. “It was precisely because of this that the United States significantly increased its support for Israel and its policies.”
Hussein’s fall destroyed a regime that brutally dominated Iraq for decades, but it also removed one of the principal Arab counterweights to Iran. Iraq’s long-suppressed Shia majority acquired unprecedented political power, while many Sunnis who occupied privileged positions under the old order suddenly found themselves marginalized.
The dismantling of the Iraqi Army and Baathist state structures left hundreds of thousands of armed and militarily trained men without a place in that order. Insurgency spread and sectarian violence followed. A new generation of jihadists that came into that landscape, now known as ISIS, built itself amid the occupation and the Sunni insurgency. By 2014, ISIS seized Mosul and proclaimed a caliphate across large parts of Iraq and Syria.
The friends America abandoned
The War on Terror did not only transform America’s enemies, it also transformed its friendships.
Across the Arab world, authoritarian governments quickly discovered the political value of becoming indispensable to America’s new struggle. Tunisia, Sudan, Yemen, Egypt, Jordan, and several Gulf monarchies expanded counterterrorism cooperation with the US, while governments increasingly presented domestic repression as part of the same fight against extremism. The distinction between jihadists and non-violent Islamist opponents could become dangerously elastic. Organizations that threatened the regime politically could be folded into a much broader security problem.
For aging authoritarian systems, the new order offered an opportunity. Lukyanov argues that some regimes came to believe that cooperation against a common enemy would buy them a kind of political absolution. “The War on Terror gave them the illusion that, by acting against a common enemy together with the United States, they would receive forgiveness for everything that had happened in the past.”
Few countries tested that proposition as dramatically as Libya.
Muammar Gaddafi spent decades as an adversary of Washington. But he was also an enemy of the jihadists seeking to overthrow him. After 9/11, this suddenly gave Tripoli and Washington something to talk about. Libya shared intelligence on Al-Qaeda and other Islamist militants with Western services; in 2003, Gaddafi renounced terrorism and agreed to dismantle his weapons-of-mass-destruction programs. Sanctions were progressively lifted, diplomatic relations restored, and in 2006, the US removed Libya from its list of state sponsors of terrorism.
For a time, the bargain appeared to work. A ruler once treated as an international pariah reinvented himself as a counterterrorism partner. Washington, meanwhile, gained intelligence cooperation and the dismantling of Libya’s unconventional weapons programs without another war.
But there was a catch. Cooperation abroad did not require meaningful liberalization at home. Libya remained brutally authoritarian even as relations with Washington improved; elsewhere, the counterterrorism imperative similarly gave security states additional room to operate. In Egypt, emergency laws allowed thousands to be detained without fair trials, while Washington tolerated serious abuses by governments it relied upon for counterterrorism cooperation.
Then, a decade after September 11, the bargain began to come apart when uprisings began in Tunisia in late 2010, and Zine el-Abidine Ben Ali fled. In Egypt, Hosni Mubarak resigned after nearly 30 years in power. And in Libya, the reversal was even more extraordinary: Gaddafi – the former enemy who dismantled his weapons programs, shared intelligence on jihadists, and rebuilt relations with the West – faced an uprising of his own. NATO intervened against his forces, and in October 2011, Gaddafi was killed.
The political vacuum produced another irony, Lukyanov said. For decades, some Arab governments portrayed Islamism as one of the principal dangers from which their rule protected both their own societies and the West. Once several of these governments fell, however, Islamist movements proved to be among the best-organized political forces left standing. Ennahda won Tunisia’s first post-revolutionary election; in Egypt, the Muslim Brotherhood emerged as the dominant electoral force and its candidate, Mohamed Morsi, won the presidency. “In the end, in both Egypt and Tunisia, for example, movements that had provided Al-Qaeda with a social and political support base came to power,” Lukyanov said.
In the places where revolutions did not produce functioning political systems, the circle became darker still. Libya descended into fragmentation and civil war; Yemen collapsed into a regional conflict; Syria became the battlefield in which local rebellion, state repression, regional competition, and transnational jihadism converged. Groups linked to Al-Qaeda, and eventually ISIS, found new territory in the wreckage.
When the War on Terror came home
Six days after the attacks, Bush visited a Washington mosque and declared that “Islam is peace,” seeking to draw a line between the perpetrators and millions of ordinary Muslims. On the ground, however, the backlash was already well underway.
Anti-Muslim hate crimes surged from just 28 in 2000 to 481 in 2001 – a more than seventeen-fold increase. Another 49 assaults and 104 incidents targeting places of worship were reported in the first week after 9/11 alone. In Chicago alone, the number of reported anti-Muslim or anti-Arab hate crimes jumped from four in all of 2000 to 51 in just the three months from September to November 2001.
The effect was measurable within Muslim communities themselves; 57% of Muslim Americans said they had experienced some form of bias or discrimination since the attacks, and 48% said their lives had changed for the worse. Yet the response was not uniformly hostile; 79% also said they had experienced an act of kindness or support from friends or colleagues of other faiths.
The consequences went beyond the immediate backlash. The security architecture built in the aftermath of 9/11 also expanded the reach and militarization of law enforcement. By 2020, nearly 65% of the roughly 18,000 US law enforcement agencies had received military equipment through the Pentagon’s 1033 program, such as weapons, ammunition, and tactical armored vehicles.
“If we return to the question of how Islam and the Islamic world have changed, Islam as a teaching has not changed,” Lukyanov stresses. “Nor have the borders of Muslim states changed. What has changed, however, is the position of Muslim communities in Western countries and in countries outside Muslim-majority regions.”
A quarter of a century later, the legacy of 9/11 extends far beyond the attacks themselves. Not only the US, but the world around it changed: Wars reshaped the Middle East politics (though did not change the region’s borders), new extremist movements emerged, regional rivalries deepened, and Muslim communities in the West faced greater suspicion and scrutiny. In that sense, perhaps the most consequential story of 9/11 for the Muslim world is not what happened on that day, but what followed in response.

articles.title: IDF's war on all fronts: How Eyal Zamir is managing threats from Iran, Lebanon, Gaza, and West Bank
articles.body:
When IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir finished 2025, he was on track as one of the most popular IDF chiefs in recent memory.
He had stormed onto the world stage in June 2025 leading Operation Rising Lion, Israel's remarkably successful massive strike on Iran's nuclear program, radars and air defenses, top military officials, and some ballistic missile sites.
Next, he was the IDF chief in October 2025 when a deal was struck with Hamas to end the Gaza War, including the return of all remaining living and deceased hostages.
But 2026 is still a work in progress, with some of Zamir's legacy in the balance.
Iran is weaker, but the threat is far from gone
Israel's early 2026 Operation Roaring Lion is viewed by most in Israel and globally as less successful than the 2025 operation. This is true even as the IDF did destroy significant aspects of Iran's ballistic missiles program, caused between $200-300 billion dollars of damage to its broader military industrial complex, and assassinated Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Regardless of the military successes, it has been highly problematic diplomatically, turning even more of the world against Israel. Also, Israel has lost additional important measures of support from the Trump administration over gas prices and the crisis in the Straits of Hormuz as well as over the fact that the Iranian regime survived and with an intransigent attitude.
So what is the overall strategic and specific threats picture?
In the view of the IDF high command, which Zamir directs, The Jerusalem Post has learned that biggest strategic win for Israel and which has been ignored by much of the global media, is Israel's advantage over Tehran after the 2026 war both in learning and advancing the other side's tactics and regarding capabilities, meaning gaining an upper hand in resupplying weapons and the ongoing arms race.
Much of the global media has focused on the US's using up significant amounts of its air defense interceptors and attack bombs, which may leave it less able to block a theoretical Chinese move to take over Taiwan.
While this is a critical debate for the US, Israel has no such disconnected second front where it would need to defend against an imminent and massive aerial enemy attack.
Rather, Israel only needs to "race" against the Islamic Republic when it comes to the volume of offensive and defensive weapons needed to prosecute an extended new offensive or defensive war.
In numbers, the Post understands that in the view of Israeli intelligence, this means that Israel has been racing ahead with new military surprises and tactics to unleash against Tehran in any potential future new conflict.
In contrast, Iran's ability to embrace and prepare new tactics is limited two-fold. It is limited by its lack of funds and preoccupation with trying to stay above water militarily after having been so severely battered. Further, it is limited by the absence of any near-term horizon or moment in which it will be economically saved and be able to fully reopen up a process for recovery and for developing new projects.
The Post understands that Zamir and the IDF high command view Israel as jumping years ahead in these areas, even if there are some other specific select areas where Iran may be able to remain more formidable.
There is another crucial development in holding Iran back from restoring its former ballistic missiles and other sources of threat power. It is a mix of the 2026 war's destruction of Iran's future production capabilities in tandem with the US's stronger than expected post-war success in blocking China from resupplying ballistic missile technology and supplies to the Islamic Republic.
The Post learned back in April that one of the greatest concerns of Israeli intelligence was to what extent China might hand over critical items to restore Iran's ballistic missile threat capabilities on a more wholesale basis.
If without Beijing, Iran was viewed as being pushed back years backward, Israeli intelligence worried that China could hand over enough ballistic missile items rapidly enough to jumpstart the recovery process forward much faster.
Although Israel does maintain that China has helped Iran recover some capabilities in this area, Zamir and the high command's view is that Washington has succeeded in blocking the vast majority of this assistance through its counter-blockade of the Straits of Hormuz. This is something which in April, no one expected would last into September or beyond.
This means that after Israel destroyed Iran's planetary mixers in 2026, which were viewed as the key to rapid mass production of ballistic missiles, that the Islamic Republic could be left with trough mixers or other slower and inferior production processes.
In contrast, if China had provided new planetary mixers and other items directly to Iran, the situation could have been much more dangerous.
Due to the damage to ballistic missile production and the US success so far with the Chinese, the IDF expects Iran to remain under 2,000 missiles even at the end of 2026, the Post has learned.
On one hand, that almost 2,000 number is very disturbing.
There were earlier hopes that Iran could be held under or around 1,000 for a longer period, and Iran has shown impressive resiliency to rebuild aspects of its missile production in a very short time after the 2026 war.
But in another sense, this is a significant near and medium term win for Zamir and Israel.
All of this comes after Tehran had somewhere between 2,500-3,000 such missiles prior to the June 2025 war.
It means that more than 18 months after that war, Iran will still have significantly fewer missiles than it had at the time.
This is even more significant when one takes into account that the pace at which Iran was moving with ballistic missile production prior to June 2025 was expected to get it to over 6,000 missiles at an earlier point in 2026 and 8,800 missiles by August 2027.
The existential ballistic missile threat has not been removed.
But it has been delayed already more than two years, and by some estimates given to the Post by as many as four years, though those most optimistic estimates make certain assumptions which could evolve.
Hezbollah is weaker, but Israel has no clear exit from Lebanon
If after the 2023-2024 war, Hezbollah was down from 150,000 rockets and mortars to 30,000-50,000, the Post has learned that it is now as low as 10,000 following the IDF's war on it in 2026.
That means Hezbollah's current arsenal is weaker than Hamas's was on October 7, 2023, when once the Lebanese terror group dwarfed the Gazan terror group in power (Hamas meanwhile has almost no rockets and has not succeeded in firing a rocket to harm Israelis in years, with its last major effective attack coming in January 2024.)
The IDF also has made it currently impossible for Hezbollah to invade Israel by seizing an approximately 10 kilometer deep security zone in southern Lebanon.
This does not mean Israel is safe from Hezbollah. There is currently no real process to disarm the group unlike in Gaza where there may be such a process with Hamas.
The Lebanese army is still terrified of having a direct conflict with Hezbollah and the Post understands that as long as the army views the 1970s Lebanese civil war as its low point, and not the recent round of fighting with Israel, this is unlikely to change.
Long-term this could leave Israel stuck in Lebanon like it was 1982-2000, something it does not want, due to military vulnerabilities and diplomatic harm from an extended occupation, and with no apparent exit strategy.
Earlier hopes that the positive relations between the Lebanese and Israeli governments might be enough to pressure Hezbollah into even partial disarmament currently look like pipedreams in the eyes of Zamir and the IDF high command, the Post understands.
But the IDF can only manage the military playing field, and converting military wins into strategic diplomatic gains, is the role of the civilian government.
In Gaza, military gains collide with political limits
This same issue is present in Gaza where the IDF has done its best to keep Hamas from making a comeback, but has no ability to force Israel's government to allow other Palestinian or international authorities into the Strip to try to replace Hamas.
If the Netanyahu government does eventually allow the International Stabilization Forces (ISF) peacekeepers and the NCAG Palestinian technocratic committee into Gaza after months of delay (by both him and Hamas), it will be only due to pressure by the Trump administration.
In the meantime, Zamir has warned that if Hamas's threat is not reduced either by diplomatic-political means or by a new major operation, the group could eventually start to reconstitute itself as a threat to Israel after years on the run.
Eyal Zamir faces a two-front battle in the West Bank
Through all of this, Zamir has inherited a multi-headed problem of terror emanating from the West Bank since early 2022.
He has tried to order harsher crack downs on certain more problematic Palestinian areas, reducing aspects of the terror threat substantially – by some estimates as much as 80% - but nothing close to stopping the threat.
At the same time, Zamir, along with the police, the Shin Bet, and the government more broadly, have lost control over several hundred violent Jewish extremists who have been regularly attacking both Palestinians and soldiers alike.
Zamir has not fought with Defense Minister Israel Katz to restore administrative detention of violent Jews, a tool the Shin Bet has consistently demanded be returned to them for use.
Rather, he has been strategic about public fighting with the defense minister, with a focus on keeping control of key IDF appointments and on pressing the government to draft more haredim. This has been despite pushes by Katz to make political-friendly appointments and to protect haredi political parties from any substantial concessions on drafting more young men from their sector into the military.
Possibly Zamir's most dramatic moment was a leak in March of a private speech he made to the cabinet about the need to draft more haredim in which he said, “I am raising 10 red flags before the IDF collapses into itself.”
More recently, he has also been more public lately about demanding government backing for combating Jewish extremist violence.
On August 27, Zamir announced that he was expanding the Israeli forces being used to maintain public order in the West Bank leading into the upcoming fall Jewish holidays.
The Post understands that the volume of forces will be more than double the pre-October 7 force size of around 11 battalions, which at times has grown to 15-20 battalions, but will temporarily grow even more.
Zamir warned the government that Jewish extremist violence has run out of control and that greater backing is needed from the government, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and others actively restraining political officials from provocative actions.
All of this takes place as IDF officials have said Jewish extremist violence has reached new levels, with hundreds of extremists recently drawing out a conflict with the IDF at the Palestinian village of Kusra for multiple weeks.
It also takes place as IDF and Shin Bet officials say that the police, after three years under Itamar Ben-Gvir, have reached highly problematic lows in terms of arresting and helping indict Jewish extremists in the West Bank.
None or almost none (the police have been at a low also in terms of transparency) of those involved in the Kusra actions were arrested.
Accordingly, Zamir has brought in the Golani Brigade and the Paratroopers Brigade to supplement the standard forces in the area, some of which have appeared too sympathetic to Jewish extremists attacking Palestinian villages.
However, without more backing from the government, Zamir has warned that even increased military forces will be insufficient.
Looking into 2027, in some ways, Zamir has succeeded in making Israel more secure than it was in the 2023-2025 period. But almost every front remains a challenge, such that he will continue to have his work cut out for him.
For a shorter version of this profile as it appears in The Jerusalem Post's 50 Most Influential Jews 2026 list, click here to read Zamir’s entry.

articles.title: Ukraine Is Losing Its Tech Edge to Russia, Former Google CEO Says
articles.body:
Ukraine risks losing its technological advantage over Russia as Moscow adapts its weapons and expands military production, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt warned Wednesday, Sept. 9.
In an opinion column for The Washington Post, Schmidt said Russia was moving toward a strategy of “total war” by mobilizing its factories and manpower while developing technologies to counter Ukrainian innovations.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Schmidt, who now chairs the Special Competitive Studies Project, said he has repeatedly traveled to Ukraine and helped its military develop battlefield technologies.
He wrote that Ukraine’s main advantage during much of the full-scale war was its ability to develop, test and modify new weapons within weeks. Decentralized networks connecting Ukrainian soldiers, engineers and defense technology companies allowed Kyiv to innovate faster than Russia’s larger military bureaucracy.
That advantage is now “rapidly diminishing,” Schmidt warned.
After Ukraine developed interceptor drones capable of destroying Russian Shahed-type drones, Moscow began deploying faster jet-powered variants that are significantly more difficult to intercept, he said.
Russia is also developing a satellite constellation intended to rival Starlink, which Ukrainian drone units use to target Russian forces in occupied territory.
While Russia previously relied primarily on its larger industrial base to counter Ukrainian innovation, it is now combining mass production with its own technological advances, Schmidt wrote.
Russia Sends Bones of Medieval Warrior to Ukraine Front to Boost Morale
Drones can become obsolete within months
Schmidt described a battlefield where thousands of unmanned systems conduct reconnaissance, transport supplies and hunt soldiers and vehicles.
He wrote that around 80% of Ukrainian military casualties occur while troops are moving between positions. Some soldiers remain underground for months after reaching the front because movement above ground has become extremely dangerous.
Weapons are also becoming obsolete at unprecedented speed. A drone that proves effective when introduced can become virtually useless within months if the opposing side changes its radio frequencies, deploys electronic warfare systems or develops faster interceptors.
Ukraine remains highly effective at adapting its technology, Schmidt said, but innovation alone cannot meet the scale of demand created by a high-intensity war.
One Ukrainian commander told Schmidt that his unit had stopped looking for additional targets because it lacked enough drones to strike those it had already identified.
Schmidt argued that producing hundreds of highly advanced drones is less valuable than manufacturing effective systems in the hundreds of thousands.
Schmidt urges West to expand Ukrainian production
Russia is building the capacity to manufacture weapons in enormous quantities and is considering another large-scale military call-up that Ukrainian officials expect could occur this fall, Schmidt wrote.
He warned that the coming winter would be critical as Russia exploits Ukraine’s shortage of air defenses capable of intercepting ballistic missiles to strike power plants and electrical substations.
Ukraine cannot match Russia’s manufacturing capacity without substantial Western involvement, Schmidt said. Kyiv urgently needs air defense interceptors, ammunition and long-range weapons, alongside investment to expand domestic production.
He urged Western governments to treat Ukraine’s defense industry as an extension of their own by jointly manufacturing weapons, resolving supply-chain bottlenecks and ensuring Ukrainian commanders do not have to ration attacks because of equipment shortages.
Closer integration with Ukraine’s battle-tested military would also allow Western armed forces to learn lessons about modern warfare and prepare for future security threats, he added.
“Lauding Ukrainian resilience is not a strategy, and courage alone cannot defend its cities or win its war,” Schmidt wrote.
You can also highlight the text and press Ctrl + Enter

articles.title: Americans are seeking a pretext for another strike on Iran’s nuclear facilities
articles.body:
Americans are seeking a pretext for another strike on Iran’s nuclear facilities
In an interview with Hassan Hanizadeh, an international affairs expert, Shargh referred to the anti‑Iran resolution passed by the Board of Governors of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). Hanizadeh said that this resolution was adopted under pressure from the United States and certain European countries to increase pressure on Iran and isolate it, and that its political dimension outweighs its technical aspects.
He stated that the resolution contains no new technical ambiguities that had not already been addressed, which indicates that Iran has taken the necessary steps toward transparency. Nevertheless, the Board of Governors and the IAEA Director General, in their reports on Iran’s nuclear activities, have focused primarily on political considerations and have ignored technical aspects. Referring this resolution to the UN Security Council could push Iran toward withdrawing from the Nuclear Non‑Proliferation Treaty (NPT)—although Russia and China may veto any resolution against Iran in the Security Council.
Iran: Let us not destroy our opportunities
The Iran newspaper spoke with Bahador Zarei, a professor of geopolitics, about Iran’s geographic and geopolitical capacities. Zarei said that although Iran is relatively small in geoeconomic terms, it is the 17th largest country in the world in terms of national power, national security, and territorial size. However, Iran is not strong in trade, with a trade volume of less than 50 billion dollars. Therefore, Iran must enter the global geoeconomic cycle and expand its commercial relations with various countries. In such a scenario, both the Caspian Sea in the north and the Persian Gulf in the south would gain strategic and geostrategic importance, enabling Iran to connect to Central Asia, the Caucasus, South Asia, West Asia, and Southwest Asia. Iran has land and maritime borders with 13 countries, which is one of the factors that makes Iran difficult to sanction effectively. If the issues surrounding the Strait of Hormuz are resolved, even if the United States seeks to impose sanctions on Iran, implementing such sanctions would not be easily feasible.
Siasat-e-Rooz: The US and Israel started the war, but Iran will end it
In its editorial, Siasat-e-Rooz focused on Iran’s regional power and its control over the Strait of Hormuz. The paper wrote that recent developments in the Persian Gulf and the US–Iran conflict show that the United States still imagines it can use its military and economic capacity to force Iran into submission and manage financial markets, hoping to reduce Trump’s economic challenges. In contrast, Iran—through new initiatives and by expanding the scope of its operations from the military domain into the technological, geopolitical, and economic spheres—is sending a clear message that control of the Strait of Hormuz remains in Iran’s hands. Ultimately, it is Tehran that determines the outcome of the war of endurance. The paper argues that no country can pass through the Strait of Hormuz or the Persian Gulf without Iran’s coordination and consent. This means that the United States and Israel may have initiated the conflict, but Iran will be the one to conclude it.
Jam-e-Jam: America’s attritional deadlock in the Strait of Hormuz
Jam-e Jam analyzed Iran’s powerful attacks on US positions in the region. According to the paper, the unprecedented damage suffered by the Pentagon and the CIA is the result of entirely flawed strategic decisions made by US policymakers in the war with Iran. The United States, by adopting an attritional strategy, has begun a new phase of continuous attacks on military infrastructure in the Strait of Hormuz. But these temporary successes have never been sustainable, as they are always met with immediate Iranian counter‑strikes, including drone attacks, while Iran’s industrial base remains intact. Applying this doctrine against a state actor exposes Washington to severe risks of miscalculation. While the US needs secure passage through the Strait, Iran can impose high costs simply by creating a sense of insecurity. This asymmetry, combined with the US inability to contain ballistic missile responses, has turned the conflict into a low‑intensity but persistent battle.
Hamshahri: The deterrence equation is on Iran’s table
Hamshahri analyzed Iran’s approach to the war with the United States, describing it as a war of equations—breaking existing equations and creating new ones. The paper argued that sustainable security has three pillars: deterrence, diplomacy aimed at reducing isolation, and national power and social cohesion. From this perspective, the Islamic Republic must maintain and strengthen deterrence, because weakening it would undermine the other two pillars and create serious risks and potential crises for the country. Deterrence has minimum and maximum levels. Iran has reached a certain level, but still has a long path ahead to reinforce it so that the very idea of attacking Iran becomes minimal.

articles.title: India Welcomes Russia, Iran Leaders for BRICS Summit Overshadowed by War
articles.body:
Leaders from Russia and Iran were in India for talks on Friday, ahead of a BRICS summit dominated by conflict and economic challenges, which Chinese President Xi Jinping will also attend.
Wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, as well as global trade turbulence and oil are expected on the agenda at the two-day annual summit that opens on Saturday, when Xi is set to arrive.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
It will be Xi’s first visit to India since 2019, and marks the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the rival neighbours, six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Tibetan border.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming again, with flights, visas and high-level contacts gradually being restored.
“China stands ready to work with India... by strengthening communication, enhancing cooperation, and properly handling differences,” Beijing’s foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said Friday.
Deep mistrust remains, with their contested Himalayan frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.
Dozens of Tibetans protested in New Delhi on Friday -- exiles, like their Buddhist leader the Dalai Lama, who has lived in India since fleeing a Chinese crackdown in 1959 -- waving placards against Xi’s visit.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is due to hold talks on Friday with President Vladimir Putin, who last visited India in December 2025. Moscow is one of New Delhi’s most important strategic partners.
Russian Chemical Giant’s Plant in Perm Targeted in Ukrainian Drone Strike
“One should engage in debate and friendship only with the virtuous, and nothing whatsoever with the unvirtuous,” Modi wrote Friday, in a social media message in Sanskrit to welcome leaders to the 11-nation summit.
Posters of a beaming Modi line streets across New Delhi, with heavy deployments of security forces across the capital and widespread traffic restrictions.
BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who arrived in New Delhi on Friday and will hold talks with Modi, said that “BRICS was established to counter unilateralism”, according to Tehran’s IRNA news agency.
- ‘Fault line’ -
As well as Iran, BRICS includes Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates -- countries with sharply differing positions on the war launched by the United States and Israel in February.
All three have been admitted to the group in recent years, joining founding member states that include India, China and Russia.
“The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the BRICS summit,” said Harsh V. Pant of India’s Observer Research Foundation.
“What was seen until last year as an achievement -- the expansion of BRICS -- today looks like a big constraint on BRICS,” Pant said.
Pezeshkian’s participation -- his first visit to India as Iranian president -- will put the Middle East conflict firmly on the agenda.
“The war in Iran will provide a stern test of the group’s cohesion,” said Shilan Shah of Capital Economics, noting the failure of the BRICS foreign ministers to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May.
UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is also expected, as is Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan, and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi.
India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.
New Delhi has navigated the energy crisis sparked by the US-Iran war in part by turning to Russia for fuel despite Western sanctions as the war against Ukraine drags on.
Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar visited Kyiv this month, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he was “grateful to India for its commitment to ending this unjust war”.

articles.title: Russia Issues Nuclear Threats to Lithuania Over Vilnius’s Plan to Lift Nuke Ban
articles.body:
Russia has threatened Lithuania with nuclear weapons as the Baltic nation is eyeing a lift of its nuclear weapons ban.
Lithuania’s parliamentary parties provisionally agreed to the constitutional amendments in July, and the parliamentary Committee on Legal Affairs voted 7-2 on the proposal on Wednesday, Sept. 9, paving the way for a final decision in early 2027.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The lifting of the ban would allow NATO, of which Lithuania has been a member of since 2004, to deploy nuclear forces on its territory.
On Friday, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov threatened Vilnius over the plan by saying the Baltic nation – once under Soviet occupation – will be “in the sights of our nuclear weapons.”
“And if there are nuclear weapons on the territory that are aimed at us, then the territory of this country will also be in the sights of our nuclear weapons,” Peskov told Russia’s Channel One on Friday, as reported by state media RIA Novosti.
Lithuania, one of Ukraine’s strongest backers in Europe, borders Russia’s exclave of Kaliningrad to the west and staunch Moscow ally Belarus to the south, with Vilnius a mere two-hour drive from Minsk, Belarus’s capital.
Russia began deploying nuclear weapons to Belarus, a non-nuclear nation, in June 2023. In December 2025, Russia also deployed its nuclear-capable Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missile (IRBM) to Belarus, whose combat use in Ukraine marked the first combat use of its kind in history.
St. Petersburg Metro Prepares 9 Stations as Civil Defense Shelters
In May, Belarus conducted a nuclear war drill with Russia, involving Belarusian military units tasked with the combat use of nuclear weapons and nuclear support operations.
In July, when discussions over the nuke ban gained traction in Vilnius’s parliament, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda attributed the need to changing geopolitical circumstances.
“The geopolitical situation is getting worse… Our constitution was written when geopolitical circumstances were totally different,” Nauseda said.

articles.title: Medvedev: NATO Will Not Invoke Article 5 if Russia Strikes Lithuania
articles.body:
Dmitry Medvedev, former president and current deputy chairman of the Russian Security Council, said Lithuania would “disappear from the map of the world” if it lifts its longstanding nuclear weapons ban.
Medvedev made the remarks on Friday, Sept. 11, after Russia had already threatened Vilnius earlier that same day.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The country’s parliamentary parties had agreed to the constitutional amendments in July, while the parliamentary Committee on Legal Affairs voted 7-2 on the proposal on Wednesday, paving the way for a final decision early next year.
“Lithuania, as I understand it, talked about opening the door for the possible placement of any weapon, including nuclear weapons,” Medvedev said, according to Clash Report.
“If God forbid, something like this happens and we have to react to their actions, no one will step in for them,” he continued, adding that NATO would not invoke Article 5 to defend the country as this would mean “a global catastrophe.”
Simultaneously, he denied the threat of Russia attacking Europe, despite an increase in Russia’s provocations, including hybrid threats and frequent drone violations of NATO’s airspace.
Advancing nuclear ban repeal despite growing threats
The lifting of the ban would essentially allow NATO to deploy its nuclear forces on Lithuania’s territory.
“The geopolitical situation is getting worse,” Lithuania’s President Gitanas Nauseda told reporters following the meeting with parliament party leaders, in which 50 MPs submitted an amendment to change the law. “Our constitution was written when geopolitical circumstances were totally different,” he continued.
Russian Strikes Kill 6, Injure 33 in Nationwide Barrage on Ukraine
The move came as Finland decided to lift its own ban just a month earlier, allowing NATO to host and transport nuclear weapons on its territory in crisis situations.
Lithuania remains one of Ukraine’s strongest backers in Europe, and it borders Russia’s exclave of Kaliningrad to the west and Moscow’s ally Belarus to the south.
In June 2023, Russia began deploying nuclear weapons to Belarus. The two countries conducted a joint nuclear war drill in May, centering on use of nuclear weapons and nuclear support operations.
Although Belarus continues positioning itself as neutral in Russia’s war against Ukraine, it remains its ally, providing territory and critical components Russia needs for weapons making.
In December 2025, Russia deployed its nuclear-capable Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missile (IRBM) to Belarus, whose combat use in Ukraine marked the first such use of its kind in history.

articles.title: Iran used AI to develop military, propaganda strategies, Anthropic report reveals
articles.body:
Iran repeatedly used American-made artificial intelligence systems to target US naval forces in the region, target Israeli and Jewish diaspora organizations, and develop phishing strategies inside the country, a Thursday Anthropic report revealed.
Anthropic described what it called an “Iran-nexus threat actor” that used Claude, the company’s flagship product, to develop targeting recommendations against US Navy targets.
The actor, according to Anthropic, used AI to identify and track naval positions and compile information, including “a roster of US personnel scraped from captions on public military photographs; publicly accessible ship and aircraft transponder identifiers; commercial satellite-imagery query scripts; and an inventory of public websites that exposed US naval movements.”
The unnamed organization also used AI to research vulnerabilities in shipboard systems, including “maritime VSAT terminals, Cisco communications equipment, and industrial control products,” according to the report.
This was one of the many findings revealed in the AI giant’s 154-page report, which delineated the dangers of US and Western adversaries such as Iran, China, and Russia utilizing the technology to pose security threats.
The report comes as debate over the dangers rages among policymakers and AI company employees, even as Anthropic refused the Pentagon’s February request to remove safety guardrails regarding mass domestic surveillance and fully autonomous weapons.
A Friday Wall Street Journal report revealed that a top researcher at Anthropic quit last week, citing fears that AI companies were developing uncontrollable systems.
'AI could kill all humans,' top Anthropic scientist says
Evan Hubinger, a top scientist at Anthropic, wrote in a social-media post, “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!”
“I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to,” the WSJ cited him as saying.
Anthropic’s report revealed that all groups showed similar methodology. “They ran multi-victim campaigns using agentic AI that would previously have required teams of operators. They built custom tools, executed intrusions, and processed stolen data at volumes no individual human operator could manage manually,” the company explained.
In addition to targeting US military assets, Iran also developed an “automated, open-source intelligence identity-profiling harness” that targeted hundreds of Israeli governmental and non-governmental individuals, as well as Jewish diaspora organizations.
The actor used the system to collect and analyze open-source data, developing a pipeline that made malware harder to detect.
Iran using AI to survey, profile Iranians
Another two “Iranian nexus actors” used the company’s model to surveil and profile 6,388 Iranians in one year. The AI company claimed that Iran built an “analyst and production studio” used to run a social network analysis of over 155,216 tweets.
Among other domestic surveillance strategies were automatic license-plate recognition, mobile-device identifier interception, and private Telegram data analysis.
These operations targeted Iranian minorities, dissidents, and opponents of the Iranian regime abroad, according to the report.
Actors also used AI to run campaigns tied to “Jihad al-Tabyin,” or explanatory jihad, to produce propaganda in what they called a “soft war” or “cognitive warfare” program: a non-military plan to shape public opinion at home and abroad, the report explained.
Several Iranian organizations, including the Islamic Culture and Communications Organization (ICCO), were using AI to distribute Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) - aligned narratives, said the report.
The organizations used the technology to build operational manuals, create persona systems, develop content strategies, and transform official government material into targeted messaging.
Yemeni group developing missiles with AI
Anthropic also claimed that a northern-Yemeni group was using Claude to develop guidance software for high-end weapons, including a multi-stage ballistic missile.
This comes as the Iranian-backed Houthis consolidate control over the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. Anthropic said that its safeguards had blocked many of the group’s requests to develop the weapons, “but not all of them.”
The company confirmed that it had taken the necessary steps to ban the account, develop detections to prevent future use, and share intelligence with government authorities.
“We hope that the findings in this report will help other developers recognize similar patterns on their own platforms, give governments and civil society a clearer view of how emerging threats take shape, and strengthen collective defenses,” it said.

articles.title: Kremlin spokesman says Lithuania would be ‘in the crosshairs of our nuclear weapons’ if it deploys a nuclear arsenal on its own territory
articles.body:
Kremlin spokesman says Lithuania would be ‘in the crosshairs of our nuclear weapons’ if it deploys a nuclear arsenal on its own territory
Kremlin Press Secretary Dmitry Peskov said Russia would aim its nuclear weapons at Lithuania if the country deploys nuclear arsenals on its own territory, speaking in an interview with the Russian state-controlled television channel Channel One.
“Obviously, these weapons will not be aimed westward: they will be aimed eastward, that is, at us,” Peskov was quoted as saying by the Russian news agency Interfax.
And if there is nuclear weaponry on that territory aimed at us, then that country’s territory will also be in the crosshairs of our nuclear weapons.
Peskov called that scenario “a very serious round of escalation and tension.”
Lithuanian authorities confirmed in June 2026 that they were negotiating the deployment of nuclear weapons on their territory. The British newspaper the Financial Times reported that the talks involve American bombers capable of carrying nuclear warheads. Lithuania’s current constitution bans deploying weapons of mass destruction or hosting foreign military bases in the country, and Lithuanian authorities said they are ready to begin discussing amendments to lift that ban.
Under a 1997 agreement between Russia and NATO, the North Atlantic Alliance pledged it has “no intention, no plan and no reason to deploy nuclear weapons on the territory of new members.”
After the full-scale war between Russia and Ukraine began, Moscow deployed tactical nuclear weapons in Belarus.

The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
