articles.title: GA-ASI’s Uncrewed Combat Aviation Portfolio Answers Call for High-End Warfare Capability
articles.body:
General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, Inc. (GA-ASI), the company that introduced the world to unmanned warfare, has systematically transformed its aircraft lineup to address the defining requirements of modern high-technology warfare: range, persistence, payload, survivability, and scale against advanced adversaries.
The portfolio now spans from the company’s enhanced MQ-9B SkyGuardian and SeaGuardian platforms capable of long-range maritime strike, to the expeditionary Mojave STOL, to the Air Force’s newly selected FQ-42A Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) — its first uncrewed fighter — and, most recently, to the Wildfire Massed Modular Aircraft (MMA), a theater-range platform engineered for affordable, attrition-tolerant combat mass.
According to GA-ASI President David Alexander, the United States has entered an era where winning demands large, capable Uncrewed Aircraft Systems (UAS) that can operate from friendly airspace into contested environments affordably, without risking aircrews.
“We’ve never been a company that rested on its laurels,” said Alexander. “The conversation around uncrewed systems has changed, and frankly, it should. The battlefield has evolved, threats have evolved, and so have we.
“We’re keeping ahead of the game, and, in the case of our FQ-42A and Wildfire aircraft, we’ve designed them from the start to overmatch threats today and into the future.”
Physics Demands Large Airframes
Losses in contested environments have prompted some observers to suggest moving away from large UAS platforms. Alexander sees those same operations as validation for continued investment in evolved large UAS.
“Yes, we’ve seen combat losses,” he said. “We’ve also heard Pentagon leaders call our Reaper the ‘MVP’ of the campaign. That tells you something important. When a system consistently delivers decisive effects, you modernize it and build on it. And I believe that’s where the Department of War is headed.”
Alexander emphasized that Reaper was purpose-built to provide persistent surveillance, long endurance, and precision strike. MQ-9A delivers these capabilities at scale and at a fraction of the cost of manned platforms that put pilots’ lives at risk, he added.
The proliferation of small drones — quadcopters, gliders, and short-range rockets — doesn’t change fundamental operational requirements, he said.
Despite the hype, smaller platforms “can’t change physics,” Alexander noted.
“Long-range, high-payload, high-endurance missions require large, hefty airframes with significant wingspan, fuel capacity, and payload volume,” he continued. “If we are serious about surveilling and targeting across wide ocean areas, tracking mobile missile units, and holding adversary assets at risk from standoff distances, large UAS modernized for contested environments are the decisive advantage.”
Wildfire: Delivering Attritable Mass at Theater Range
Wildfire represents GA-ASI’s answer to a critical requirement: affordable combat mass that can sustain losses while maintaining operational pressure across contested theaters.
This theater-range, high-production UAS is designed specifically for high-threat environments:
Combat payload and range: Wildfire can carry two Long Range Anti-Ship Missiles (LRASM) or four Joint Strike Missiles (JSM) for meaningful combat distances and has a ferry range that exceeds 8,000 nautical miles. This enables delivery of weapons, sensors, electronic warfare capabilities, or communications relay deep into contested battlespace.
Modular architecture: Open interfaces and modular payload hard points enable modularity to support rapid mission reconfiguration, allowing commanders to adapt as threats and priorities shift during operations.
Volume production: Leveraging more than 5 million square feet of manufacturing capacity and advanced production processes, Wildfire is engineered to be built and fielded in numbers sufficient to absorb attrition while maintaining persistent theater-wide pressure.
Combined with Gambit Series capabilities, Wildfire delivers what defense leaders call “attritable mass”— large numbers of capable systems whose loss does not constitute strategic setback because they are affordable, uncrewed, and replaceable.
Gambit Series: Autonomous Combat Jets for Peer Threats
The Gambit Series represents GA-ASI’s family of autonomous jets for high-end contested operations. Built around a common core comprising roughly 70 percent of key components, the platform’s modular architecture drives down costs while simplifying production, logistics, and sustainment.
Recently selected by the U.S. Air Force for its CCA program, the FQ-42A — designed to fly alongside fighters like the F-22 — is a variant of GA-ASI’s Gambit 2.
Across six missionized Gambit variants, the architecture supports:
- Long-endurance ISR in contested airspace
- Air-to-air combat
- Adversary training for advanced threat replication
- Stealth reconnaissance in denied areas
- Carrier-based naval operations
- Penetrating air-to-ground strike and suppression of enemy air defenses
All Gambit aircraft are designed for human-machine teaming with advanced fighters and other UAS, extending sensors, adding weapons capacity, and imposing complex targeting dilemmas on adversary defenses — precisely the type of effects envisioned in modern Air Force operational concepts.
Mojave STOL: Airpower, Hold the Tarmac
Built on GA-ASI’s other pioneering aircraft, Mojave STOL addresses a critical vulnerability in modern combat: dependence on large runways.
Short Takeoff and Landing (STOL) capability: Mojave STOL operates from austere, unprepared locations — open fields, dry riverbeds, even amphibious assault ship decks — generating uncrewed combat airpower from sites adversaries cannot easily target or predict.
Advanced sensor integration: Controllable via human-portable, laptop-based ground control systems, Mojave STOL carries cutting-edge radar, electro-optical/infrared, and signals intelligence payloads, providing a comprehensive operational picture for precise targeting and situational awareness to support dispersed forces.
In a combat environment where large runways are vulnerable to adversary strikes, Mojave STOL establishes airfields without airports. Its rugged construction enables persistent ISR and strike capability sourced from improvised mobile launch and recovery sites.
MQ-9B: Evolved Flagship Platform for Standoff Operations
MQ-9B SkyGuardian and SeaGuardian remain GA-ASI’s flagship multi-mission ISR platforms, now upgraded for long-range contested operations and integration into distributed kill chains.
Long-range weapons integration: New pylons with 30-inch lug spacing accommodate larger standoff munitions, including LRASM and JSM. Combined with MQ-9B’s advanced ISR suite, this transforms the aircraft into a long-range strike and maritime interdiction platform capable of engaging far outside adversary standoff ranges.
Resilient communications: Integration with proliferated Low Earth Orbit (pLEO) satellite constellations provides low-latency, high-bandwidth, jam-resistant connectivity. In combination with DoD-standard cybersecurity, MQ-9B maintains secure command-and-control and sensor links globally, even under electronic attack.
For Air Force and joint planners, MQ-9B has evolved beyond counterinsurgency roots into a standoff sensor-shooter that functions as a resilient node in distributed operations.
Urgency Driven by Evolving Threats
Alexander noted that changing battlefield conditions have continually driven the company to advance its technology and operational concepts.
“When you look at the threats we’re seeing in Ukraine and Iran, we already knew our aircraft would need to evolve, and we’ve been pushing ahead there for years now,” he said. “But it seems like every morning the news puts fresh urgency behind delivering that vital combat capability while finding ways to strip out some of what drives up costs.”
That urgency is backed by unmatched operational experience. To date, GA-ASI has accumulated nearly 10 million flight hours, the vast majority in combat operations.
Taken as a whole, Alexander said, the aircraft portfolio shows that GA-ASI is serious about retaining its position as the leading provider of UAS to the United States and its allies.
“We know, to our core, what it takes to deliver relevant systems,” he said. “We have the people, infrastructure, and capacity in place, today, to do it at scale.
“GA-ASI is ready to answer the call.”

articles.title: Yemen’s Houthis Capture Red Sea Port City, Threatening New Front in War
articles.body:
Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels have reportedly captured the strategic Perim Island that sits in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait as they aim to tighten their grip on the critical maritime chokepoint.
The Houthis took Perim on Friday, four Yemeni government sources told Reuters. The capture was also relayed to the Associated Press by a senior military official with Yemen’s internationally recognized government. The reports come a day after the Houthis captured Yemen’s port city of Mokha from Saudi-backed government forces.
Perim Island divides the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a vital trade route situated between Yemen and Djibouti and Eritrea in the Horn of Africa, that links Asia and Europe via the Red Sea and Suez Canal. Its capture would risk a grave escalation in the widening regional conflict. If the Houthis were to assume control of the Bab el-Mandeb, it could give Iran an advantage in its war with the U.S. The active hostilities between Washington and Tehran are largely focused on another critical trade route, the Strait of Hormuz.
In a statement shared Friday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea declared the “success” of a military operation launched on Sept. 3 that intended to expel "Saudi-backed forces" along the western coast of Yemen. He went on to assert that “maritime navigation is safe for all companies, with the exception of Saudi ships.” The statement made no mention of Perim Island.
The escalation comes after weeks of fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed government of Yemen, shattering a four-year informal cease-fire in the country's civil war.
Yemen’s government on Thursday reportedly launched airstrikes west of Taiz in response to the capture of Mokha and warned civilians to avoid roads between Taiz and Mokha. Houthi-owned Al-Masirah TV reported that Saudi-backed forces launched 40 airstrikes on the provinces of Taiz, Jawf, Hodeida, and Marib.
Observers and Yemeni residents fear the escalating fighting could renew an all-out civil war in Yemen.
“This renewed war should alarm us all,” Hans Grundberg, the U.N. special envoy for Yemen, said at an emergency meeting of the U.N. Security Council on Thursday. “It effectively marks the end of the relative calm that Yemen has experienced for over four years since the U.N.-brokered truce.”
Capturing the southwestern port and Perim—also known as Mayun—would significantly strengthen the Houthis’ ability to threaten shipping via the Bab el-Mandeb, a waterway through which 8.1 million oil barrels a day passed during the second quarter of 2026, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
The Houthis previously disrupted shipping in 2024, in response to Israel’s occupation and bombardment of Gaza, and made a global impact. The move prompted the U.S. and U.K. to carry out strikes against Houthi rebel targets.
The Bab el-Mandeb has become even more important since Iran militarized the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation for the U.S. and Israel’s Feb. 28 strikes.
Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer of defense studies at King’s College London, tells TIME that any Houthi takeover of these Red Sea areas would be “hugely significant" for the wider region.
In the 2024 disruption, the Houthis “were striking shipping from further inland, now they're controlling the coastline, very close to shipping, particularly Perim Island,” he says.
Perim offers a “vantage point from which the Houthis can operate with far less sophisticated technology, drones, and missiles in order to strike shipping,” Krieg says, adding that “they could even use small skiffs in a sort piracy fashion to harass shipping.”
How is Iran connected?
The Houthis reportedly received direct guidance and weapons from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Iran reportedly told the Houthis last week to escalate their attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Iran publicly maintains that the Houthis are “not a proxy.” The country’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement Friday that the conflict in Yemen must be resolved through dialogue instead of military action.
Iran’s First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref on Friday said that Tehran was “delighted by the victories of the heroic Yemeni nation” and put a call to unity “around the banner of Islam.”
Krieg explains how the Houthis may want to keep their targets solely on Saudi shipping in order to not draw out an international coordinated maritime response.
“They could widen the conflict to not just Saudi shipping, but any shipping going through the Bab el-Mandeb. But it would be an own-goal for the Houthis, because you're then giving the international community a mandate to basically support the Saudis,” he says.
Axios reported Friday that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had called Trump twice the previous day to request that he launch strikes against the Houthis—a request Trump is said to have declined.
"The United States is focused on protecting our core national security interests—such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea—while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges,” a senior Administration official told TIME when asked about the reports. “We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen Government regarding regional stability."
The Houthis’ advance comes as Tehran has sought new ways to counter Washington’s economic pressure campaign and military attacks. A stronger Houthi position along the Red Sea coast could further constrain global energy supplies, raise shipping and insurance costs, and push up oil prices. Even if the Houthis are acting in their own interest, Iran could gain significant leverage over Washington in conjunction with continued pressure on traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
The capture of Mokha came hours after President Donald Trump on Wednesday suggested that Iran’s government was prolonging the war in an attempt to affect Republican prospects in the U.S. midterm elections in November. He nevertheless insisted Iran is on the verge of collapse and that the war will end “immediately after” the vote.
The Houthis are “not necessarily doing the bidding of the Iranians; they're doing what is in their interests. Nobody really controls the Houthis,” says Krieg, but this escalation very well could benefit Tehran in negotiations.
“Ultimately this gives, even by extension or by proxy, the Iranians another part to play if they feel their terms are not being met, or if they feel that they need to dial up the pressure,” Krieg concludes.
More shipping disruptions
From Mokha, which lies around 80 km north of Bab el-Mandeb, and Perim Island, which sits directly in the waterway around 26 km from shore, the Houthis would have a stronger position to disrupt shipping, particularly targeting vessels travelling to and from Saudi Arabia, which is the world’s biggest crude exporter and a close U.S. ally.
Saudi Arabia has routed more oil to its Red Sea port of Yanbu after the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz. But the Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia on July 20 and began attacking Saudi shipping and energy infrastructure. Saudi crude exports have reportedly fallen to their lowest level in 13 years, with production dropping 23% from July to August. Overall vessel traffic through Bab el-Mandeb fell around 24% in the week following the July blockade.
The kingdom has responded with airstrikes in Yemen’s north and warned Iran to rein in the group. It has supplied its Yemeni allies with arms, intelligence, and logistical assistance.
Experts tell TIME that whilst the Houthis have shown their “intent and capability" to strike shipping, the tightening of their grip on the Bab el-Mandeb is sufficient to rattle energy markets and supply chains.
“This just adds another layer of uncertainty, very likely increasing the insurance payments, and that will increase shipping costs,” says Krieg, which would make it “very problematic for global energy trade.”
The advance could also force the U.S. to devote military resources towards protecting a second maritime chokepoint and assisting its ally, potentially complicating efforts to limit or swiftly end U.S. involvement in the Middle East.

articles.title: EU Approves €6.1 Billion Ukraine Defense Package, Unlocking PAC-3 Patriot Purchases
articles.body:
The European Commission approved a €6.1 billion ($7.1 billion) tranche of defense funding for Ukraine on Sept. 11, including exemptions allowing Kyiv to use the money to purchase US-made PAC-3 interceptor missiles for Patriot air defense systems.
The approval allows Ukraine to draw on the EU’s €90 billion ($104 billion) support loan to purchase PAC-3 interceptors, among the few weapons capable of intercepting Russian ballistic missiles.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The decision does not, however, mean the missiles will be delivered immediately. Ukraine faces a global shortage of Patriot interceptors as it prepares for another winter of Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure.
European Commissioner for Defense and Space Andrius Kubilius confirmed the decision at a press conference in Brussels on Friday, according to a Ukrinform report, the Commission had formally approved the package after EU member states backed the measures earlier this week.
“Today, the Commission officially approved €6.1 billion for Ukraine for air defense, drones and missiles from the Ukraine Support Loan,” Kubilius said.
The latest approval means the EU has now allocated all €28.3 billion ($32.9 billion) earmarked for Ukraine’s defense under the sprogram.So far, €8.4 billion ($9.7 billion) has been disbursed. Kubilius said another €4.7 billion ($5.5 billion) is currently being processed.
Fires, Explosions Reported Across Russia as Ukrainian Drones Target Refineries, Ozon Hubs
The €90 billion support loan, approved by EU countries in April, is intended to cover around two-thirds of Ukraine’s defense and budgetary needs in 2026 and 2027 and will be delivered in tranches.
PAC-3 missiles global shortage
This latest decision allows Ukraine to bypass some of the loan’s standard procurement requirements.
Under the rules, weapons purchased with the loan are generally required to come from the EU or Ukraine sources, with equipment containing more than 35% of components sourced from third countries requires explicit approval.
Kubilius said the Commission had granted five such exemptions: three for Ukrainian companies to source drone components from outside the bloc and two for US-made equipment, including PAC-3 interceptor missiles.
“Ukraine’s military edge depends on the rapid availability of critical products in the required quantities and within very short time frames,” Kubilius said.
The commissioner said speed is particularly important for air defense, given Ukraine’s immediate needs and the limited global supply of Patriot interceptors.
The European Commission estimates that Ukraine needs around 2,000 PAC-3 interceptors annually to defend against Russian ballistic missile attacks, while global production is only gradually increasing.
Kubilius said allies are exploring ways to provide Ukraine with missiles from existing stockpiles while waiting for new production.
One option under discussion is for EU member states that already have PAC-3 missiles to transfer them to Ukraine immediately and receive replacement missiles under agreements planned for 2027.
EU relaxes sourcing rules for Ukrainian drones
Three of the five exemptions approved by the Commission relate to Ukrainian drone manufacturers.
The Commission did not specify from which countries the components covered by the exemptions would be supplied. However, an earlier exemption approved in April allowed Ukraine to source drone components from China.
The remaining two exemptions cover US-made equipment, including PAC-3 missiles, with purchases potentially coordinated through NATO.
The decision comes as Ukraine and its allies seek to strengthen air defenses before winter, when Russia is expected to again target Ukraine’s energy infrastructure with large-scale missile and drone attacks.

articles.title: Money, not engineering, is what stands between Ukraine and Russia’s fastest drones, Zelenskyy says
articles.body:
Ukraine has not had enough of the right weapons to shoot down Russia's jet-powered drones, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said at a press conference with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in Calgary on 10 September. He put the remaining obstacles at time and money rather than engineering, and used the appearance to press partners for joint production. Russia attacks Ukrainian cities with drones every night, and the defense against the fastest of them is still being built.
"We did not have enough means"
Zelenskyy was answering a question about the Russian drone found at Leipzig airport in Germany and the drone that delayed his own flight out of Moldova.
"We have to be very frank: we did not have enough means to destroy all these fast drones," he said. "Yes, we are on the way, more than 60 companies are already working on this. Yes, we will get a result, but it takes time."
Three days earlier, he noted that only three to five of the firms show real results.
Germany blames Moscow for Leipzig drone attack, closes consulate and cultural center among sweeping diplomatic measures
The bottleneck is money
He then went past the engineering.The problem is not only technology, he said, but the funding to build thousands of interceptors every single day.
That arithmetic sends Ukraine abroad with its blueprints.
"That is why we talk about joint production, about production lines in one country or another," Zelenskyy said.
Russia now builds about 3,000 jet-powered drones a month, by Ukrainian military intelligence's count, and fired some 800 of them in four days at the end of August. They fly faster than propeller Shaheds and are harder to bring down, which has stretched air raid alerts nationwide. Ukraine's Air Force cannot yet rely on usual interceptor drones against them.
One drone, of the kind that turned up at Leipzig or crossed Moldova, is not a problem for Ukraine, Zelenskyy said. Thousands of fast drones a day are.
One Russian drone held up seven flights in Moldova, Zelenskyy’s trip to Norway for King Harald V’s funeral among them
What a night without enough interceptors looks like
The same night, Russia sent 161 long-range attack drones at Ukraine, decoys among them, along with a cruise missile.That is an ordinary night now, and its damage spreads thin across the map instead of landing in one place.
A Russian strike set a nine-story apartment block alight in Kyiv, burning the facade up to the fifth floor and a flat on the second. Firefighters carried seven people out and handed seven more to medics. Russian drones injured eight people in the capital overnight.
North of the city, Russia burned warehouses in the Bucha district, then struck the same site again while the crews were still dousing the flames.
In Dnipro, the drones kept coming back, more than ten times from the evening on, damaging a plant and a row of garages and injuring seven people.
Farther out, Russia injured a mother and her son in Zaporizhzhia and damaged a plant in Zhytomyr Oblast, and the waves ran west far enough that NATO jets went up over Romania.

articles.title: World leaders in India for BRICS summit overshadowed by Iran war
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
World leaders in India for BRICS summit overshadowed by Iran war
Leaders of China, Iran, Russia, and more are gathering in India on Friday for talks ahead of an 11-member BRICS summit dominated by conflict and economic challenges,
The US-Israeli war on Iran and Russia's invasion of Ukraine, as well as global trade turbulence and oil are expected on the agenda at the two-day annual summit that opens on Saturday, when Chinese President Xi Jinping is set to arrive.
It will be Xi's first visit to India since 2019, and marks the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the rival neighbours, six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Himalayan border.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming again recently, with flights, visas and high-level contacts gradually being restored.
However, deep mistrust remains, with their contested frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.
"One should engage in debate and friendship only with the virtuous, and nothing whatsoever with the unvirtuous," Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi wrote Friday, in a message in Sanskrit to welcome arriving leaders on social media.
Modi is due to hold talks later on Friday with Putin, who last visited India in December 2025. Moscow is one of New Delhi's most important strategic partners.
India has navigated the energy crisis sparked by the Iran war in part by turning to Russia, its most controversial fuel supplier in recent years.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is also expected on Friday, and is due to hold talks with Modi.
'Fault line'
Posters of a beaming Modi line streets across New Delhi to welcome the leaders, with heavy deployments of security forces across the capital and widespread traffic restrictions.
BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.
It has since expanded and now includes Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates—three countries with sharply differing positions on the war launched by the United States and Israel in February.
"The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the BRICS summit," said Harsh V. Pant of India's Observer Research Foundation.
"What was seen until last year as an achievement—the expansion of BRICS—today looks like a big constraint on BRICS," Pant said.
It will be Pezeshkian's first visit to India as Iranian president, and will put the US-Israeli war firmly on the agenda.
"The war in Iran will provide a stern test of the (expanded) group's cohesion," said Shilan Shah of Capital Economics, noting the failure of the BRICS foreign ministers to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May.
United Arab Emirates President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is also expected, as is Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan, and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi.
India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.
New Delhi has navigated the energy crisis caused by the Iran war in part by turning to Russia, one of its most important strategic partners and its most controversial fuel supplier in recent years as the war against Ukraine drags on.
Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar visited Kyiv this month, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he was "grateful to India for its commitment to ending this unjust war".

articles.title: Iranian strikes force UAE to dismantle plans for its AI mega-campus
articles.body:
Iranian strikes force UAE to dismantle plans for its AI mega-campus
TEHRAN — The United Arab Emirates is quietly dismantling its blueprint for a 5-gigawatt artificial intelligence project, abandoning plans for a centralized campus in Abu Dhabi in favor of a dispersed network of hardened facilities.
Iranian missile and drone operations have permanently altered the security calculus for regional autocracies hosting American forces.
Originally envisioned as a 10-square-mile computing hub built in partnership with U.S. tech firms, the project is undergoing a total strategic redesign.
According to a Reuters report on September 11, 2026, Emirati officials are now calculating the financial burden of moving sensitive infrastructure underground into the rugged mountain ranges of Ras Al Khaimah and Fujairah, equipping dispersed sites with blast-resistant concrete and electronic jamming apparatus.
Retaliation shatters the safe haven myth
The sudden overhaul follows retaliatory strikes by Iranian forces targeting infrastructure linked to foreign military presence across the region.
In March, drone strikes damaged two Amazon Web Services data centers in the UAE alongside a major facility in Bahrain, triggering prolonged disruptions across regional cloud networks and banking systems.
The impact demonstrated how quickly commercial digital infrastructure collapses when tied to Western military footprint.
Pressure intensified in April when Iran’s armed forces released targeting footage explicitly identifying Stargate UAE, the project’s $30 billion first phase.
The video confirmed the exact coordinates of the site adjacent to Al Dhafra Air Base, an enclave housing U.S. troops that has been targeted repeatedly since the wider war began in February.
The cost of subservience
The flagship project was built on a geopolitical bargain. Spearheaded by G42, an entity controlled by Emirati national security adviser Tahnoun bin Zayed, Abu Dhabi agreed to sever technological ties with China in exchange for advanced Nvidia microprocessors and infrastructure deals with American corporations such as OpenAI, Oracle, and Cisco.
By embedding critical digital infrastructure next to active launchpads for U.S. military operations, Abu Dhabi tied its economic future directly to Washington’s regional warfare.
When the U.S. and Israel launched their campaign of aggression against Iran, the UAE’s decision to host and abet hostile forces, provide basing and logistics for operations against Iran, and make itself complicit in Washington’s anti-Iran bloc transformed its high-tech megaprojects into vulnerable targets.
Scattered infrastructure and mounting financial costs
Emirati planners are now scrambling to break the 5-gigawatt masterplan into fragmented sites across multiple emirates.
Workloads handling military and government data will be buried inside disused mines and subterranean mountain vaults.
Planners are also integrating localized missile interceptors, blast walls, and redundant power networks to survive potential strikes.
These physical modifications carry immense financial and logistical burdens. Splitting a unified mega-campus into isolated, blast-proof facilities multiplies energy consumption, physical security perimeters, and specialized cooling requirements at every single site.
While G42 and its Western partners claim the build proceeds as planned, the physical reality tells a different story.
Abu Dhabi traded its national sovereignty for American hardware and military promises, only to discover that no Western air defense shield can protect infrastructure erected in the shadow of U.S. military bases.

articles.title: Turkish combat drone gets a longer-range strike weapon
articles.body:
- Baykar has integrated Roketsan's new 300-ER air-launched ballistic missile onto its Akıncı combat drone, with a test launch expected soon.
- The missile can strike targets more than 500 km away and extends a family of shorter-range weapons already fired from the Akıncı.
Turkish drone maker Baykar has fitted its Akıncı unmanned combat aircraft with Roketsan’s new 300-ER air-launched ballistic missile, with a first launch from the drone expected soon, according to Ulusavunma.
Roketsan first showed the 300-ER publicly at the IDEF defense show in Istanbul in July 2025, presenting it as the longest-range weapon yet in a family of air-launched missiles that began with the shorter İHA-122 and İHA-230. The missile can hit targets more than 500 km (310 miles) away, depending on the altitude it is launched from.
The 300-ER measures about 5 meters (16 feet) long, weighs 900 kg (1,980 lb) and carries a warhead of more than 150 kg (330 lb) inside a 370 mm-diameter body. It navigates using GNSS and inertial guidance and switches to a TV camera seeker for the final approach to the target, a setup Roketsan says is built for precision strikes on radars, armored vehicles, air defense systems and command centers.
The missile extends a lineage Roketsan built from its ground-launched artillery rockets. The company adapted its 122 mm and 230 mm-class rockets into the air-launched İHA-122 and İHA-230, both of which Baykar has already test-fired from the Akıncı, hitting targets roughly 55 km and 100 km away in past trials. The 300-ER carries that same approach out to a much longer range, inside a larger airframe.
That range matters because it lets a large drone like the Akıncı release a weapon and turn away before coming within reach of many surface-to-air missile systems built to intercept aircraft rather than incoming ballistic threats. Roketsan has said the missile is also intended for use on fighter jets and on Baykar’s jet-powered Kızılelma combat drone.
Roketsan told Turkish media in April 2026 that it expected to complete initial test firings of the 300-ER and deliver the missile to the Turkish Armed Forces within the year. Baykar’s September 10 statement does not say whether that test launch has already taken place or specify a date for it, and neither company has disclosed when the missile might enter regular service.

articles.title: Why Yemen government forces collapsed ahead of Houthi offensive
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Why Yemen government forces collapsed ahead of Houthi offensive
Yemen's Houthi movement has taken control of the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait after seizing Mayyun Island and government forces withdrew from Perim Island, following a rapid collapse of positions held by forces aligned with the internationally recognised government.
The developments came a day after the Houthis took control of the Red Sea city of Mokha, following about a week of heavy fighting.
The speed of the reversal has raised questions over the state of government forces on Yemen's western coast. Until shortly before the withdrawals, reports from the area had pointed to government advances. Their lines then collapsed within hours.
A Houthi official told The New Arab on Friday that the group had taken control of Mayyun Island and completed its control of Bab al-Mandab.
Reuters, citing two government sources, reported that Yemeni government forces had withdrawn from Perim Island.
The strait is one of the world's most important maritime chokepoints, connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean.
The latest reversal followed a series of withdrawals by government forces along Yemen's western coast.
On Thursday, forces loyal to the internationally recognised government withdrew from Mokha, near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, after earlier withdrawals from the districts of Hays and al-Wazi'iyah.
Government sources told The New Arab that orders had been issued on Wednesday evening for troops to leave Mokha, without an explanation being given for the immediate reason.
The withdrawal was described to the troops as part of a "redeployment".
Government forces then began leaving the headquarters of the Joint Forces formations in the city.
On Thursday morning, Presidential Leadership Council member Lieutenant General Tareq Saleh said forces on the western coast had been ordered to "reorganise their ranks".
He said the Joint Forces had established a command centre south of Mokha after what he described as "Houthi forces breaking through the various fighting fronts under intense fire pressure in which the Houthis used various types of weapons".
Saleh added that "the armed forces on the western coast, the National Resistance, Giants and Nation's Shield forces, in addition to units of the Taiz axis west of the governorate, have paid a heavy price, in martyrs and wounded, throughout the past days as they confronted the Houthi attack".
"We directed the formation of an alternative command centre in a safe location that would regroup the forces in consultation with the leadership of the Arab coalition and the Leadership Council," he said.
No official clarification followed about Saleh's location, the status of the forces under his command or the site of the command centre he said had been established south of Mokha.
Unconfirmed reports suggested it could be in the Dhubab area.
The Presidential Leadership Council, Joint Forces command and defence ministry also issued no further statements explaining the fate of the forces after the announcement that they were reorganising.
The lack of clarity has prompted widespread questions in Yemen about what happened, particularly after the government forces had announced advances before the balance on the ground changed rapidly.
Why Mokha matters
Mokha had been under heavy pressure in the days before the withdrawal.
The city was struck by dozens of missiles and explosive drones, while the Houthi advance accelerated after the movement deployed thousands of fighters to fronts west of Taiz.
Mokha lies in the far south-west of Taiz governorate, about 90km from the provincial capital and roughly 60 to 70km south of the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Its proximity to one of the world's main maritime routes for energy trade and oil tankers gives it major strategic importance and links its security directly to shipping through the Red Sea.
The city had also housed the headquarters of the Joint Forces, one of the most important military groupings aligned with Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council.
The formations include the National Resistance led by Tareq Saleh, the Southern Giants Brigades led by Presidential Leadership Council member Abu Zara'a al-Muharrami, and the Tihama Resistance Brigades.
The Joint Forces comprise about 30 military brigades.
They were reorganised and restructured at the beginning of 2026 into five main divisions and forces under direct Saudi supervision. These include the Guardians of the Republic, Tihama Brigades, Zaraniq Brigades and Giants Brigades, as well as a naval formation and specialised security forces.
Observers had regarded the formations as a major strike force and an integrated military institution protecting the southern gateway to the Red Sea.
Houthis say navigation remains safe
Hizam al-Assad, a member of the Houthi political bureau, told The New Arab that "what our Yemeni armed forces have carried out in some coastal areas is an internal national operation within the framework of imposing Yemeni sovereignty and dealing with the challenges and ambitions that threaten civil peace".
He added that "freedom of navigation and the movement of international trade in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab are safe and regular, and there is no need for any international concern about them, as there is no danger to them from the Yemeni side".
"The operations currently taking place have specific objectives in accordance with what was previously announced and come within the defensive framework," Assad said.
Asked whether the movement intended to impose fees at Bab al-Mandab after taking control of it, he said: "We have no such intention."
Yasmine al-Eryani, executive director for knowledge production at the Sana'a Center for Strategic Studies, said government forces had remained largely defensive in the previous period, with the exception of counter-operations in al-Jawf intended to disperse Houthi forces and ease pressure on Mokha.
She said the Houthis' determination to advance towards the city and their willingness to sustain heavy losses suggested they were seeking a rapid operation rather than a prolonged battle.
Eryani said the timing of the attack was significant in the context of regional escalation, arguing that Houthi moves appeared to coincide with "Iran's escalation ladder".
She warned that any attempt to impose fees or service arrangements at Bab al-Mandab could set a dangerous precedent and reshape the rules governing global maritime navigation.
Saudi calculations remain unclear
On the performance of government forces, Eryani said that despite some relative improvement in their capabilities and cohesion, the battle had tested whether the government had succeeded in unifying its military command.
"And it is clear that it has not done so yet," she said.
She said confronting an experienced fighting force such as the Houthis required a flexible military strategy, unified command and a disciplined defensive doctrine.
The growing use of drones and air power had altered the nature of the confrontation, she said, but was not sufficient on its own to determine the outcome.
Eryani also pointed to fragile military morale during the fighting.
She said the Houthis had invested in an information campaign that deepened doubts over whether reinforcements would arrive from other units.
Any military advance against the Houthis required simultaneous and coordinated mobilisation across multiple fronts, she said, something that did not happen during this confrontation.
Despite the setback, Eryani said the fighting reflected expectations among broad sections of Yemenis that advancing towards Sanaa and restoring state institutions could once again be possible, at least at a psychological level.
She cautioned, however, that it was too early to draw final conclusions from a battle taking place in a highly volatile environment where all scenarios remained open.
Eryani said Saudi Arabia's calculations remained unclear.
Riyadh had not indicated full support for a broad military operation and continued to stress that diplomatic channels remained open, despite what she described as Houthi provocations.
At the same time, Saudi Arabia had continued to provide the Yemeni government with relatively high levels of support and was likely to have been part of the calculations preceding the decision to respond militarily.
Eryani said no outside state could ultimately decide the conflict on behalf of the Yemeni side.
Regional and international interests in maritime security and deterring cross-border attacks could provide the government with allies, she said, but could not substitute for unified Yemeni political will to build a stable state.
"No one will put their full weight behind a weak link," she added.
This article is an edited translation from our Arabic edition

articles.title: Ukraine and Canada Sign 100-Year Partnership and Drone Deal
articles.body:
Ukraine and Canada signed a Declaration on 100-Year Partnership, which provides for expanding cooperation to the level of a comprehensive strategic partnership.
This became known following the meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in Calgary, the Office of the latter reported.
As part of the agreements, the states are launching their first deal on unmanned systems (Drone Deal) with a country in the Americas.
In Alberta, the leaders inspected drone models that will be the first to be deployed as part of this defense initiative.
The agreement provides for Canada to order large quantities of drones, with 30% of the manufactured equipment to be supplied to Ukraine.
The parties expressed their intention to establish a long-term defense-industrial partnership for the joint production of unmanned systems, counter-drone systems, and electronic warfare systems.
In addition, the Canadian side confirmed a new military aid package aimed at strengthening Ukraine’s air defense.
Canada will focus on supplying the necessary air defense systems and interceptor missiles, while continuing to provide ammunition and military equipment.
The partners extended the Operation UNIFIER training mission to prepare Ukrainian service members through 2029.
Both countries will deepen cooperation in intelligence, cyber defense, countering hybrid threats and foreign information manipulation.
It is worth recalling that on January 16, Volodymyr Zelensky and former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer signed an agreement on a century-long partnership between the two countries.
During a joint press conference, the President of Ukraine announced an agreement on continued annual military assistance and an expansion of the training program for Ukrainian troops.

articles.body:
Putin arrives in India for BRICS summit set to be dominated by Middle East, Ukraine wars
Russian President Vladimir Putin arrived in New Delhi on Friday for a two-day BRICS summit expected to focus on wars in Ukraine and the Middle East and economic challenges. Putin and Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian are due to meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi, while China’s Xi Jinping is also expected to hold talks.
Russian President Vladimir Putin arrived in the Indian capital on Friday ahead of an 11-member BRICS summit set to be dominated by wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, as well as economic challenges.
Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian were due to hold talks with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, while Chinese President Xi Jinping was also expected to meet him on the sidelines of the two-day meeting, according to Indian diplomatic sources.
Putin arrived at Palam Air Force Station in New Delhi, where he was greeted by India's Minister of State for External Affairs Kirti Vardhan Singh, according to footage broadcast by Russia's Ria Novosti news agency.
For China's Xi, it will be his first visit to India since 2019 and marks the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the rival neighbours, six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Himalayan border.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming again recently, with flights, visas and high-level contacts gradually being restored.
However, deep mistrust remains, with their contested frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.
Read moreChina, Russia conclude BRICS+ naval drills in South Africa amid controversy
'Fault line'
Posters of a beaming Modi line streets across New Delhi to welcome leaders, with heavy deployments of security forces across the capital and widespread traffic restrictions in central districts. Delhi police have urged people to be patient and cooperative.
BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.
It has since expanded and now includes Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates – three countries with sharply differing positions on the war launched by the United States and Israel in February.
"The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the BRICS summit," said Harsh V. Pant of India's Observer Research Foundation.
"What was seen until last year as an achievement – the expansion of BRICS – today looks like a big constraint on BRICS," Pant said.
Read moreXi calls on Mideast nations to be ‘masters of their own affairs’ in rare Egypt visit
It will be Pezeshkian's first visit to India as Iranian president, and will put the Middle East conflict firmly on the agenda.
"The war in Iran will provide a stern test of the (expanded) group's cohesion," said Shilan Shah of Capital Economics, noting the failure of the BRICS foreign ministers to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May.
India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the Iran war in part by turning to Russia, one of its most important strategic partners and its most controversial fuel supplier in recent years as the war against Ukraine drags on.
Putin last visited India in December 2025, but he also met Modi in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, this month.
Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar visited Kyiv this month, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he was "grateful to India for its commitment to ending this unjust war".

articles.title: ‘Go home, man. You’re embarrassing.’ U.S. officials are reportedly eager for the CIA director to take over Russia–Ukraine talks from Witkoff.
articles.body:
‘Go home, man. You’re embarrassing.’ U.S. officials are reportedly eager for the CIA director to take over Russia–Ukraine talks from Witkoff.
CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s potential emergence as Washington’s chief negotiator on the Russia–Ukraine war has energized many U.S. officials, even though the White House has officially denied any such plan, Politico reported.
The Financial Times wrote on September 9 that Ratcliffe would take on a “larger role” representing the United States in the negotiations. American officials had shared that information with their European counterparts, according to the paper.
Steve Witkoff would continue participating in the negotiations alongside Ratcliffe, the FT wrote, while Jared Kushner could shift his focus to settling the war in Gaza and the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran. The White House press office called the Financial Times report “totally fake news.”
Politico’s sources describe Ratcliffe as a stronger negotiator than Witkoff. But one of them stressed that simply replacing the special envoy won’t be enough to change the situation: nothing will shift until the United States starts putting real pressure on Russia through tougher sanctions and increased military aid to Ukraine.
“If Ratcliffe gets involved, he knows Russian issues very well,” Matthew Boyse, who worked on Eurasian affairs at the State Department during the first Trump administration, told the outlet. He also cautioned against expecting quick success in negotiations under Ratcliffe, since Vladimir Putin believes time is on his side and therefore “is showing no interest in moving off fixed maximalist positions.”
Many in Washington also welcome Ratcliffe’s potential appointment, viewing Witkoff’s approach as amateurish. After a recent meeting with Putin, for instance, Witkoff said: “When we retire, we’ll have all these incredible stories and incredible memories, and yours will be right at the top of it all.” An unnamed Washington official responded: “Who talks about retirement in literally one of the most critical meetings, ever? Go home man, you’re embarrassing.”
A Politico source in Ukraine said they had no information yet indicating Ratcliffe would take charge of the Russia–Ukraine issue but stressed that Kyiv has been “working with the U.S. at every level, including the CIA.”
Ratcliffe flew to Moscow in late August, though the purpose of the trip remains unclear. Officials in both the United States and Russia downplayed its significance, describing it as a routine visit within the framework of intelligence agency contacts. Western media outlets have offered widely differing accounts of the trip’s real purpose, ranging from a call to scale back cooperation with Iran to a warning against attacking NATO countries.

articles.body:
Necva Taştan Sevinç
11 September 2026•Update: 11 September 2026
The European Commission on Friday approved an additional €6.1 billion ($7.1 billion) for Ukraine to procure defense products, including air and missile defense systems, ammunition, drones and electronic warfare equipment.
The funding is aimed at strengthening Ukraine's ability to counter intensified Russian ballistic missile and drone attacks.
“Today, we have approved €6.1 billion to help Ukraine procure different defence products in the field of air and missile defence, ammunition, drones and electronic warfare,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on US social media company X.
“With this approval, Ukraine can now also purchase the Patriot equipment it needs to better protect its skies from Russia’s indiscriminate attacks,” she added.
The package will finance purchases from both EU and Ukrainian defense companies and allow Kyiv to procure PAC-3 missiles for Patriot air defense systems.
The funding comes under the EU's €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan for 2026-2027, of which €60 billion is earmarked for defense and €30 billion for budgetary assistance.
With Friday's decision, the €28.3 billion allocated for Ukraine's defense support in 2026 has been fully assigned, covering specific equipment, suppliers, quantities and implementation timelines.
The bloc has already disbursed €8.35 billion in defense funding for Ukraine this year.
The announcement came as the EU and Ukraine also held the first board meeting of a new defense industry initiative aimed at jointly developing drone and counter-drone technologies.
EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said the initiative seeks to strengthen Europe's drone capabilities by drawing on Ukraine's battlefield experience.
Kubilius said Europe must learn from Ukraine not only about drone technology and production but also about accelerating manufacturing processes and rapidly scaling up production capacity.
The EU currently produces around 1.5 million drones annually, compared with roughly 10 million each in Ukraine and Russia, he said.
Europe should be prepared to increase its production to 10 million drones or more annually in the event of a crisis or war, Kubilius added.
The initiative's board includes representatives from nine EU member states and nine Ukrainian companies, selected from around 400 applications.
Its priorities include accelerating joint ventures between EU and Ukrainian companies, securing supply chains, expanding testing capabilities and speeding up research, development and procurement.
Kubilius said the initiative should go beyond being a consultation platform, with the first concrete results expected by the end of the year.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Russian Aircraft Engine Plant, Pantsir Air Defenses – General Staff
articles.body:
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian defense-industry plant producing components for military aircraft engines, along with air defense systems, a radar station and drone facilities, the AFU General Staff said on Friday, Sept. 11.
The strikes hit Russian military targets in several regions and occupied Ukrainian territories, according to Ukraine’s military.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The most significant target was the Snizhne Machine-Building Plant in the occupied Donetsk region. The facility produces components for gas-turbine engines, including compressor and turbine blades, and supplies parts used in Russian military aviation.
Ukrainian forces also targeted two Pantsir-S1 air defense systems in Taganrog, Rostov Oblast, a Russian radar station in Berezki, Bryansk Oblast, and a facility in Donetsk used to store, prepare and launch attack drones.
In the occupied Luhansk region, Ukrainian forces struck an FPV drone operator training center and a unit of the Chechen Akhmat forces in Petropavlivka.
The General Staff did not provide details on the extent of damage at the targeted sites, saying the results were still being assessed.
The strikes are part of Ukraine’s ongoing campaign against Russian military infrastructure and the defense-industrial network supporting Moscow’s war against Ukraine.
Part of wider Ukrainian drone campaign
The reported attack came amid a broader wave of overnight Ukrainian drone strikes against Russian industrial infrastructure.
‘Weeks, Not Months’: Ukraine’s FP-7 Ballistic Missile Could Soon Strike Russia
In Perm, a major chemical plant was reportedly targeted by Ukrainian drones early Friday, Sept. 11, with footage appearing to show a drone diving toward the facility.
In Saratov, a fire was reported at the Rosneft-owned Saratov Oil Refinery, while an Ozon logistics center also reportedly caught fire.
In Volgograd, regional authorities reported damage to an industrial facility and an apartment building, with two people hospitalized.
Ozon logistics hubs have increasingly been targeted since late August. Seven warehouses have reportedly been hit across Samara, Rostov, and Belgorod oblasts, Krasnodar Krai, Bashkortostan, and Dagestan.
The attacks also come as Ukraine continues to target Russia’s oil-refining sector. Ukrainian drones have struck Russian refineries at least 70 times since the beginning of 2026, according to Bloomberg, contributing to a sharp decline in refining output and growing gasoline shortages.
At least 17 Russian regions have introduced restrictions on fuel sales, while Russia has increasingly turned to imports from India, Morocco, Turkey, and Belarus to cover the shortfall.
The Russian defense ministry had not released a tally of intercepted drones from the latest wave, while Ukraine had not officially claimed responsibility for the reported attacks.

articles.title: GUR: Around 25,000 DPRK troops already rotate through Russian army ranks
articles.body:
Approximately 25,000 North Korean troops have already rotated through the Russian armed forces, Lieutenant General Oleh Ivaschenko, Chief of the Main Intelligence Agency (GUR) of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, said in an interview with The Times.
Currently, according to Ivaschenko, about 8,000 DPRK troops are present in Russia's Kursk region.
"Today, there are approximately 8,000 DPRK troops in Russia's Kursk region. Our intelligence indicates that their numbers could rise to around 50,000," he said.
Overall, the GUR estimates that Russia has already recruited more than 28,000 foreign fighters—including individuals from African nations drawn by promises of high pay. However, the GUR believes the number of North Korean troops within Russian forces could increase sharply.
North Korea is also supplying ballistic missiles to Russia.
As of August last year, the GUR estimated that Pyongyang had supplied at least 150 KN-23 or KN-24 missiles, with another 120 promised.
As previously reported, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy noted that Russia plans to deploy between 30,000 and 50,000 troops from the DPRK on its territory.

articles.title: Air defenses down 777 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 11. /TASS/. Air defenses downed 777 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions, the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea last night, the Defense Ministry said in a statement.
"On-duty air defenses intercepted and destroyed 777 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles between 8:00 p.m. Moscow time on September 10 and 8:00 a.m. Moscow time on September 11 (5:00 p.m. - 5:00 a.m. GMT). The drones were shot down over the Bryansk, Kursk, Belgorod, Oryol, Kaluga, Voronezh, Tula, Ryazan, Lipetsk, Nizhny Novgorod, Saratov, Rostov, Samara, Perm, Mari El and Udmurt regions, as well as Crimea, the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea," the statement reads.
Russian forces strike Ukrainian data centers, port infrastructure, logistics hubs
Russian forces struck Ukrainian defense industry sites, logistics hubs and data centers overnight, as well as port infrastructure and vessels carrying military cargo, the Defense Ministry said in a statement.
"Last night, the Russian Armed Forces carried out group strikes involving high-precision air-launched weapons and attack unmanned vehicles, striking Ukrainian defense industry sites and logistics hubs involved in the production and storage of drones, as well as data centers in the city of Kiev, the Kiev, Khmelnitsky and Dnepropetrovsk regions, and port infrastructure facilities for unloading and storing cargo intended for the Ukrainian army, and seagoing vessels carrying military cargo and fuel for the Ukrainian military," the statement reads.
Russian forces strike logistics hub in Dnepropetrovsk Region storing fixed-wing drones
Russian forces have struck a logistic hub in Ukraine's Dnepropetrovsk Region storing fixed-wing drones and their components, the Defense Ministry said in a statement.
"Strikes involving high-precision air-launched weapons and attack unmanned aerial vehicles hit the Dnepr logistics hub in the Dnepropetvosk Region used to store fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles and their components," the statement reads.
Russian forces strike cargo ship carrying military supplies to Odessa
Russian forces struck a dry cargo ship carrying military supplies for the Ukrainian army to the port of Odessa, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"In addition, a dry cargo vessel delivering supplies for the Ukrainian armed forces was hit while at sea en route to the port of Odessa," the ministry said.
Russian forces strike data center storing intelligence intended for Ukraine army
Russian forces have struck the Bi Mobile data center that stored and transferred data, including intelligence, and ensured the operation of the Ukrainian army’s network equipment, the Defense Ministry said.
According to the ministry, the Russian Armed Forces continued to carry out group strikes on Ukraine’s defense industry sites, logistics hubs, data centers and seaports overnight.
"Strikes involving high-precision air-launched weapons and attack unmanned aerial vehicles hit the following targets in Kiev and the surrounding region: the Bi Mobile data center, which ensured the storage and transfer of data, including intelligence, and the operation of network equipment used by the Ukrainian army," the ministry specified.
Russian forces strike Nova Poshta terminal storing UAVs in Khmelnitsky
Russian forces struck an innovative terminal at the Nova Poshta logistics center in Khmelnitsky, which was being used to store unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"As a result of strikes using precision air-launched weapons and attack drones, the following targets in the Khmelnitsky region were hit: an innovative terminal of the Nova Poshta logistics center in the city of Khmelnitsky, used for the storage and distribution of fixed-wing UAVs and their components," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian forces strike foreign drone parts warehouse in Odessa Region
Russian forces struck a warehouse storing components for foreign-made drones near Vizirka in the Odessa Region, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"Strikes with precision-guided air-launched weapons and attack drones hit targets in Odessa and the Odessa Region, including a warehouse in Vizirka storing components for foreign-made unmanned aerial vehicles intended for the Ukrainian armed forces," the ministry said.
Russian forces strike Gostomel logistics hub storing drone components
Russia forces have struck the Gostomel logistics hubs in the Kiev Region storing components for drone production, the Defense Ministry said in a statement.
"Strikes involving high-precision air-launched weapons and attack unmanned aerial vehicles hit the Gostomel logistics hub used to store and distribute components for the production of long-and medium-range drones," the statement reads.
Russian forces strike two dry cargo ships, motor boat at Chernomorsk port
Russian forces have struck two dry cargo ships carrying supplies for the Ukrainian army and a motorboat at the port of Chernomorsk, the Defense Ministry said in a statement.
"Strikes involving high-precision air-launched weapons and attack unmanned aerial vehicles hit two dry cargo ships carrying military cargo for the Ukrainian army and a motorboat at the port of Chernomorsk, as well as fuel tanks and a storage facility for supplies intended for the Ukrainian armed forces," the statement reads.
Russia hits automotive parts plant in Odessa repairing equipment for Ukrainian military
The Russian Armed Forces struck an automotive parts plant in Odessa where equipment for the Ukrainian military was being repaired, the Defense Ministry reported.
"As a result of strikes with high-precision air-launched weapons and strike drones, the following targets were hit: an automotive components plant in the city of Odessa and the Odessa region that repairs and maintains military equipment for the Ukrainian military," the statement said.
Russia strikes territorial defense brigade’s deployment point in Sumy Region
Russian forces used a Kh-39 light multipurpose guided missile to strike a temporary deployment point of the 119th Separate Territorial Defense Brigade near Lesnoye in the Sumy Region, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"A temporary deployment point of the 119th Separate Territorial Defense Brigade in Lesnoye in the Sumy Region was also hit with a Kh-39 light multipurpose guided missile," the ministry said.
Russian forces strike Ukrainian drone control points in Sumy Region with aerial bombs
Russian forces have struck Ukrainian drone control points in the Sumy Region using FAB-500 high-explosive aerial bombs, the Defense Ministry said in a statement.
"The Russian Defense Ministry has released footage showing five FAB-500 high-explosive aerial bombs equipped with the unified glide/adjustment module hit the drone control points of the Ukrainian National Guard’s Fourth Separate Rapid Response Brigade near the settlement of Lesnoye in the Sumy Region," the statement reads.

articles.title: Russia has fired its Oreshnik with six warheads at Ukraine three times. State Duma defense committee member says “hour is not far” before fourth one
articles.body:
A member of Russia's parliament has threatened a fresh strike on Ukraine with the Oreshnik, Russia's intermediate-range ballistic missile. Andrei Kolesnik, of the State Duma's defense committee, says the "hour is not far" when Ukraine will "feel what Oreshnik is," casting the strike as revenge for a Ukrainian attack on the Russian city of Sochi, Russian state media reported, according to UNIAN.
Russia has already fired the Oreshnik at Ukraine three times, starting with Dnipro in November 2024, then the Lviv Oblast in January, a strike that landed roughly 70 kilometers from the Polish border and NATO's edge, and again near Bila Tserkva in Kyiv Oblast in May.
Kolesnik frames a strike as revenge
Kolesnik cast the coming strike as an answer to what he called Ukrainian terrorism against civilians. He pointed to a recent Ukrainian attack on Sochi, noting that Ukraine's forces used unmanned naval boats rather than drones.
"This is a terrorist attack in its purest form," he said, adding, "I think the hour is not far when the Ukrainian side will feel what Oreshnik is."
But what Kolesnik did not mention in his threats is that Russia hits Ukraine daily. Kyiv has been under a constant attack by jet-powered drones that trigger an air alert almost hourly since 27 August. Russia also fires presumably two ballistic missile attacks on the Ukrainian capital two times a week, inflicting $12 million in damages per strike and killing civilians. Meanwhile, other regions come under Russian attacks with the same intensity and suffer from Russian advances in the east and south of Ukraine.
The missile is a message more than a weapon
The Oreshnik carries six warheads and flies at around Mach 11. All three strikes were launched from the Kapustin Yar range in southern Russia, according to Ukraine's air force.
Russia has kept up that pressure by deploying a missile brigade to Belarus, positioning that would put more of Europe within the missile's reach.

articles.title: Russia offers war-tested drones and missiles for export – expert
articles.body:
Russia offers war-tested drones and missiles for export – expert
Can Kasapoglu, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, said this in an analytical review on the situation in the Russian-Ukrainian war.
"Russia is converting its industrial and operational experience gained in Ukraine – including mass-produced affordable munitions, cruise-missile-drone hybrids, and saturation attacks using mixed strike packages – into an increasingly competitive defense-export portfolio," the expert said.
Russia presented some of its export products at the El Alamein International Airshow 2026, held in Egypt on September 8-10.
"Russia dispatched its combat-tested drones and missiles to Egypt to promote them for export," Kasapoglu said.
One example is the export version of the Banderol cruise-missile-drone hybrid. Russia displayed the Dan-T loitering munition. A derivative of the Banderol missile, the turbojet-powered Dan-T weighs up to 272 kg, has a range of approximately 450 km, and can be launched from fixed-wing drones or rotary-wing manned aircraft – primarily Mi-28 variants. Kronstadt JSC, the manufacturer of the Orion reconnaissance-strike drone, produces Banderol.
Russia began testing the system in secret in 2024. Its first documented use against Ukraine came in spring 2025, when Ukrainian intelligence reconstructed the hybrid from debris.
According to the expert, Banderol resembles a scaled-down Kh-101, with deployable wings and radar-signature-reducing shaping.
The expert points out that Banderol's architecture combines a Chinese Swiwin turbojet and inertial-navigation system, American, European, and Japanese electronics, and Russia's Kometa-8 controlled radiation pattern antenna. It costs an estimated $50,000-$150,000, compared with roughly $2 million for the Kh-101 and $1.5 million for the Iskander-K. It reaches some 595 km/h per hour, travels 500 km, and carries a 113-kg high-explosive fragmentation warhead
"The Ukrainian military is trying to find interception weapons to counter the Banderol, including products from the Shahed-hunter Wild Hornets drone technology group," Kasapoglu wrote.
The expert also noted that the Russian defense industry sent an export version of the Lancet drone, the Lancet-E, to Egypt. The system has warhead variants weighing approximately 2.7 kg and 4.5 kg. The basic version of the Lancet has an operational range of about 40 km and contains a significant number of Western-made components.
In July, Russia planned to produce 120 Bandеrol missiles per month, but the plant had not yet reached its target production rate. In August, the Ukrainian Defense Ministry's Main Intelligence Directorate reported that Russia was capable of producing up to 80 Bandеrol missiles per month.

articles.title: The EU approved a €6.1 billion loan for Ukraine for weapons
articles.body:
The EU approved a €6.1 billion loan for Ukraine for weapons
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine will be able to purchase PAC-3 missiles for Patriot systems, drones, and electronic warfare equipment. The funds will be provided under the Ukraine Support Loan.
The European Commission has approved an additional €6.1 billion loan for Ukraine to purchase various defense products. In particular, this concerns a package that enables Ukraine to procure PAC-3 missiles for Patriot systems, as well as finance Ukrainian drones and their components. This is reported on the European Commission’s website, UNN reports.
Details
Today, the European Commission approved the allocation of an additional €6.1 billion to Ukraine for the purchase of various defense capabilities in the fields of air and missile defense, ammunition, drones, and electronic warfare systems. This urgently needed funding will help strengthen Ukraine’s ability to withstand the ongoing intensification of Russian strikes with ballistic missiles and drones
The funds will be used to purchase defense products from both EU companies and Ukrainian companies. The decision also gives Ukraine the opportunity to purchase PAC-3 missiles for Patriot systems.
The aid package, financed במסגרת the €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan, provides for five exceptions to the standard conditions for the provision of assistance: three for Ukrainian-made drones and components whose cost exceeds the established thresholds, and two for U.S.-made equipment, including PAC-3 missiles, including through the NATO-coordinated PURL mechanism.
The European Commission added that this year it has already allocated €8.35 billion to finance Ukraine’s defense, and additional funds will be allocated soon.
We remind you
The European Commission approved Ukraine’s application to purchase missiles for Patriot air defense systems במסגרת the Ukraine Support Loan. The application concerns approximately €3.2 billion to strengthen Ukraine’s air defense.

articles.title: European Commission allows Ukraine to buy Patriot missiles with EU loan originally restricted to European-made weapons
articles.body:
European Commission allows Ukraine to buy Patriot missiles with EU loan originally restricted to European-made weapons
The European Commission has approved a 6.1 billion euro transfer to Ukraine under the Ukraine Support Loan program to buy air defense systems, missiles, and drones, EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said. Kyiv can now use the European loan to purchase PAC-3 interceptor missiles for its Patriot systems.
EU authorities cleared the 90 billion euro Ukraine Support Loan for 2026–2027 in April, with 30 billion euros earmarked for budget support and the remaining 60 billion for defense procurement. Under the loan’s rules, Ukraine can only buy weapons with at least 65% of their components made in Europe or Ukraine. Anything that falls short requires separate authorization.
The Commission had already carved out one exception, for Chinese-made drone components. It has now agreed to five more: three for Ukrainian-made drones and components whose cost exceeds the allowed threshold, and two for American weapons, including PAC-3.
Clearing PAC-3 purchases for European funding doesn’t mean Ukraine will get the missiles quickly, the Ukrainian news outlet Kyiv Independent reported. Kyiv is currently contracting for roughly 1,000 Patriot missiles, but much of that order won’t be filled for years.
Kubilius also said the EU and NATO are discussing a swap arrangement: countries would hand Ukraine missiles from their own stockpiles now and receive interceptors in return once Kyiv’s 2027 batches arrive. Germany had already promised days earlier to send Ukraine missiles from its own reserves.
A shortage of Patriot missiles remains one of the most serious threats to Ukraine’s air defenses. Without these interceptors, Ukrainian forces have essentially no way to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles.
That shortage will become especially critical as winter sets in. Analysts believe Moscow plans to escalate attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure during the cold months to strengthen its position at the negotiating table.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
