articles.title: Houthis seize Yemen's Red Sea coast in lightning offensive
articles.body:
We're closing this live page now.
Join us back here from 0900 tomorrow for more live coverage of developments in the Middle East.
Thanks for following.
 
This live blog has now ended. Make sure to follow us for the latest news on Facebook, X, and Instagram.
You can catch up on events from earlier today by visiting our previous live blog here.
These were the key events on Friday:
• The Houthis have seized Yemen's Red Sea coast following a lightning offensive against government forces, deepening the Iran-backed group's control over the crucial Bab al-Mandeb shipping lane.
•    Saudi Arabia was forced to take its crucial East-West oil pipeline offline after it was struck by drones launched from Iraq.
•    Iran, Gulf states and Iraq will hold a regional meeting in Oman on Monday to discuss the Strait of Hormuz.
•    Israel has killed at least one person and injured another nine in its latest attack on Gaza.
The next round of negotiations between Israel and Lebanon in Rome have been delayed until October, a US official said Friday.
While the talks will not go ahead as planned in September, the Lebanese and Israeli ambassadors will meet at the State Department in Washington next week "to discuss ongoing developments and the continued implementation" of a framework deal agreed in June, the official said on customary condition of anonymity.
An Iraqi military commander was dismissed early on Saturday after investigations confirmed the latest drone attacks targeting Saudi Arabia originated from Iraq, according to a statement by Iraq's prime minister's office.
The commander led operations in Maysan province in southern Iraq, according to the statement.
Iraq welcomed Saudi Arabia's decision to hold off on retaliation after Riyadh said drones launched from Iraqi territory struck its East-West pipeline.
Iraq condemned any attack threatening Saudi security and said its prime minister had ordered an investigation into those responsible, according to a statement from its armed forces.
Saudi Arabia said drones launched from Iraq attacked its East-West pipeline, but said it would not retaliate for now following a request from Iraq's prime minister, while reserving the right to take all necessary measures to protect its sovereignty, security and critical facilities, according to a Saudi foreign ministry statement.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan discussed regional developments and recent attacks targeting Saudi Arabia in a call with his Saudi counterpart Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud, a Turkish diplomatic source said on Friday.
Last month, NATO member Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a joint defense agreement that includes a mutual defense clause similar to NATO's Article 5.
Lebanon's army on Friday arrested a relative of ousted Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad, as well as the son of famous Lebanese drug lord Nouh Zaiter, a security source told AFP.
The source, requesting anonymity, said that the military "arrested three people, including Suleiman Hilal al-Assad, the son of ousted Syrian President Bashar al-Assad's cousin" while they were caught using drugs in the eastern Bekaa region.
"Among those arrested was also the son of Nouh Zaiter," who is named Ali, the source added, referring to a famous Lebanese drug lord who was captured by the army last year.
The source also said that "the Syrian detainee is a civilian" and not a former officer.
Saudi authorities shut the East-West oil pipeline in the Riyadh and Medina areas after it came under attack, injuring a number of people, an energy ministry official told state media on Friday.
"The East-West pipeline in the Riyadh and Medina regions was subjected to several attacks on Thursday morning," the official told the SPA news agency, adding: "The pipeline was stopped as a precaution, and the attacks resulted in some injuries."
Ten Iranian fishermen who went missing in August off Iran's southern coast and were later found in the neighbouring United Arab Emirates will return home on Friday, state media reported.
The anglers went missing as fighting raged in the Middle East war, with the Strait of Hormuz a major flashpoint between Tehran and Washington, which are vying for control of the strategic waterway.
"These 10 Iranians left Dubai a few minutes ago," Iranian state news agency IRNA reported earlier today, citing the Iranian consulate general in the UAE.
They were returning to Iran by plane to the port city of Bandar Abbas on the other side of the Gulf, IRNA said.
A spokesperson for Yemen's military says it had launched airstrikes on the road between Taiz and Mocha, the coastal city seized by Houthi forces on Thursday.
Israel has carried out multiple airstrikes on the south Lebanon town of Nabatieh al-Fawqa, Lebanon's state-run news agency has reported.
The National News Agency also reported raids in Al-Mansouri in Tyre district.
An adviser to Iran's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei called the advance in Yemen by Tehran-backed Houthi fighters a "resounding victory" on Friday, after they seized a key island in the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait.
"Congratulations on this resounding victory, Ansar Allah," Mohammad Mokhber wrote on X, referring to the Houthis by their formal name.
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis have seized control of the country's entire Red Sea coast, a military official from the internationally recognised government told AFP on Friday, consolidating the group's control of the vital waterway.
The official said that all territory under government control "on the western coast has fallen", after the Houthis seized the strategic Mayyun Island and the Greater and Lesser Hanish islands in the Bab al-Mandab strait as they seek to choke off Saudi oil exports.
Iran's foreign ministry said the country would meet with Gulf states in Oman on Monday to discuss the strategic Strait of Hormuz, which the Islamic republic has blockaded during the Middle East war.
"This meeting is intended to promote better understanding among the countries of the region and help strengthen shared regional security," the ministry said in a statement on Friday, adding: "Iraq and other littoral Persian Gulf states" will participate.

articles.title: EU approves funding for Patriot missiles for Ukraine
articles.body:
EU approves funding for Patriot missiles for Ukraine
EU Commissioner for Defense and Space Andrius Kubilius said this at a press conference in Brussels on Friday, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
"Today, the Commission officially also approved EUR 6.1 billion for Ukraine air defense drones and missiles from the Ukraine Support Loan. This is really a very important step forward. We worked a lot with member states and Ukraine to this goal," the commissioner said.
He stressed that the decision is a crucial step toward ensuring the Ukrainian military's combat capability and protecting critical infrastructure from Russian attacks.
According to the official, the decision will allow Ukraine to urgently address shortages of precision weapons and missiles for Patriot air defense systems through exemptions from the general procurement rules.
"The decision officially enables Ukraine to procure PAC-3 missiles for Patriots. Funded under the Ukraine Support Loan, the package includes five derogations from standard eligibility conditions – three for Ukrainian-made drones and components exceeding cost thresholds and two for U.S.-made equipment, in particular PAC-3 missiles, including we as a NATO-coordinated portal mechanism," Kubilius said.
The EU commissioner noted that the speed of deliveries is now a decisive factor, and that the partnership between the EU and Ukraine should ensure a steady supply of the weapons needed on the battlefield.
"Ukraine's military edge depends on the rapid availability of critical products in the required quantities and within very short time frames. Accelerating EU deliveries through desk stocking, reprioritizing orders, and ramping up the production remains crucial," he said.
Asked about the timeline for the delivery of PAC-3 missiles, Kubilius stressed that allies are looking for flexible solutions to immediately meet Ukraine's needs until new batches leave the factory.
He said the question now was whether it is possible to reach agreements with member states that already have PAC-3 missiles in their stockpiles to transfer these missiles from their stocks to Ukraine now and then receive replacements under Ukraine's agreements for 2027.
As reported, under the approved decision, the European Union has fully allocated the EUR 28.3 billion planned for this year to finance Ukraine's defense under the Ukraine Support Loan.
The European Commission is currently processing a request for the disbursement of another EUR 4.7 billion tranche, after EUR 8.3 billion had already been transferred.
According to European Commission estimates, Ukraine's annual needs to defend against ballistic attacks amount to around 2,000 PAC-3 interceptor missiles for Patriot systems, while global production capacity is only gradually increasing, requiring flexible solutions from NATO and EU allies.

articles.title: Iran-backed Houthis seize Red Sea port, putting another key trade route at risk
articles.body:
Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels seized the Red Sea port of Mokha and captured the nearby Perim island on Friday, tightening their grip around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait while the U.S.-Iran war chokes another of the world’s critical shipping routes at Hormuz.
The swift advance marks the Houthis’ biggest territorial expansion in years. According to reports from the Associated Press, fighters swept south along Yemen’s western coast as Saudi-backed government forces withdrew, prompting Saudi airstrikes on Mokha airport.
That surge puts the Houthis in a strong position around Bab al-Mandeb, the narrow southern gateway to the Red Sea and Suez Canal through which roughly 10 to 12 percent of global trade passes.
Advertisement
At its narrowest, the strait is only about 30 kilometers wide. Yemen’s internationally recognized President Rashad al-Alimi warned Thursday it “must not be allowed to become another Strait of Hormuz.”
The Iranian-supported rebel advance raises the prospect of simultaneous disruption at two of global trade’s most vital chokepoints, potentially compounding shipping delays, supply shortages and inflationary pressure worldwide.
Tehran on Friday voiced support for Yemen’s "independence, national sovereignty and territorial integrity," while blaming the country’s crisis on blockade and foreign military intervention. The Iranian foreign ministry's statement, published on official state-run news agency IRNA, did not address the Houthi advance or Bab al-Mandeb.
The Houthis’ military capabilities have also drawn fresh scrutiny. A weapons cell based in Northern Yemen, a large part of which is controlled by the Houthis, used Anthropic’s Claude AI to develop guidance, navigation and control software for rockets and ballistic missiles, the tech giant reported in a memo published Thursday.
Western concerns are growing over the ramifications of the Iran war spreading further across the region.
Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot warned Friday in a post on X that “Bab al-Mandab is not a bargaining chip.”
Advertisement
“Blocking or disrupting this vital artery puts global supply chains at risk,” he said, warning of higher prices and shortages of “food, fuel and other essential goods.” Prévot urged Iran to use its influence “for de-escalation rather than confrontation.”
Beginning in 2023, the Houthis launched a sustained campaign of attacks on shipping in the southern Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb, which they said was in solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza during the Hamas-Israel war.
That prompted major shipping firms and oil companies — including Hapag-Lloyd, MSC, Maersk, BP and Frontline — to reroute vessels away from the Suez Canal and around Africa instead. Traffic has still not returned to pre-2023 levels, although some companies had begun testing a return to the route this summer.
According to a report by Axios, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called U.S. President Donald Trump twice Thursday to urge immediate U.S. strikes on the Houthis. Trump declined direct military action for now.
On the other side of the Arabian peninsula, U.S. forces struck three Iranian oil tankers on Sept. 5 and another five days later, while Iran says it has retaliated against commercial vessels using what it considers unauthorized routes.

articles.title: Why Turkey is opening channels with Hezbollah
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
How Israel is pushing Turkey and Hezbollah closer
Turkey and Hezbollah are quietly expanding channels of communication as Ankara seeks to manage the group and stop it from playing any destabilising role in Syria, while also trying to deter what it sees as growing Israeli threats in the region, according to analysts.
The contacts come as tensions between Turkey and Israel deepen over their competing interests in Syria, and as President Recep Tayyip Erdogan seeks to expand Turkey's influence across the Middle East.
But Turkey’s engagement with Hezbollah does not signal that Ankara has embraced the Iran-backed militant group. Omer Ozkizilcik, from the Atlantic Council think tank, said Turkey remained deeply sceptical of Hezbollah because of its relationship with Iran and its role during the Syrian conflict.
"We have to assess the two biggest disputes between Turkey and Hezbollah – firstly, the relationship of Hezbollah with Iran, and secondly, the role that Hezbollah played in Syria," Ozkizilcik told The New Arab.
"With Hezbollah being kicked out of Syria, the second biggest area of dispute has been resolved," he added.
The Hezbollah problem and Israeli threat
Turkey has emerged as a key player in Syria following the ouster of former dictator Bashar al-Assad and has maintained a troop presence in the north of the country. Ankara has close relations with the new administration in Damascus, which resents Hezbollah for fighting alongside Assad during Syria’s 13-year civil war.
Turkey and Hezbollah have not always been on good terms.
During the Syrian war, more than a dozen Hezbollah fighters were killed during Operation Spring Shield, a cross-border military operation carried out by Turkish forces in the Idlib Governorate against the former Syrian regime’s military and allied militias.
The operation was launched in late February 2020 in direct response to the Balyun airstrikes – a joint Syrian-Russian attack on a Turkish army convoy in Idlib.
But Assad's fall has fundamentally changed the regional equation. Hezbollah has lost its main supply route through Syria, while its military capabilities were significantly reduced during its 2024 war with Israel.
Against that backdrop, Ankara’s immediate concern appears to be ensuring that Hezbollah does not seek to re-establish a hostile presence in Syria or threaten the country’s new government, led by President Ahmed al-Sharaa.
Hezbollah has acknowledged that it held meetings with the Turkish ambassador to Beirut, while its leadership has also signalled a willingness to engage with Syria’s new rulers.
"What the Turkish government is trying to do is not to mediate between Sharaa and Hezbollah but to first of all ensure Hezbollah will not play a hostile and negative role against the Syrian government," Ozkizilcik said.
He added that recent statements by Hezbollah chief Naim Qassem expressing a willingness to meet with Syria’s new leadership had been welcomed in Ankara.
For Turkey, keeping Hezbollah and Syria from entering into confrontation is also tied to a much broader dispute with Israel.
Israel has warned that it will not allow Turkey to gain a foothold on its borders, while Israeli officials have dubbed Ankara the "new Iran" and accused it of seeking to expand its influence in Syria.
In August, Israel struck a base in northern Syria that it claimed was being used by Turkish troops, an allegation Ankara denied. There have been past Israeli airstrikes on the Turkish presence in Syria.
Erdogan has meanwhile warned that Israeli attacks on Syria and Lebanon are becoming a threat to Turkey. He said his country's security did not begin in Hatay, Turkey's southernmost province, but rather in Aleppo, Damascus and Beirut.
"We will not allow a fait accompli in our brotherly countries, and we will not turn a blind eye to any attacks targeting them," Erdogan cautioned in June.
But Ankara's response to Israel is not necessarily to strengthen armed groups confronting it. Instead, Ozkizilcik said Turkey viewed the continued presence of proxy groups as a potential justification for Israeli aggressions on neighbouring countries.
"Turkey believes that non-state armed actors are very effective pretexts for Israel to invade neighbouring countries," he said.
From Ankara’s perspective, Hezbollah’s presence in Lebanon is therefore itself part of the problem.
Turkey is opposed to Hezbollah’s role in Lebanese politics and does not support the group’s military presence. But it also wants Israel to withdraw from southern Lebanon and southern Syria, and sees stronger central governments as the means of achieving that.
"From a Turkish perspective, Hezbollah’s presence is problematic," Ozkizilcik said. "Turkey wants to empower statehoods and central governments."
That position could explain why Ankara is simultaneously communicating with Hezbollah while working with Washington, Damascus and Beirut on a potential arrangement that would see the group disarm.
Ozkizilcik said Turkey was working with Syria, Lebanon, the United States, Saudi Arabia and other Gulf allies, as well as Lebanese political actors, to reshape Lebanon’s political landscape and facilitate Hezbollah’s disarmament.
The proposed formula would involve Hezbollah giving up its weapons and Iran’s supply routes to the group being cut, in exchange for an Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon. However, whether such an arrangement is possible remains uncertain.
"Under the current Israeli government, it is very difficult," Ozkizilcik said, adding that the situation could change following Israel’s elections at the end of October.
Top Israeli officials have repeatedly said their troops will remain on Lebanese and Syrian land.
Is Turkey facilitating money transfers to Hezbollah?
The question of Iran’s support for Hezbollah has also become increasingly important since Assad’s fall.
Lebanon banned all flights from Iran following warnings that money shipments to Hezbollah via Beirut airport could put the facility at risk of Israeli attack. Individuals were subsequently arrested at the airport while attempting to smuggle millions of dollars in cash into Lebanon, with at least one reportedly travelling from Istanbul.
Reports have since emerged alleging that Turkey was facilitating the transfer of money and weapons to Hezbollah as Iran’s ability to do so diminished.
Those claims have not been independently confirmed.
Ozkizilcik said some of the reported transfers could instead have involved individuals within Turkey’s Islamist political spectrum who sympathise with Iran, Hezbollah and other members of the so-called "axis of resistance."
He stressed, however, that such activity did not represent Ankara’s policy.
"It is not the Turkish government’s policy to aid or facilitate aid to Hezbollah," he said.
According to Ozkizilcik, the Turkish government has also taken measures, including in coordination with Washington, to prevent individuals sympathetic to Iran and Hezbollah from providing financial support to the group.
Will Syria intervene in Lebanon?
This distinction matters for understanding Ankara’s current approach. Turkey may be opening channels with Hezbollah, but its objective is not necessarily to preserve the group as a powerful armed actor.
Instead, Ankara appears to be seeking to contain Hezbollah’s role in Syria, limit the possibility of a wider regional confrontation and create conditions in which Lebanon and Syria can regain greater control over their territory.
That also explains why Erdogan may not need to pressure Syria as heavily as some reports have suggested.
The Turkish president has reportedly pushed back against US pressure on Damascus to become involved militarily against Hezbollah in Lebanon. But Ozkizilcik said Ankara did not necessarily need to "rein in" Syria because the new Syrian government itself had no interest in sending forces into its neighbouring country.
"I don’t think Erdogan has to rein in Syria as the Syrian government has genuinely zero interest in intervening in Lebanon," he said.
A direct confrontation between Syrian forces and Hezbollah could nevertheless weaken both Syria and Lebanon and create an opportunity for Israel to exploit divisions between the two countries.
For Turkey, that would risk further destabilising the region while bringing Israeli military activity closer to its own sphere of influence.
Could Turkey and Israel go to war?
The more immediate danger for Ankara, however, may be the growing friction between Turkey and Israel itself.
While both countries have reasons to avoid a direct military confrontation, their ambitions in Syria are creating new points of friction. Turkey wants to preserve its influence over the post-Assad order, while Israel has made clear that it will act against what it considers threatening military infrastructure near its borders.
Ozkizilcik said a direct clash remained unlikely.
"Geopolitics predicts that a direct clash is unlikely, but Netanyahu is unpredictable," he said, arguing that the Israeli prime minister could still do "something crazy" for electoral reasons.
For now, Turkey’s contacts with Hezbollah appear less like the formation of a new alliance than an attempt to manage an increasingly complicated regional balance.
Ankara does not view Hezbollah as a trusted partner, nor does it appear interested in strengthening the group militarily. But with Hezbollah still an important Lebanese actor, Turkey has an interest in keeping channels open – particularly as it seeks to prevent a confrontation with Syria, push for Israeli withdrawals and expand the influence of the Lebanese and Syrian states.

articles.title: Ukrainian Flamingo missiles strike chemical plant in Russia's Volgograd, Fire Point says
articles.body:
Ukrainian Flamingo missiles strike chemical plant in Russia's Volgograd, Fire Point says
Ukraine carried out an FP-5 "Flamingo" missile strike on Russian military-industrial facilities in Volgograd overnight on Sept. 11, according to Ukrainian missile manufacturer Fire Point.
"Flamingos paid a little visit to Volgograd last night," Fire Point said in a social media statement. "Ukrainian sanctions, as always, proved to be the most effective."
The company said direct hits on the facilities sparked a "massive fire."
The FP-5 Flamingo is a Ukrainian heavy cruise missile manufactured by Fire Point that first entered service in August 2025. While early versions were relatively inaccurate, the missile has since undergone modifications and upgrades and has been used in several attacks on Russian military-industrial facilities.
"The Flamingo was fairly inaccurate in the beginning," Fabian Hoffmann, a senior research fellow at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, told the Kyiv Independent, explaining that Fire Point has since modified and upgraded the missile. "The missile is now operationally more useful," he said.
Footage posted by monitoring channels on social media showed fires apparently coming from the facility, although the extent of the damage remained unclear.
Volgograd Region Governor Andrey Bocharov acknowledged that a Ukrainian missile strike had taken place in the city, claiming that "an industrial facility in southern Volgograd" was damaged by "falling debris."
"Good results from our long-range strikes aimed at reducing Russia’s capacity to wage war. An enterprise and an oil industry facility were hit in the Saratov and Volgograd regions … Thank you to everyone who is developing Ukraine’s strength so that there will be no safe havens left in Russia for anything that supports the war," President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sept. 11.
Ukraine also struck targets in the Black Sea, Dagestan, Udmurtia, and the Tula, Nizhny Novgorod, Perm, and Samara regions, he added.
Volgogradpromproekt LLC is a chemical company based in Volgograd that is under U.S. sanctions for supporting Russia's military. According to the U.S. sanctions designation, the company "produces ferrocene-containing combustion catalysts and technology for the production of chemicals."

articles.title: Western partners should treat Ukraine's defense industry as extension of their own – ex-Google chief
articles.body:
Western countries should treat Ukraine's defense industry as an extension of their own, jointly producing weapons, resolving supply chain bottlenecks, and guaranteeing Ukrainian troops the quantities of strike capability they need, former Google CEO and chairman Eric Schmidt argues.
According to a column by Schmidt published in the Washington Post, the U.S. needs to recognize that Russia is pursuing a total-war strategy, mobilizing its factories and manpower.
He said that for most of the full-scale invasion, Ukraine's great advantage was its ability to adapt and innovate, while the enemy had greater numbers of troops, funding and industrial capacity.
"That advantage is rapidly shrinking. When Ukraine developed interceptors capable of destroying Russian Shahed drone swarms, Russia adapted by fielding faster, jet-powered Shaheds that are much harder to intercept," the former Google CEO said.
He said Russia is now deploying a satellite constellation that could rival Starlink, which Ukrainian drone units use to strike Russian forces in occupied Ukrainian territory.
He said that for years the enemy's strategy was to counter Ukrainian innovation with its own industrial scale, but Russia is now combining scale of production with its own innovation as well.
Schmidt also pointed to the rapid pace of technological competition in the war, in which a drone can be effective the moment it appears but lose its edge within a few months as the adversary adapts.
He said Ukraine is successfully adapting to such changes, but that innovation alone is not enough to scale production and meet the demands of a full-scale, high-intensity war.
"A brilliant drone built in the hundreds is interesting, but a good drone built in the hundreds of thousands can change the course of a war," Schmidt said.
He stressed that Russia is preparing for total war, considering a large-scale mobilization and building up industrial capacity for weapons production.
According to Schmidt, Ukraine cannot withstand these Russian capabilities on its own.
"The coming winter will be decisive. Russia is already exploiting Ukraine's lack of defenses against ballistic missiles to strike power plants and substations, aiming to soon plunge Ukrainians into darkness, cold and suffering," the former Google CEO said.
He said Ukraine now needs more interceptors, ammunition and long-range strike capability, as well as investment to expand its own production capacity.
"Closer engagement with them (Ukraine's military — Interfax-Ukraine) would let Western militaries help secure Ukraine's victory, absorb hard-won lessons about modern warfare, and strengthen the international order against the threats that will shape events in the decades ahead," he wrote in the column.
At the same time, he said that praising Ukrainian resilience cannot be a strategy, since courage alone cannot defend cities or win a war.
"We cannot allow it to face another winter alone under Russian bombs," Schmidt added.

articles.title: Iran used American AI to track US Navy ships in the Middle East
articles.body:
Iran used artificial intelligence models developed in the United States in an attempt to locate U.S. Navy ships in the Middle East, according to a report by Anthropic warning of emerging national security threats, whose main findings were reported by The Wall Street Journal. According to the report, an Iran-linked group gathered information from ship and aircraft identification and tracking transmitters, military imagery and commercial satellite images to track U.S. warships and look for vulnerabilities in their communications.
Anthropic said it had managed to thwart the Iranian operation, which used an advanced version of its Claude model. The U.S. newspaper said the finding was one of several threats detailed in the 154-page report, which offered a kind of playbook for how U.S. adversaries are using artificial intelligence in new ways that pose a serious threat to national security: developing new missiles, conducting aggressive disinformation campaigns, spying on dissidents and even exploring the possibility of developing biological weapons.
In recent days, U.S. President Donald Trump was asked whether he was concerned that artificial intelligence could lead to the extinction of humanity. No, I don’t have any [concerns]," he replied. What worries him, he explained, is the possibility that the United States will not win the global AI race.
At almost the same time, Anthropic published its report describing what is already happening on the ground: Scientists used the Claude model for research intended to assist in the development of biological weapons, while actors linked to hostile states such as Iran, Yemen and Russia also used it for weapons development, espionage, propaganda and surveillance.
Anthropic reported five cases of this type of biological research that it identified in recent months. The company said this was the first time a private AI company had published findings about the possible use of its platform to develop biological weapons. At the same time, Anthropic stopped short of concluding that the cases involved terrorist plots. The names of the scientists, operatives, institutions and countries where they were operating were not disclosed.
According to the report, in some cases users circumvented geographic restrictions and concealed their objectives in order to evade Claude's safety mechanisms. Although tests conducted in 2025 showed that Claude models were unable to provide significant assistance with dangerous biological research, more advanced and potentially more dangerous models have since been released. Anthropic said it had added additional safeguards and blocked the accounts it identified.
The report was published two days after Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old researcher who worked at Anthropic, announced his resignation and publicly criticized the company. “Neither company is acting responsibly,” he wrote. “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”
Coxon made clear that existing models do not currently pose an extinction risk but warned that the pace of progress could quickly change that. Evan Hubinger, who leads research at Anthropic on aligning AI models with human goals, publicly agreed and estimated that there is a greater than 10% chance that artificial intelligence will wipe out humanity within the next decade.

articles.title: India, Russia vow to boost ties when Modi, Putin meet in New Delhi
articles.body:
India said Friday that Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to further strengthen the special relationship between their countries, discussing areas such as energy and defense.
New Delhi is balancing diplomatic ties, maintaining strong relationships with the U.S., Gulf Arab states, Russia, Iran and Israel, while facing shipping and trade disruptions from the Ukraine and Iran wars.
The leaders met for the second time in two weeks. The meeting occurred on the eve of the annual BRICS leaders summit in the Indian capital, which Chinese President Xi Jinping, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian and others are scheduled to attend. The bloc seeks to raise its profile even as its members are divided over the Iran war.
Modi and Putin "discussed conflicts in West Asia and the Black Sea region that have affected maritime trade and the safety and security of Indian seafarers," India's Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
Modi reiterated that conflicts should be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy and that India stands ready to assist in peace efforts, the ministry added.
"The two leaders agreed to remain engaged to further strengthen the special and privileged strategic partnership between the two countries," the Foreign Ministry statement said.
India, along with China, is one of the biggest buyers of Russian oil, helping Moscow replenish its budget since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and sweeping Western sanctions.
India has resisted pressure to scale back trade, arguing its large population and economy need secure, affordable and reliable energy supplies. New Delhi has also said the Ukraine conflict can be resolved only through dialogue and diplomacy, not by some countries stopping energy, metal or fertilizer trade with Russia.
Russia's share of Indian crude imports rose in 2023, reaching a record 51% in July, as disruptions to Middle East supplies increased Indian refiners' reliance on Russian oil. That share likely moderated in August as China stepped up Russian oil purchases, Indian media reported.
Friday, Modi said he presented Putin with a Russian translation of the Thirukkural, a revered classical text in India's Tamil language comprising 1,330 couplets on virtue, governance and love, attributed to the poet and philosopher Thiruvalluvar.
The two leaders also visited an India-Russia industrial fair showcasing Russian technology, AI, aviation, space, nuclear science, heavy engineering, mining, and banking companies.
India and Russia aim to raise bilateral trade to $100 billion by 2030 from nearly $70 billion in 2024-25.

articles.title: We’re on the brink of world war that ends with nuclear weapons – Carlson to GU (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.body:
We’re on the brink of world war that ends with nuclear weapons – Carlson to GU (EXCLUSIVE)
Conservative journalist Tucker Carlson has warned that the world is on the brink of a global conflict that could ultimately end with the use of nuclear weapons in an interview with Going Underground host Afshin Rattansi broadcast on RT on Saturday.
Carlson argues that the US is already effectively at war with Russia through Ukraine and warns that further escalation risks a nuclear confrontation.
“The CIA is running the war. The US intelligence services are running the war out of Ukraine against Russia,” he says. “The United States is at war with Russia, and the only kind of conceivable end stage if this continues is a nuclear exchange in which everyone is killed.”
The Ukraine conflict and the US-Israeli war on Iran “have merged into a global war,” he argued, warning that the confrontation now risks the very existence of the United States.
Carlson also accuses the Trump administration of abandoning the agenda it campaigned on, saying Trump and his advisers have “almost systematically betrayed the people who voted for him in 2024.” He describes the shift as “the greatest betrayal that I’m aware of in the history of American politics.”
The interview also covers political censorship in the US, the rise of BRICS, China’s growing global influence, and the changing balance of power internationally.

articles.title: Trump Loses the Other Strait
articles.body:
Trump Loses the Other Strait
The Houthi advance is bad news for the U.S., and even worse news for Saudi Arabia.
As recently as last week, the Iran war appeared to be turning slightly in America’s favor. The Houthis—the Yemen-based militia that is Iran’s most formidable remaining ally in the Middle East—were under pressure from their local rivals, and the Saudi air force was pounding them with air strikes. The president of Yemen’s internationally recognized government issued a triumphant statement declaring that the Houthis’ miscalculations “will open the door to their complete collapse.” With their Houthi partners wounded, Iran’s leaders would have one more reason to back down and agree to Donald Trump’s terms.
Yesterday morning, those delusions drifted away like smoke as Houthi forces broke through their enemies’ defenses and seized the towns and islands around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the most important maritime choke points in the world.
That loss leaves Trump, who had been hoping to win back control of the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, with a bitter surprise. His enemies now control both of the two important straits in the Middle East, through which a combined total of about a third of the world’s oil shipments pass every day.
It also underscores a stubborn fact: For all the setbacks suffered by Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” over the past year or two, its forces retain an ideological fervor and an esprit de corps that is sorely lacking on the other side. The Gulf states’ failure to work together against the Houthis has been catastrophic, and it echoes Trump’s own failure to devise a plausible or coordinated strategy against Iran.
Although the Houthis already had the ability to threaten shipping in the Red Sea, the capture of the Bab el-Mandeb “means you can literally sit on the coast and fire at passing ships,” April Longley Alley, a Yemen expert at the Washington Institute on Near East Policy and the former political adviser to the United Nations special envoy for Yemen, told me. “It makes it easier and cheaper, and it solidifies, from a military and political point of view, that they have a stranglehold on the strait.”
The United States might not be able to do much about this, even if the Pentagon launches a new round of air strikes on the Houthis. (The Saudi leader, Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman, called Trump twice yesterday urging him to strike the Houthis, Axios reported.) Bombs and missiles would achieve little without a ground force to take advantage of them, and America’s Yemeni allies are now battered and divided. The Trump administration waged a seven-week war against the group last year, and although it succeeded in killing some Houthi commanders, it did not dislodge the group or alter its ability to wage war, as Trump had promised.
The Houthi advance is even worse news for Saudi Arabia. For many years, the Saudis have been struggling to tamp down the Houthi threat on its border. Now the Houthis have inherited a great deal of Saudi and Emirati supplies left behind by the official Yemeni government’s retreating forces. A video circulated yesterday of Mohammad Ali al-Houthi, one of the group’s top commanders and a cousin of its supreme leader, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, riding though Mokha in an Emirati armored vehicle.
The mess that Saudi Arabia faces in Yemen is partly of its own making. The Houthis were born three decades ago in reaction to Saudi meddling in Yemen’s religious and political sphere. In December, tensions between the Saudi and Emirati leadership led Riyadh to demand that the Emiratis—their nominal allies—withdraw from Yemen, leaving the Saudis in charge of a patchwork of militias with divided loyalties. The various Yemeni factions continued to squabble among themselves even as their Houthi enemies were at the gates.
“There was no coordination between commanders, between the intelligence and the drones, between the coast guard and the army—nothing,” Farea Al-Muslimi, a Yemen specialist at the think tank Chatham House, told me.
The Houthis have clearly benefited from the Gulf’s disunity. “Last time the Houthis made a breakthrough at Marib in 2022, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia were able to jointly support a devastatingly effective Yemeni-government counterattack,” Michael Knights, the head of research at the consultancy Horizon Engage, told me.
The Houthis, meanwhile, were disciplined and focused. “They sacrificed hundreds if not thousands of fighters,” a member of Yemen’s officially recognized government, who asked not to be identified for fear of repercussions, told me. “Our bullshit activists were putting out fake news about victories, while the Houthis were working in silence.”
With the momentum on their side, the Houthis could now go on to seize more terrain in other parts of Yemen, including Marib province, where much of Yemen’s oil is located. They could also extend their power bloodlessly, by cutting deals with tribal and regional leaders in the south and east. All of this would further consolidate their power and strengthen their Iranian patrons.
The Houthi victories have already put into doubt the value of the Mecca Alliance, the mutual-defense pact formed in August by Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey. Islamabad and Ankara have shown no inclination to help the Saudis, despite a rash of recent Houthi strikes on targets in southern Saudi Arabia.
Iran’s vaunted Axis of Resistance is not a bulletproof covenant either. The Houthis were absent earlier this year when the United States and Israel started bombing Iran.
But unlike their enemies, the Houthis and the Iranians have a deep ideological bond, one that their soldiers willingly die for. And the Houthis do not need to win every battle. As long as they can sink an occasional oil tanker, they will hold a whip hand over their Saudi neighbors, and over the rest of the world too.

articles.title: NATO member risking nuclear standoff – Kremlin
articles.body:
NATO member risking nuclear standoff – Kremlin
Russia will respond to any deployment in Lithuania of nuclear weapons aimed at the country by adjusting its own posture accordingly, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has warned.
The Baltic NATO state is currently moving to abolish a constitutional ban on hosting weapons of mass destruction, which President Gitanas Nauseda described as outdated in July. Speaking to Russian TV on Friday, Peskov said Vilnius would cause another rise in tensions with the proposed move.
“If you host nuclear weapons, they are aimed at somebody. Those won’t be aimed to the west. They will be aimed to the east, i.e. at us,” Peskov said. Consequently, “our nuclear weapons will be aimed at” the hosting nation.
Lithuanian media has described the proposed constitutional reform, which could be approved as soon as this winter, as creating a legal framework for a proposed EU nuclear-sharing scheme. France, the only nuclear power in the economic bloc, is considering moving some of its weapons to other member states.
NATO already has a nuclear-sharing arrangement under which US nuclear bombs are stored in non-nuclear countries, including Belgium, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Türkiye, and the UK.
Earlier this week, a Lithuanian parliamentary committee on legal affairs approved a proposal to amend the constitution, with two MPs voting against. The opposition argued that the change should be put to a referendum, while Nauseda’s government said approval by parliament is sufficient. Constitutional amendments in Lithuania require two separate votes in parliament at least three months apart.
The provision outlawing weapons of mass destruction also bans foreign military bases and was included in the basic law to safeguard the post-Soviet republic’s neutrality. Lithuania joined NATO in 2004 along with Latvia and Estonia. Germany is currently working to deploy a heavy tank brigade in the country.
Russia has described NATO’s expansion in Europe as a key cause of current tensions with the US-led military bloc. Moscow views the forward deployment of nuclear-capable weapons near Russia’s borders as a major risk because it significantly reduces the time available to determine whether a detected attack is a false alarm or an actual strike warranting nuclear retaliation.

articles.title: Russian forces kill 9, injure 145 across Ukraine over past day as Moscow expands gas station strikes to Kyiv
articles.body:
Russian forces kill 9, injure 145 across Ukraine over past day as Moscow expands gas station strikes to Kyiv
At least nine people were killed and 145 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day, local authorities said.
The Ukrainian Air Force reported that Russia launched 161 attack drones of various types overnight, including jet-powered drones, as well as one S-8000 "Banderol" low-cost cruise missile. According to the Air Force, Ukrainian forces shot down or suppressed 138 drones using electronic warfare, with hits recorded at 19 locations, while falling debris from downed drones struck three additional sites.
During the Russian attack on Odesa early on Sept. 11, Romania scrambled F-16 fighter jets to monitor drones or missiles approaching the Romanian border. No violations of Romanian airspace were ultimately recorded, the Romanian Defense Ministry said.
In Pavlohrad, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, a Russian strike on a shopping center in the middle of the day caused a mass-casualty incident, according to Ukrainian authorities. At least five people were killed and 67 others injured, including at least three children.
Across the rest of the region, two people were killed in Russian attacks on the regional capital, Dnipro, on Sept. 10, while five others, including a 6-year-old girl, were injured, local authorities reported.
Two more men were injured in overnight attacks in Dnipro, while one person was injured in the Nikopol district, according to Governor Oleksandr Hanzha.
In Donetsk Oblast, Russian attacks killed one resident of Kramatorsk and injured 29 other residents of the region over the past day, according to Governor Vadym Filashkin.
In Kyiv, Russian jet-powered drone strikes continued, hitting several civilian targets, including a gas station. Four people were injured in attacks on Sept. 10, while eight more were injured in an overnight drone strike on a residential building, city authorities reported.
The Sept. 10 strike marked the first time Russian forces targeted a gas station in Kyiv, after similar attacks had largely been concentrated in frontline regions. The expanding campaign is complicating fuel distribution, with potential consequences for both civilians and military personnel who depend on passenger vehicles to get around.
The attacks continued as Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski arrived in the Ukrainian capital by train.
A woman was also killed in a Russian drone strike in Kyiv Oblast's Vyshhorod district on Sept. 11, according to Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Regional State Administration.
In Kharkiv Oblast, a 49-year-old man was wounded by Russian shelling in the settlement of Zolochiv, according to local authorities.
In Kherson Oblast, nine people were injured in various Russian attacks, local authorities reported.
In Odesa, a Russian attack damaged a warehouse containing humanitarian aid and injured two people, Governor Oleh Kiper said.
In Sumy Oblast, 12 people, including four children, were injured in Russian glide-bomb strikes, while a woman was wounded in a separate drone strike, local authorities reported.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, five people, including two children, were injured in Russian attacks on the city of Zaporizhzhia and the surrounding district, according to local authorities.

articles.title: “Credit to the Russians, they know how to scale,” Ukrainian military spokesperson says. Ukraine’s jet-drone interceptors show early promise, but harder job ahead
articles.body:
Ukraine is getting closer to home-built interceptors designed to hunt down Russia's fast jet Gerans. Those interceptors have shown very positive early results, and the harder job now is producing enough of them to match the speed at which Ukraine downs the slower drones, Serhii Bratchuk, spokesperson for the Ukrainian Volunteer Army, said on Radio NV.
The jet-powered Geran is the problem Ukraine has been racing to solve. It flies too fast for the mobile gun teams and light interceptors that bring down the slower, piston-engine version. Alongside ballistic missiles, those drones have already done strategic damage: they helped Russia destroy about 90 percent of Ukraine's modern warehouse capacity.
A working interceptor changes that only if Ukraine can field it in numbers, which is why Bratchuk framed the fight ahead as one of production rather than invention.
Interceptors show early promise
However, Bratchuk would not put a date on their release, saying that "right now, our developers are testing our jet interceptor drones."
"We can't talk about details, but from what I know and what I see, the results are very positive, and we are counting on them," he shared.
Four Ukrainian companies already have interceptor drones in field trials, and President Zelenskyy has said that 67 firms in all are working to shoot down the jet drones en masse.
Production must catch up
Ukraine has to lift jet-drone interception to the level it has reached against the conventional Gerans, Bratchuk said, the ones Ukrainians nickname "mopeds" for their buzzing engines. Only then, he argued, can Ukraine say it is closing the sky to the fast drones as it has to the slow ones.
Russia keeps firing both types, in the south and elsewhere, and often at night, precisely to overload Ukraine's air defenses.
Russia scales, and Ukraine must too
Bratchuk gave Russia its due on the one thing that will decide this contest, its ability to turn out weapons in volume.
"Credit to the Russians. They know how to scale," he said.
Ukraine has to learn the same lesson, he argued, and he believes it can, having pulled off fast build-ups before.
"There are examples where we really do learn fast and scale up the relevant processes. So when it comes to jet interceptor drones, we very much want that scaling," he added.

articles.title: Russia-linked hackers used Claude agents to target Ukraine and steal military drone technology, Anthropic report finds
articles.body:
A Russia-linked hacking group used Claude as part of a large-scale espionage campaign targeting Ukrainian government agencies and military drone manufacturers, as well as various organizations in Europe, according to a new report by its creator, Anthropic, titled “Detecting and countering misuse of AI.”
The company said its identification of the group is consistent with public reporting on Midnight Blizzard, a hacking operation that the U.S. and the UK have linked to Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR). According to Anthropic, the group targeted more than 20 organizations, including government ministries, intelligence and defense agencies, embassies, think tanks, and defense industry companies. Most of the targets were in Ukraine and Europe.
The hackers automated a significant share of their operations using AI agents built on Claude. The agents were used for reconnaissance, phishing, gaining access to systems, and stealing data. The hackers also scanned email services and remote access systems used by more than two dozen Ukrainian government organizations.
One of their main targets was Ukraine’s drone industry. The hackers extracted the contents of email accounts belonging to at least two manufacturers of drone components, attacked a military drone producer, and stole a software development kit (SDK) for a drone computer-vision system.
They then spent several days studying the system, reconstructing the product’s architecture, identifying its components and supplier dependencies, and obtaining information about a product that had not yet been publicly unveiled. Anthropic said the hackers showed particular interest in firmware related to military drone control and machine vision — technology that allows drones to interpret visual information from cameras and other sensors.
AI agents were used at nearly every stage of the attacks. They gathered information on potential targets, helped build and maintain phishing infrastructure, executed commands inside victims’ systems, stole credentials, and processed hundreds of gigabytes of stolen data.
Some tasks were performed autonomously. For example, the agents monitored whether security tools were detecting the group’s malware. If the software began to be recognized, the agents modified and rebuilt it on their own, repeating the cycle after new detections.
Anthropic said one of the group’s operators speaks Russian and uses the handle JackPoterz. The company said the operator’s methods and choice of targets were characteristic of Russian state-backed cyberespionage campaigns.
The hackers also breached at least three providers of hotel Wi-Fi networks. After obtaining administrative access, they redirected hotel guests’ internet traffic through servers under their control and attempted to infect Windows, Android, and iOS devices. They were particularly interested in people connected to Ukraine, including government officials and employees of drone manufacturers.
Anthropic noted that Microsoft described the same technique in July under the name CaptiveCrunch. According to an August report by Microsoft Threat Intelligence, hackers linked to Midnight Blizzard intercepted hotel Wi-Fi traffic around the world and installed malware on victims’ devices by disguising it as browser or operating system updates. Microsoft said at the time that artificial intelligence had helped conduct a significant portion of the group’s operations.
Anthropic’s new report provides additional details about the operation — for example, the fact that the hackers hijacked WhatsApp accounts and covertly extracted Russian- and Ukrainian-language conversations, targeting at least two former senior Ukrainian officials using that method. The group also identified vulnerabilities in video surveillance services that allowed it to access live camera feeds.
Another target was a government technology organization in a North African country. Anthropic said the hackers gained control of its central account server and stole a database containing more than 300,000 national identity records, as well as registry data on more than 500,000 companies.
Anthropic said it blocked accounts linked to the group and shared information about the operation with state authorities and industry partners.

articles.title: ‘Up to mobilization’: Belarusian President Lukashenko says it’s time to ‘shake up’ Belarus’s army
articles.body:
‘Up to mobilization’: Belarusian President Lukashenko says it’s time to ‘shake up’ Belarus’s army
Alexander Lukashenko said the Belarusian armed forces will continue undergoing readiness inspections.
“I’ve already said it in plain terms: the army needs shaking up, the time has come. The whole army. We’ll check everyone. Up to mobilization,” Lukashenko said.
Inspections have already been carried out in tank and motorized rifle units, he said, and are now underway in an artillery brigade. “We are preparing for war so that there won’t be one,” Lukashenko added.
Lukashenko said his youngest son, Nikolai, is also serving in the army. “No one even knew. Viktor [Belarusian Defense Minister Viktor Khrenin] drafted him. He’s serving in the army like everyone else, as he should. He’s a lieutenant. I won’t say where, but in the toughest unit,” Lukashenko said.
Ukrainian officials have repeatedly warned that Belarus poses a threat. In April 2026, Volodymyr Zelensky pointed to increased military activity in the neighboring country and suggested Russia might try to draw it into the war. By June, he said Belarus was nearing completion of road infrastructure and facilities for storing ammunition and fuel along the border with Ukraine. “We know that Russian documents describe this specifically in the context of the objectives of the so-called SVO,” he added.
Zelensky also demanded that Lukashenko remove the relay stations guiding Russian drone strikes along the border with Ukraine, warning, “if he doesn’t do it, we will.” Less than a week later, he said the relay stations had stopped working.

The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.

articles.title: Russian air defence stocks significantly depleted
articles.body:
Russian long-range air defence interceptor stocks have been depleted to the point where Moscow is having to make serious decisions about where it deploys them, a Western official has told the UK Defence Journal.
We asked whether the assessment is that Russian air defence stocks are genuinely running down to a point that would leave Russian cities and infrastructure more vulnerable than they have been, or whether the decline reported by Ukrainian intelligence in S-300 and S-400 interceptor reserves is being offset by external supplies.
“No, absolutely, 100 per cent. They’ve been depleted,” the official said.
The explanation offered was that the stockpiles were never intended for this. Those reserves existed “for defence of Russia in a campaign from NATO, not some sort of regional conflict with Ukraine”, the official said, with the consequence that “absolutely those numbers are dwindling, and Russia is having to make some really serious prioritisation decisions about where they employ those air defence assets.”
The depletion was explained by reference to a series of Ukrainian operations that Russian planning had not anticipated. Reflecting on how much has changed, the official said an intelligence officer five years ago would not have thought the present situation realistic, and that the same applies looking at it from the Russian side. Ukrainian drone strikes reaching the vicinity of the St Petersburg International Economic Forum, and Russian oil refining capacity down by 40 per cent at its peak, were described as completely unforeseeable by Moscow.
One measure of how acute the problem became was legislative as Russia introduced a law to mobilise reservists specifically for the air defence of oil refineries, the official said, a step taken late last year in response to the success Ukraine was having against those targets.
On whether a point of exhaustion can be identified, the official was careful, telling me “I don’t think we’ll be in a position yet to say what that pivot point is,” they said, declining to predict a date by which reserves might run out while maintaining that Russia faces very difficult choices.
Officials described Russian use of North Korean KN-23 ballistic missiles as significant in itself. “The fact that Russia is having to use North Korean missiles is quite significant. It says a lot about Russia’s ability to resource its own conflict,” one official said, declining to give numbers.

articles.title: Russia strikes data center in Kiev – MOD
articles.body:
Russia strikes data center in Kiev – MOD
Russia has struck a commercial data center in Kiev and infrastructure in the Ukrainian port of Odessa, the Defense Ministry in Moscow has said.
The 4,500-square-meter Be Mobile facility in the Ukrainian capital was among a string of military-linked industrial, logistics, and port targets hit overnight with precision weapons and attack drones, according to the ministry’s morning update on Friday.
In Kiev Region, Russian forces struck a site near the town of Gostomel that the ministry said was used to store components for long-range drones. 
Kiev deploys kamikaze drones for strikes deep inside Russia on a daily basis.
Multiple videos circulated by Ukrainian media show a fire reportedly caused by a jet-powered drone strike.
Footage shows bright sparks and apparent secondary explosions, fueling speculation that munitions may have been stored at the site.
The incident comes amid growing tensions in Ukraine over the military’s use of facilities close to residential areas to store explosives.
In late August, a Russian strike on an ammunition depot in the village of Milaya northwest of Kiev triggered a massive detonation that killed 35 people and damaged hundreds of nearby homes. This week, a security official responsible for setting up and operating the depot was formally accused of negligence.
Russia’s latest operation also reportedly targeted two logistics hubs in Khmelnitsky Region and Dnepropetrovsk Region, both of which the ministry said were used to store drone parts.
In Odessa Region, the ministry said multiple targets were struck, including a repair shop servicing Ukrainian military hardware, another storage facility for drone components, as well as several cargo ships and fuel depots linked to the Ukrainian military.
Ukraine made attacks on Russian civilian ships a key part of its attempted “pressure campaign” during the summer. Russian retaliation has since virtually paralyzed shipping through ports in Odessa Region.

articles.title: EU approves EUR 6.1 bln support loan for drones, Patriot air defense missiles
articles.body:
The European Commission has officially approved providing Ukraine with a EUR 6.1 billion support loan to purchase drones and missiles for Patriot air defense systems, EU Commissioner for Defense and Space Andrius Kubilius said.
"Today I'll share news about our decisions under the Ukraine support loan. Today the European Commission officially approved allocating EUR 6.1 billion from this loan for the purchase of drones and missiles for Ukraine's air defense systems," he told reporters in Brussels on Friday.
Kubilius called this a genuinely important step forward, saying the Commission had worked hard with member states and Ukraine to reach this point, and that the decision formally allows Ukraine to purchase PAC-3 missiles for Patriot systems.
He explained that for EU funding to be used to purchase weapons from third countries, member states must adopt a separate decision. This package, financed under the Ukraine support loan, involves five departures from standard procurement eligibility rules, he said: three concern drones and components of Ukrainian manufacture whose cost exceeds set limits, and two concern equipment made in the United States, including PAC-3 missiles, among them procurement carried out through a joint purchasing mechanism coordinated by NATO.
The commissioner said Ukraine's military edge depends on the rapid availability of critical equipment in the necessary volumes and on very short timelines. Speeding up the delivery of needed equipment by drawing on existing stockpiles, reprioritizing orders and scaling up production remains a decisive task, he stressed, adding that today's decision means the full EUR 28.3 billion allocated this year from the Ukraine support loan has now been assigned to the country's defense needs.
He said the European Commission is currently processing payment requests worth EUR 4.7 billion, in addition to the EUR 8.3 billion already disbursed earlier. The disbursement process is therefore also moving forward, he said, noting that before transferring funds, the Commission verifies contracts to ensure they comply with the terms of the Ukraine support loan and with procurement rules agreed with member states.

articles.title: BRICS Summit 2026: Putin, Modi reaffirm partnership
articles.body:
BRICS Summit 2026: Putin, Modi reaffirm partnership
Published September 11, 2026last updated September 11, 2026
What you need to know
- Putin and Modi discuss a wide range of issues, including the Ukraine-Russia conflict, energy cooperation and trade across several sectors
- Modi again urges Putin to end the war in Ukraine
- Modi calls for maritime trade to be protected during bilateral talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in New Delhi
- Pezeshkian warns Iran coming under 'critical, dangerous' US economic pressure
Here is a roundup of some of the top headlines from the BRICS Summit 2026 in India:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
We are pausing our coverage
It's past midnight in New Delhi, so we are pausing our coverage for tonight.
We will be back on Saturday for the start of the two-day BRICS leaders' summit.
IN DEPTH: India's BRICS strategy tested with Xi, Putin set to visit
New Delhi's "America Plus" approach sees India deepening its ties with China and Russia, while also trying to keep BRICS from turning into an anti-Western platform.
But with BRICS both growing in size and increasingly troubled by internal divisions, the forum might limit Narendra Modi's diplomatic gains.
Find out more about India's diplomatic balancing act between BRICS members China and Russia and the West in this report by DW's Mural Krishnan.
Modi urges Putin to end Ukraine war
India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi again appealed to Russian President Vladimir Putin to enter negotiations to end the war in Ukraine.
During their meeting in New Delhi on the eve of the BRICS summit, Modi told Putin that dialogue and diplomacy are the right way to resolve conflicts, the Indian Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
Russia's war in Ukraine and its impact on shipping in the Black Sea have affected India, a major buyer of Russian oil and grain. Indian sailors have also been caught up in drone attacks.
The war, which the Indian Foreign Ministry has referred to as conflicts "in the Black Sea region," is on the agenda for the two-day summit.
India has adopted a typically pragmatic approach to the conflict, seeking to balance ties with the West and with Russia.
However, during an August meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) in Kyrgyzstan, Modi urged Putin to end the war, which was in its fifth year.
IN DEPTH: India looks to steer BRICS away from anti-Western turn
The BRICS summit 2026 takes place in Delhi this weekend. Unlike last year, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are expected to attend. Can India keep the expanded bloc united?
Find out more in this report by DW's Arthur Sullivan.
Modi meets Iranian president Pezeshkian
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has met with Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian on the eve of the BRICS leaders' summit.
According to a statement by India's Foreign Ministry, Modi thanked Pezeshkian for taking part in the summit "despite the challenging circumstances" for Iran, which remains at war with the US and Israel.
Despite that conflict and economic pressure from the US to cut trading ties, India has sought to balance maintaining its relationship with Tehran and with Israel and Arab Gulf states.
Modi called for regional peace and stability to be restored and maintained and for maritime trade routes to be protected, amid the US and Iran's competing blockades of the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran facing 'critical, dangerous' pressure — Pezeshkian
Iranis currently experiencing "critical, dangerous" levels of pressure, President Masoud Pezeshkian said.
The pressure comes as a result of the US sanctions on the country, according to Pezeshkian.
"Iran has been subjected to heavy sanctions in recent years," the Iranian leader said ahead of the BRICS summit in India.
"This pressure has reached critical and dangerous stage in recent months following the military aggression by the US and Israel," he added.
Pezeshkian also said that the world is going through a period of "unprecedented complexity."
Putin blames West for attempting to reclaim 'former leadership'
Russian President Vladimir Putin blamed Western countries for attempting to reclaim their "former leadership" in an "unseemly" fashion,
According to Russia's leader, the West is focusing on destroying facilities and pipelines, as well as seizing vessels, in an attempt to maintain its economic leadership.
Putin made these comments while speaking at the BRICS business forum in India.
Modi, Putin reaffirm partnership on issues of mutual interest
Indian PM Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin held bilateral talks on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit that will begin on Saturday.
The two leaders "exchanged views on India-Russia engagement in the multilateral sphere, in particular in BRICS under India’s Chairship for 2026," a statement by India's Ministry of External Affairs said.
In the meeting, the leaders also exchanged views on "key regional and global issues of mutual interest, including the conflicts in West Asia and the Black Sea region which have impacted maritime trade and the safety and security of Indian seafarers."
Reaffirming their ties, the two leaders committed to "remain engaged in an effort to strengthen further the Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership between the two countries," the statement added.
Pezeshkian arrives for BRICS Summit
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian landed in Delhi to attend the BRICS Summit.
This is the first visit by an Iranian President to India in over eight years.
Pezeshkian is scheduled to hold bilateral talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi at 6.15 p.m. local time Friday to advance two-way trade and strengthen overall ties.
His participation at the BRICS Summit and bilateral talks with Modi holds significance as it comes at a time when tensions are rife in the Middle East and energy market disruptions have shaken the economy worldwide.
WATCH — India's difficult BRICS chairship
With BRICS nations now representing nearly 3.7 billion people and close to 40% of global GDP, leaders are meeting amid rising geopolitical tensions, trade disputes and energy challenges.
While the expanded bloc is seeking a stronger voice in the global economy, disagreements over an alternative payment system and China's dominant role could test unity. Renewable energy and green infrastructure financing are emerging as key areas to watch.
Former UN diplomat: BRICS is 'voice of Global South,' but 'contradictions remain'
Speaking to DW about the BRICS Summit, former UN diplomat Shashi Tharoor said that the expansion of the bloc has made it the voice of the Global South.
The BRICS coalition started out with four member countries; Brazil, Russia, India and China but now has 11 members and partner countries after the economic bloc decided to open up membership for more countries in 2023.
Tharoor noted that while Iran joined the coalition, US strategic partners Egypt and Ethiopia also joined
"The expansion that took place in Johannesburg turned out to be one in which both sets of geopolitical points of view were accommodated," Tharoor noted in an interview with DW.
He argued that, "in some ways the expansion has made it much more the voice of the global south."
However, he also said that while the majority of the world is represented in the new 11-member BRICS, the chances of having a consensus has also decreased.
"I would say that BRICS is functioning, but the contradictions remain, and some contradictions have become even more apparent," he said.
He said that when BRICS leaders met this year, they "could not agree on any particular language, and so the chair, India, issued a chair statement instead… it wasn't just Iran, it was also Ukraine that they couldn't agree on."
Tharoor noted that the bloc has a "built-in set of geopolitical divergences which will crop up whenever issues divide the members."
Piyush Goyal proposes 'borderless' digital trade at BRICS
Indian Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal on Friday urged BRICS member countries to link their payment systems, encourage trade in local currencies, and make digital trade more accessible globally.
Addressing the opening ceremony of the BRICS Business Forum on Friday, Goyal highlighted India's digital payments ecosystem, including the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), as a potential foundation for deeper cross-border financial cooperation among BRICS economies.
"Today, it is also accepted in 11 countries and I would urge the Brics member countries and partner countries to link our payment systems, trade in each other's local currencies, make digital trade global and build together for the future emerging technologies," Goyal said as reported by Indian newspaper Deccan Herald.
Modi, Putin to meet on the sidelines of BRICS
Russian President Vladimir Putin landed in Delhi on Friday to attend the BRICS Summit being held at the Bharat Mandapam on September 12 and 13.
He will be meeting Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in the afternoon. Talks are expected to focus on enhancing cooperation in a range of areas, including defence, energy, technology, pharmaceuticals and people-to-people exchanges.
"Warmly welcome President Vladimir Putin of Russia for the 18th BRICS Summit. He was received by MoS K V Singh at the airport. India and Russia share multifaceted and longstanding ties anchored in Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership," Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said in a post on X.
This is Putin's first in-person participation at a BRICS Summit held outside Russia since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Later in the evening, Modi will also be holding a bilateral talk with Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian.
Welcome to our coverage
Hello! This is Midhat from the New Delhi bureau, bringing you the biggest headlines emerging from across India.
With just one day to go before the BRICS Summit kicks off, Delhi is all geared up and welcoming the dignitaries — several of whom have already arrived in the capital, including Russian President Vladimir Putin.
From Friday onwards, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi will be holding bilateral talks with several leaders, including China's Xi Jinping, Iran's Masoud Pezeshkian and Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.
Security in the capital has been intensified with thousands of personnel deployed. All schools in Delhi, including government, and private schools will remain closed on September 11 due to the BRICS Summit.
Commuters in Delhi will see traffic restrictions and diversions over the bext three days. Authorities have advised travelers to plan journeys and use the Metro where possible.
Stay tuned as we bring you more on the BRICS Summit and everything else making a buzz in the country.

articles.title: Pro-Palestine groups 'blockade' UK insurers over Elbit ties
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Pro-Palestine groups 'blockade' UK insurers over ties to Israeli arms firm Elbit
Pro-Palestine activists have carried out protests outside five UK offices belonging to two of the world's largest commercial insurance and reinsurance providers over their alleged links to Israeli arms manufacturer Elbit Systems.
Chubb and Sompo offices in Manchester, Glasgow, London and Maidstone faced disruption from campaigners who say that the insurers have provided underwriting for Elbit Systems and its subsidiary, UAV Engines, in Britain, as well as Elbit's US operations.
Elbit, Israel's largest arms manufacturer, supplies drones, surveillance systems and other weapons to the Israeli military, including during Israel's genocidal war on Gaza, which began on 7 October 2023.
According to the groups involved in the direct action, including Manchester-based Palestine Resistance Collective (PRC), Mothers Against Genocide Scotland and Boycott Bloody Insurance, protesters gathered outside Chubb's Glasgow office carrying banners and formed a 'red line' around the building while distributing leaflets to passers-by and office workers.
A speech was delivered inside the building's lobby, and a letter was handed to Chubb's management calling on the insurer to sever its relationship with Elbit.
In Manchester and London, protesters blockaded office entrances while making the same demand.
In a statement, Andrew Taylor, a member of Boycott Bloody Insurance, a campaign group calling on insurance companies to end their support for "destructive companies",, said: "Israel relies on Elbit’s weapons and technology to enact its genocide and occupation in Palestine – and Elbit wouldn’t be able to operate without insurance from Chubb."
He added: "People of conscience all over Britain will continue to reject Chubb’s complicity in war crimes until they see it come to an end."
Boycott Bloody Insurance has also accused Chubb of having significant exposure to companies it considers destructive, ranking it among the worst-performing insurers for underwriting weapons, fossil fuel and border detention and surveillance companies.
The group says this includes providing insurance to Lockheed Martin and several UK suppliers of components for F-35 fighter jets, which are also used by Israeli forces in military operations in the occupied Palestinian territories.
The latest action follows moves by two other insurance firms, Allianz and Aviva, to end underwriting for Israel's largest arms manufacturer following sustained direct action by banned activist group Palestine Action.
Allianz's coverage of Elbit Systems UK ended last November, while Aviva's employment liability insurance coverage for UAV Engines Ltd, an Elbit subsidiary, ended in last September.
Elbit Systems UK is now reportedly receiving employer's liability insurance from Aspen Insurance, while UAV Engines is insured by Chubb.

articles.title: €1,000 Shot: Estonia Develops Tempterno CP260 Multi-Target Mini-Rocket
articles.body:
Estonian company Tempterno Defence has developed the Tempterno CP260 multi-mission, multi-target unguided mini-rocket designed to destroy aerial and ground targets.
The new development was unveiled at the MSPO international defense exhibition in Poland, Militarnyi reports.
The about 1-kg munition has a maximum range of up to 2.5 km and an effective range of 200 to 500 meters. The developers cite its low cost per shot, at around €1,000, as one of its main advantages.
The rocket can be launched from multicopters, fixed-wing UAVs, ground launchers, or manually from the shoulder. The launcher for the missile is being developed by another Estonian company.
In its air defense configuration, the rocket uses a proximity fuze that detonates at a distance from the target, creating a cloud of tungsten pellets.
Естонська компанія Tempterno Defence розробила легку багатоцільову мініракету Tempterno CP260 pic.twitter.com/SYhBv6ZXJB
— Владислав (@Vladislav110528) September 10, 2026
For engaging ground targets, including personnel and vehicles, high-explosive, inflaming, and anti-armor warheads are being developed.
“Instead of simply using a kamikaze drone to destroy a single target, you can arm a UAV with rockets and destroy several targets in a single flight,” a Tempterno Defence representative said.
The missile is currently guided manually using a camera mounted on the launcher, but the developers are working to automate target detection and acquisition with artificial intelligence.
The company is already in contact with Ukrainian enterprises regarding cooperation on integrating warheads and software for automated target acquisition.
The rocket itself is already ready and undergoing test flights, while development and testing of the warhead lineup are expected to be completed by the end of this year or early next year.
As Militarnyi previously reported, the Estonian-Ukrainian company DoD Solution and Estonian company Defsecintel will develop joint systems for detecting and intercepting drones.
Also in December 2025, Latvia successfully tested a similar Estonian Mark 1 micro-missile designed to counter drones.
