articles.title: Ukrainian drones reportedly strike Russian oil refinery, Ozon warehouse in Saratov
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones hit oil refinery, Ozon warehouse as Russia's Saratov comes under attack
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Ukrainian drones struck the Russian city of Saratov overnight on Sept. 11, hitting a local oil refinery and a logistics hub operated by e-commerce giant Ozon, according to Ukraine's General Staff and satellite imagery published by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL).
Videos circulating on social media appeared to show drones and Russian air defenses in operation in the region.
The attack on an oil refinery owned by Russian energy giant Rosneft sparked a fire at the facility, Ukraine's General Staff said, adding that the extent of the damage was still being assessed.
The Saratov Oil Refinery has been repeatedly targeted during Ukraine's long-range strike campaign against Russia's energy infrastructure. The facility, which is part of state oil company Rosneft, has an annual processing capacity of roughly 4.8 million metric tons of crude oil.
Saratov Oblast Governor Roman Busargin posted on Telegram around 2 a.m. local time about a threat from unmanned aerial vehicles, claiming that emergency services had been placed on full alert.
Soon after the strike on the refinery, a logistics hub belonging to Russian e-commerce giant Ozon was also reported to be set ablaze in Saratov. Video published by Exilenova+ appeared to show a major fire emanating from the facility shortly after explosions were heard.
Satellite imagery published later in the day by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL) showed the Ozon warehouse had been completely gutted by fire following the Ukrainian attack. The logistics center covers 100,000 square meters.
"Good results from our long-range strikes aimed at reducing Russia’s capacity to wage war. An enterprise and an oil industry facility were hit in the Saratov and Volgograd regions…Thank you to everyone who is developing Ukraine’s strength so that there will be no safe havens left in Russia for anything that supports the war," President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sept. 11.
Ukraine also struck targets in the Black Sea, Dagestan, Udmurtia, and the Tula, Nizhny Novgorod, Perm, and Samara regions, he added.
A prominent Ukrainian defense company, Fire Point, which manufactures the FP-1 long-range drone, confirmed that its drones were used in the attack on the warehouse.
"Last night, Ukraine's Defense Forces used FP-1 drones to erase another Ozon warehouse complex, this time in Saratov," the company said in a statement on social media. "Eighty-five thousand square meters wiped out. Over 30 million items out of stock permanently."
The facility is the seventh Ozon logistics hub to have been damaged or destroyed by Ukrainian forces since Aug. 22, when Ukraine first struck the company's hub in Chapayevsk, Samara Oblast. The number rises to 33 when attacks on logistics centers operated by Ozon's competitor Wildberries are included, according to RFE/RL.
Ozon is Russia's second-largest e-commerce marketplace, behind Wildberries, and operates an extensive network of warehouses, fulfillment centers and delivery infrastructure across the country.
Elsewhere in Russia, explosions were also heard in the port city of Kaspiysk in the Dagestan Republic. No information was immediately known as to the outcome of the reported attack.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the reports or the extent of any damage.
Saratov is located approximately 460 kilometers (285 miles) east of the Ukrainian border with Russia, near Luhansk Oblast in eastern Ukraine.
Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have emerged as one of the most economically significant aspects of Kyiv's long-range drone campaign, contributing to fuel shortages and pushing Russian production down sharply over the summer.
Russian refinery throughput fell to about 3.8 million barrels per day in August, down from around 5 million barrels per day a year earlier, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing Energy Aspects.
Ukraine has increasingly targeted Russian refineries in an effort to disrupt fuel supplies and reduce energy revenues that help finance Moscow’s war.

articles.title: Defense Forces strike three more Russian air defense systems and drone operator training center in Luhansk region
articles.body:
Defense Forces strike three more Russian air defense systems and drone operator training center in Luhansk region
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported this on Telegram, according to Ukrinform.
Specifically, two “Pantsir-S1” anti-aircraft missile and gun systems were struck in Taganrog, Rostov Oblast, Russia, and a radar station was struck in Berezki, Bryansk Oblast.
In the temporarily occupied city of Donetsk, a facility used by the Russian army for the storage, preparation, and launch of attack drones was struck.
Also, in the temporarily occupied part of the Donetsk region, the Snizhne Machine-Building Plant—a facility specializing in the production of parts for gas turbine engines, including compressor and turbine discs and blades—was struck. Russia uses it to manufacture military-grade products, including components for aircraft engines.
In the temporarily occupied town of Petropavlivka in Luhansk Oblast, a training center for drone operators belonging to the “Akhmat” unit was struck. It specializes in training operators of FPV drones and other unmanned systems.
Assessments of the extent of the damage are ongoing.
As reported by Ukrinform, the Defense Forces recently struck three Russian “Nebo-SV” radar stations in the Bryansk region.

articles.title: Yemen's Houthis take over vital Bab al-Mandeb strait
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Yemen's Houthis take over Bab al-Mandeb strait vital to global shipping
The Houthis seized control of Yemen's entire Red Sea coast and captured three strategic islands on Friday, in a lightning offensive that cemented their hold on a vital shipping corridor linking Europe and Asia.
The developments are likely to deepen the US-Israeli war's impact on international commerce, as Saudi Arabia shut down an oil pipeline following attacks, and after months of Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
Following a week-long offensive that has left hundreds dead, government officials said the Iran-backed group seized the Yemeni side of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal.
A local official with Yemen's Saudi-backed government said on Friday that the Houthis had "completed their takeover of the Bab al-Mandab area and Mayyun Island".
A government military official later reported the group had also seized Greater and Lesser Hanish, the last two islands in the narrow waterway not under their control, as well as all of the neighbouring Red Sea coastline.
"Everything that was under our control on the western coast has fallen," the military official added.
A witness told AFP that gunmen were "deploying along the Bab al-Mandab shore and are driving around in military vehicles".
The capture of the islands, particularly Mayyun in the middle of the strait, heightens the Houthis' ability to attack Saudi tankers, which they have been targeting since July.
Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest oil exporter, has relied on the Red Sea ever since Iran's Hormuz blockade choked off its shipments via the Gulf.
Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iranian supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei, congratulated the Houthis on their "resounding victory" on Friday.
Farea Al-Muslimi, research fellow at Chatham House, told AFP: "Now the Iranians don't only control... the Strait of Hormuz, but they control the other most strategic chokepoint in the Middle East."
Oil prices have soared past $100 a barrel this week, while average US diesel prices topped $6 for the first time on Friday -- a potential headache for President Donald Trump ahead of midterm elections.
The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Saree, said navigation through the Bab al-Mandab Strait was "safe" for all but Saudi Arabia following the latest advances.
'Great victories'
The Houthi offensive has killed more than 500 people, according to sources on both sides.
It has also displaced about 46,000 people, the UN migration agency said on Friday.
It is part of renewed hostilities in Yemen's civil war that began with the group's takeover of the capital Sanaa in 2014.
Houthi supporter Abdulhamid Dhaifallah lauded the group's "great victories" in and along the strait.
"They have been preparing for this front for four years," the Sanaa resident said.
Satellite images from Copernicus Sentinel Data taken on Thursday showed black smoke billowing near Medina, along the general route of the East-West pipeline that carries Saudi oil to its Red Sea coast.
The Saudi energy ministry on Friday announced that attacks led to the closure of the pipeline -- which it had been increasingly using to bypass Hormuz -- adding that injuries were recorded.
"The East-West pipeline in the Riyadh and Medina regions was subjected to several attacks on Thursday morning," a ministry official told the SPA news agency, adding: "The pipeline was stopped as a precaution, and the attacks resulted in some injuries."
Before the Red Sea offensive, the Houthis already controlled a large part of Yemen's north.
They have recently attacked government-held areas in Hodeida and Taiz provinces and swept down the coast, seizing the port city of Mocha and Zuqar Island, north of Bab al-Mandab, on Thursday.
Mohamed, 46, who fled Mocha in the middle of the night, told AFP there was an "apocalyptic" atmosphere in the historic city.
Dangerous conflict
On Friday, the spokesman for the Yemeni government forces, Majed Abdullah Al-Nazili, said they had begun shelling areas along the Taiz-Mocha road, while residents told AFP they heard airstrikes.
While Saudi Arabia has also hit back with airstrikes and ordered troop reinforcements from Aden, where the internationally recognised government is based, it has failed to stop the Houthis' advance.
Houthi media said two Saudi strikes hit Mocha's airport on Friday, while a local official said the city's seaport was hit by six missiles of unknown origin.
"I think the Saudis have tried everything they can to avoid this war, but I don't think they have any more choice," said Al-Muslimi.
The ongoing exchanges risk reviving a war that killed hundreds of thousands of Yemenis and sparked one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
The Houthis, after seizing Sanaa and forcing out the government, fought a Saudi-led coalition from 2015 until a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022.

articles.title: Polish MEP takes axe to Ukrainian Nazi-linked memorial (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Polish MEP takes axe to Ukrainian Nazi-linked memorial (VIDEO)
A Polish MEP has taken an axe to a memorial honoring Nazi-linked Ukrainian nationalist paramilitaries responsible for massacring Polish civilians during World War II.
In a video posted on X on Thursday, Grzegorz Braun can be seen repeatedly striking a stone obelisk in Bialystok, near Poland’s border with Ukraine, which commemorates members of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA).
The UPA was the armed wing of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN), a WWII-era ultranationalist movement led by Stepan Bandera which collaborated with Nazi Germany. UPA fighters massacred tens of thousands of ethnic Polish civilians in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia, now largely in western Ukraine.
”The UPA monument in the Dolhobyczow municipality in Hrubieszow County is to be dismantled,” he wrote. “The obelisk offending the memory of the victims of the Ukrainian genocide against Poles should be removed... immediately after documenting the crime of Banderism,” Braun added.
Pomnik UPA w gminie Dołhobyczów w powiecie hrubieszowskim do likwidacji❗️
Obelisk obrażający pamięć ofiar ukraińskiego Ludobójstwa na Polakach powinien zostać usunięty profesjonalnymi narzędziami natychmiast po udokumentowaniu przestępstwa banderyzmu!#StopBanderyzacjiPolski… pic.twitter.com/8Q4QZ2z5vJ
According to Braun, local Poles feared Ukrainian retaliation if they removed the memorial. He said one proposal to dismantle it was met with the response: “We’re afraid they’ll set us on fire.”
The memorial stands over a burial site containing 41 UPA members killed in a clash with Soviet forces in February 1946. According to Polish records, a Ukrainian memorial was erected there without authorization in the 1990s. The stone monument honoring the UPA fighters was added later and has also faced questions over its legal status.
The site has repeatedly been vandalized. Unidentified people damaged inscriptions on the obelisk earlier this month, while the Ukrainian Embassy expressed “deep outrage” after another attack in July.
The OUN and UPA massacres remain a major source of tension between Poland and Ukraine. Warsaw recognizes the killings of predominantly Polish civilians in Volhynia, Eastern Galicia, and neighboring regions in 1943-1945 as genocide and estimates that up to 100,000 Poles were killed.
The dispute has intensified amid Kiev’s continued honoring of WWII-era Ukrainian nationalists. Vladimir Zelensky took part in the May reburial of OUN leader Andrey Melnik as part of efforts to establish a “Pantheon of outstanding Ukrainians” and later granted a Ukrainian military unit the honorary title “Heroes of the UPA.”
Polish President Karol Nawrocki responded by stripping Zelensky of the Order of the White Eagle, Poland’s highest state honor. Warsaw has also warned it will not support Ukraine’s EU membership bid unless Kiev changes its approach.
Polish MEP Ewa Zajaczkowska-Hernik has meanwhile called for an end to free weapons deliveries to Ukraine, arguing that Warsaw has provided some $4.6 billion in military aid only to be repaid with a “Banderite pantheon of heroes.”
”Let’s stop being suckers for Ukraine!” she wrote on X.
Russian President Vladimir Putin weighed in last month, arguing that the neo-Nazi nature of the Ukrainian government has become so visible that even Poland’s strongly anti-Russian authorities can no longer ignore it. Warsaw, he said, faces an “obvious demand” from its population to confront the issue.
Public attitudes toward Ukrainians in Poland have also deteriorated. A July CBOS poll found 52% of Poles opposed accepting Ukrainian migrants, against 42% in favor – the first time opponents had outnumbered supporters since tracking began after the 2014 Western-backed coup in Kiev. Support has fallen from 94% in 2022 to 42% this year.
An August IBRiS survey separately found that 67% of Poles support deporting unemployed Ukrainian men of military age.

articles.title: Russia spent 18 months building the road to Sloviansk. Ukraine spent three taking it back
articles.body:
- Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps has retaken 150–240 sq km north of Lyman since May
- It erased 18 months of Russian groundwork for a northern march on Sloviansk
- Almost nobody reported it for three months—not even Russian war correspondents
- The fighting continues north of Lyman, but on Ukraine's terms
On 22 May, a mechanized battalion of Ukraine's 3rd Assault Brigade—backed by at least two more brigades, the 60th Mechanized and the 66th, attached to the 3rd Army Corps for the operation—attacked Russian positions around the village of Nove, 15 km north of the town of Lyman in eastern Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast. Russian drones were heavily jammed that day. Roughly five Ukrainian vehicles were hit, most by fiber-optic drones—the only kind still able to fly.
Nobody outside the Ukrainian army reported it for three months. The first fragmentary accounts surfaced in late August; the full picture only this week. By then the 3rd Army Corps had taken back somewhere between 150 and 240 sq km and wrecked Russian plans for a northern siege of Sloviansk, one of the last two big free cities in Donetsk. Observer Thorkill, writing in Polish, called it a success on an operational scale.
The presence of that Ukrainian armor around Nove, which at the time anchored the right flank of a 100 sq km salient held by regiments of the Russian 20th Combined Arms Army, was an ominous sign for the Russians. After months of careful preparation by the 3rd Army Corps, the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) were strong north of Lyman. Russian forces were weak.
"The moment AFU could start moving vehicles through the area, the battle was basically over," mapper Vitaly wrote three months later. "Vehicles didn't win it, they showed up because the conditions that had made vehicle movement impossible were already gone." Ukrainian drones were everywhere. And Russian drones, effectively jammed by electronic warfare, could barely fly.
Not everyone reads those months the same way. Thorkill, who tracked the sector throughout, puts the breakthrough at 17 to 18 August, and writes that for most of July and early August the 3rd Corps' attacks were repelled by the Russian 144th Motor Rifle Division. On that account the slow months were not a steady advance. What turned them, he says, is not clear: someone on the Ukrainian side made the difference north of Kolodiazi. He is candid about the limits of what can be seen. Some sources say the Russians withdrew, others deny it, others say they were partly cut off. What he can confirm from satellite imagery is that Ukrainian forces retook Serednie and Zelena Dolyna.
Overextended and pummeled by drones, the Russians barely clung to their salient north of Lyman, which sat between the Nitrius and Zherebets rivers. They were especially exposed at its western edge, where they had pushed across the Nitrius. The Russians had hoped the salient would be a "base for an offensive on Lyman, which could have allowed further offensives to Izium and Sloviansk [and] threatened the northern supply road to Donbas," according to mapper Clément Molin.
Instead, the salient became a trap as the Ukrainian 3rd Army Corps relentlessly—but quietly—exploited the fragility of the Russian 20th Combined Arms Army. The Russians have now been pushed back toward the Zherebets, leaving behind their uncounted dead ... and their ambitions for a quick northern march on Lyman and then Sloviansk and neighboring Kramatorsk.
It had taken Russian forces 18 months to set the conditions for a push toward Sloviansk from the north. In the three months beginning with that mechanized assault around Nove, the Russians "apparently lost 1.5 years of progress in the area," Vitaly concluded. Estimates of the ground retaken vary: Molin puts it at more than 200 sq km, the AKM Mapping account at 151, and Konrad Muzyka of Rochan Consulting at around 240.
The appearance of Ukrainian armor around Nove in late May was a strong indication that the 3rd Army Corps had the momentum. But that doesn't mean the Corps' eventual victory in the battle for the Lyman salient was a foregone conclusion. On paper, the Russians have a manpower and firepower advantage in Donetsk.
A bridgehead too far
The 20th Combined Arms Army advanced too far, too fast. And the terrain favored the Ukrainian defenders, who could pluck at the Russians' supply lines from entrenched positions until the time was right for a counterattack.
"Russia putting itself inside a deep, narrow pocket only made the final phase easier," Vitaly explained. "Once AFU had enough control over the surrounding movement, every new Russian mission sent into the area walked into a reinforced perception trap—troops committed to hold positions that existed far more convincingly in reports than as a functioning front."
The silence
What kept the trap working was that nobody talked about it. The Ukrainian general staff said nothing. Pro-Ukrainian analysts, who normally map every advance within hours, held their tongues until late August. So did the Russians.
Observer Andrew Perpetua, who has followed Ukraine's other quiet operations around Kupiansk and in southern Donetsk, called this one tighter still. The Lyman operation "seemed even more protected since even the most in the know and honest Russian reporters seem to be missing it. Or at least silent about it," he wrote. "It was honestly shocking to watch how out of the loop the Russians really were, which I think is in large part due to the collective action of OSINT to avoid speaking about the situation."
Perpetua's reading is that the lying is heaviest exactly where Russian forces are being pushed back. Nearby Sviatohirsk is the case in point. Vladimir Putin recently announced its capture. On 7 September, the commander of the 3rd Army Corps, Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi, walked around the town on camera.
The 3rd Army Corps cut across the salient around three weeks ago, reaching the northern edge of Kolodiazi and trapping an unknown number of Russian stragglers between the Ukrainian vanguard and the old Russian bridgehead. Most of the encircled Russians appear to have escaped. "There is a large area where there may still be Russian soldiers," Molin warned. "Most of the villages westwards have been cleared, but not the treelines."
On 24 August the Ukrainians mounted a second mechanized attack, so the operation has not stopped. But the 3rd Army Corps is likely shifting from attacking to consolidating and defending—and clearing out the Russian stragglers that, left alone, could sow chaos in the new gray zone that was once a Russian salient.
Russian channels have started to admit the problem. Rybar wrote of "problems near Lyman," conceding that Ukrainian units have been attacking southward from Ridkodub for months and that Russian forces "do not even control the airspace immediately near the front line." The fighting continues, but on Ukraine's terms, for now.
How much it changes is the one thing the analysts do not agree on. "This is one of the most important victory for Ukraine in 2026," Molin wrote, a victory that "will delay the offensive on northern Donbas." Thorkill, in the same post that called it an operational-scale success and rated it larger than the 7th Rapid Reaction Corps' gains near Velyka Novosilka in July, ends on the opposite note: it will not, he writes, affect in any way the situation of Ukrainian forces on the direction that matters most at present, the Kramatorsk agglomeration.

articles.title: Ukrainian air defense shoot down 138 of 161 enemy targets; hits recorded at 19 locations
articles.body:
Ukrainian defense forces destroyed 138 enemy targets overnight into Friday, with enemy aerial assets striking 19 locations, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
"According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense units had shot down or suppressed 138 enemy UAVs—including Shahed and Gerbera types, as well as other drone models," the message reads.
In total, overnight into September 11 (starting from 18:00 on September 10), the enemy launched an attack involving 161 strike UAVs—including Shahed (including jet-powered versions), Gerbera, and Parodiya-type decoy drones—from the following directions: Orel, Kursk, and Primorsko-Akhtarsk (Russian Federation), as well as occupied Donetsk and Hvardiyske (occupied Autonomous Republic of Crimea).
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Ukrainian defense forces.
Meanwhile, impacts by enemy aerial assets were recorded at 19 locations, while debris from shot-down targets fell at three locations.

articles.title: Russia attacked Ukraine with 161 drones: air defense destroyed 138 targets
articles.body:
Russia attacked Ukraine with 161 drones: air defense destroyed 138 targets
Kyiv • UNN
Overnight, Russia launched 161 attack UAVs and S8000 drones at Ukraine. Air defense destroyed or suppressed 138 targets; hits were recorded at 19 locations.
During the night of September 11, Russian invaders attacked Ukraine with S8000 "Banderoль" drones and 161 Shahed- and Gerbera-type attack UAVs, as well as Parody-type decoy drones. This was reported by the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, UNN reports.
Details
The enemy launched drones from Russia's Belgorod, Oryol, and Kursk regions and Krasnodar Krai, as well as from the occupied Crimea and Donetsk.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine's Defense Forces.
Air defense shot down/suppressed 138 enemy Shahed- and Gerbera-type UAVs and drones of other types.
Hits by enemy air attack weapons were recorded at 19 locations, as well as the fall of downed targets (debris) at 3 locations.
We would like to remind you
The total combat losses of Russian troops since the beginning of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine have reached approximately 1,503,880 personnel. In the past 24 hours alone, Russia lost another 1,490 people.

articles.title: Ukrainian companies increasingly integrating AI into missiles
articles.body:
Ukrainian companies increasingly integrating AI into missiles
Several Ukrainian companies are working on missile systems that use artificial intelligence, Brave1 CEO Andrii Hrytseniuk told Business Insider.
Source: Business Insider
Details: According to Hrytseniuk, AI is now "increasingly being integrated into missile systems as well".
"...although this has not yet reached the scale of hundreds of solutions that we see in the drone sector, we are already seeing the first successes and many developments that are currently under way," the Brave1 chief said.
Ukrainian companies are already widely integrating artificial intelligence into drones and combat robots, including for decision-making, navigation and targeting.
"Initially, AI began to be used on a large scale in drones. It is not that fast – it is sufficient for drones, but missiles require significantly higher speeds," Hrytseniuk said.
In an interview in May, Hrytseniuk said that more than 200 Ukrainian companies were developing AI-powered components for missiles, drones, radars and other systems.
Efforts to integrate AI into missiles appear to have intensified as Ukraine invests in developing long-range strike weapons, which are frequently used to attack military and energy facilities in Russia.
It is currently unclear exactly how Ukrainian companies are using artificial intelligence in missiles or how far the relevant developments have progressed. Brave1 said the technology would expand Ukraine's capabilities but would not remove humans from the process entirely.
Background:
- Ukrainska Pravda reported that the Ruta Block 2 missile, developed with support from Brave1, is undergoing flight testing in Ukraine. For the prospective Ruta Block 3, the developers say it will feature autonomous navigation in degraded GNSS environments and a terminal guidance system.
- Ukraine is testing drones equipped with AI-based autonomous terminal guidance. According to the Defence Ministry, the number of strikes using AI-assisted guidance has increased tenfold since the beginning of 2026.
Subscribe on Patreon to back our journalism long-term.

articles.title: Russian recruiters lure foreigners with jobs in construction and IT, kidnap them, and send them to war, Amnesty International finds
articles.body:
Russia tricks and coerces foreign nationals into fighting on Moscow’s side in the war against Ukraine, exploiting their dire economic situations and precarious migration status. A study by Amnesty International published on Sept. 10 asserts that some of the documented cases qualify as human trafficking under the definition of the UN Palermo Protocol.
According to data provided by Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, by April 2026 Ukraine had identified at least 28,391 foreigners from 136 countries who had taken part in combat as part of the Russian army (not counting those from regular North Korean units). Amnesty International itself notes that it could not independently verify these figures.
While conducting the study, human rights researchers made six visits to two prisoner-of-war camps in western Ukraine, where they spoke with citizens of Brazil, Colombia, Cuba, Egypt, Sierra Leone, Sri Lanka, Somalia, and South Africa. Amnesty International also collected testimony from foreigners still serving in the Russian army, as well as from their relatives and lawyers.
According to Amnesty International, foreign citizens were lured to Russia with promises of high pay and expedited citizenship in connection with jobs in security, logistics, construction, IT, and other fields. However, upon their arrival in the country, some were made to sign documents in Russian, a language they did not speak. Among those documents was a contract with the Russian army.
Nalin, a Sri Lankan national (name changed by Amnesty International), says a middleman promised him work as a security guard. He came to Moscow with 58 other Sri Lankans. The group was met at the airport and taken to an office, where they were told to quickly sign documents in Russian without translation. According to Nalin, he did not understand what was happening. Among the papers he signed was a military contract. After a brief training, he was sent to the front. Nalin’s account matches the testimonies of two other Sri Lankans interviewed by Amnesty International, who added they never even received the promised pay.
In late 2025, a South African national referred to in the study as Joseph responded to an online job posting for a driver in Poland. An intermediary explained that he first had to fly to Moscow, pick up a truck there, and drive it to Poland. After Joseph departed, the agent stopped responding. According to Joseph’s wife, upon his arrival in Moscow he had “everything taken away.” He was told he would not be going to Poland and that he “was a soldier now.” The family says Joseph was never paid for his service either.
Another interviewee, Brazilian IT specialist Pedro, was offered a well-paid job in his field in Russia. Instead, he ended up at the Avangard training center. According to Pedro, his captors confiscated his phone, laptop, and passport. He could not leave the center on his own. When he asked the commander to let him go, the commander reportedly replied: “If you try to run, you’ll either go to prison, or we’ll kill you ourselves.” Pedro spent 11 months in the Russian army before being captured by Ukrainian forces. He, too, says he never received the payments he was promised.
Colombian national Jorge told a similar story. He saw a job posting for civilian work in Russia and flew to Ufa via Istanbul in November 2025. There he was given documents to sign in Russian, with people repeatedly saying “quickly, quickly” and “later.” He was then driven by bus for three days to an unknown location, given a rifle and a uniform (despite his protests that he was a civilian), and ultimately delivered to a trench on the front line.
Another Colombian told Amnesty International that his passport was taken from him at the airport in Ufa. He also spent several days on a bus — along with seven other Colombians and 35 Africans — eventually arriving at a military training ground. According to him, rumors circulated among the recruits that people who refused to go to the front were “disappeared.” When his group was sent forward, he saw that everyone from the previous group had been killed; his group was ordered to keep moving.
The study also describes a different scheme, using Peru as an example. According to a group of Peruvian lawyers, since 2025 intermediaries have been receiving about $2,000 for each recruit they deliver for Russian military service. After arriving in Russia, people were made to sign not only military contracts but also powers of attorney valid for up to 15 years (and sometimes indefinitely). Amnesty International notes that such documents could give third parties access to recruits’ money. Such schemes also operated through agencies in Colombia, and The Insider previously reported on a similar scheme involving stolen payments to Brazilians.
The same Peruvian lawyers told the human rights group that they are assisting 200 families whose relatives went to Russia after being promised civilian jobs. They know of at least 300 more such cases and say that the Peruvian embassy in Moscow has returned at least ten former recruits home. In one instance, a father who had already been caught up in a scheme warned his son to contact the embassy before he, too, was shipped to the front. Recruiters failed to find the younger man, and he ultimately managed to escape Russia.
Yet another scheme involves foreigners already living in Russia. According to Amnesty International, migrants with expired visas or other legal difficulties were offered a contract with the army as a way to avoid detention or deportation — and even to obtain a residence permit or citizenship. Foreign prisoners were also offered the opportunity to join the army instead of serving time. Two Egyptians detained on drug charges said they were threatened with lengthy imprisonment and offered military service as an alternative. A Cuban national sentenced to six years agreed to a contract because he faced deportation after his release from prison.
A refugee from a Central African country told Amnesty International that his temporary protection renewal was denied after he refused to sign a contract with the Russian army. After losing his appeal, he was placed in detention, where representatives of the army approached him and other detainees with new contract offers. A lawyer interviewed by Amnesty International confirmed that Russian immigration offices offer foreigners the chance to legalize their status and obtain Russian citizenship through military service. Human rights defenders argue that when the practical alternative is detention or deportation, this cannot be described as fully voluntary consent.
All of the foreigners interviewed by Amnesty International reported severe restrictions on freedom of movement after signing a military contract — regardless of whether they had joined up voluntarily. People had their passports, phones, and other devices confiscated and were barred from leaving their housing. Some said they were woken up at night, put on buses, and driven for several days to an unknown destination without being told where they were going.
Training before deployment to the front usually took about two weeks. Interviewees complained of equipment shortages and a language barrier that often prevented them from communicating properly with their commanders. Amnesty International believes this practice is part of a Russian effort to increase the number of troops at the front by any means possible.
“The level of exploitation and coercion involved led us to conclude that in many cases this amounts to human trafficking, as defined under the UN’s Palermo Protocol,” Amnesty International Secretary General Agnès Callamard said.
In its conclusions, Amnesty International notes that the migration units of Russia’s Interior Ministry and the Russian Ministry of Defense may be directly implicated in these practices. The organization could not establish the exact structure of ties between all of the foreign intermediaries and Russian state bodies involved in the coerced recruitment efforts, but as the report makes clear, the recurrence of identical schemes across different countries points to possible coordination or cooperation between recruiters and the Russian state agencies that send foreigners to the front. Amnesty International stresses that Russian authorities have, at the very least, created favorable conditions for these schemes to flourish and that the Russian military benefits from their existence as a means of replenishing its manpower.

articles.title: Trump's war cascades into a multifront battle for regional order
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump's war cascades into a multifront battle for regional order
Iran has widened its war in the Gulf. Israel, meanwhile, continues its war in the Arab Levant and is also preparing for a greater role in the Gulf.
Tel Aviv is openly declaring that it will continue its war against Iran and its regional axis, while Benjamin Netanyahu continues to speak of bringing down the Iranian regime. Tehran, weakened and in retreat across parts of the Levant, is seeking to expand its influence in the Gulf, not only through the Strait of Hormuz but also by opening a new front around the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
It has already laid the groundwork through a series of military operations against Gulf states and appears to be preparing for further action if the US blockade continues and military strikes persist.
The world is holding its breath. Donald Trump is threatening to strike Pickaxe Mountain, the heavily fortified nuclear facility near Natanz. Netanyahu, meanwhile, continues to say that Israel is ready to carry out further operations against Iran as Tehran seeks to restore its nuclear programme.
Israel is working to provoke Iran further and draw it into a renewed war. Netanyahu appears to see escalation as the main route through which to fight his electoral battle, and therefore prefers to continue military operations in pursuit of achievements that could improve his political standing.
What Netanyahu wants is a renewed war stretching from Lebanon to Syria, alongside renewed confrontation between the United States and Iran. He is also seeking a greater Israeli role in the Gulf, particularly in the Yemen war.
Israeli reports point to concern in Tel Aviv that the Houthis could consolidate control over Bab al-Mandab and gain greater influence over shipping in the Red Sea. The Israeli military has also conducted exercises in Eilat simulating naval warfare.
Redrawing West Asia for good?
What the United States is doing amounts to redrawing the map of the Middle East, and of a significant part of the wider region. Israel, for its part, repeatedly says that it has already changed the Middle East and intends to continue doing so.
The shared US-Israeli objective is to draw the states of the region further into Israel’s orbit and into the Abraham Accords. Israel will seek to impose this through military pressure, whether in Lebanon, Syria or later on other states, including Gulf countries.
Saudi Arabia is particularly important in this regard, as Trump continues to push for it to join the Abraham Accords.
Lebanon, meanwhile, remains under sustained military and political pressure aimed at pushing it in the same direction.
This cannot be separated from remarks by the Israeli president about his ambition to meet the Lebanese president, visit Beirut and announce a peace agreement. Nor is it different from US statements that openly point towards an eventual peace agreement between Lebanon and Israel.
The framework agreement between Lebanon and Israel is increasingly being presented as the basis for governing that relationship, with Hezbollah’s disarmament across Lebanese territory treated as a central condition.
In this way, Washington is effectively giving Israel political cover to remain militarily active until Hezbollah is disarmed.
The US position coincided with Israel’s destruction of tunnels at Ali al-Taher, north of the Litani River, a clear indication that Israeli military operations may continue in other areas.
Netanyahu himself said that the Israeli army had destroyed tunnels around Beaufort Castle and Ali al-Taher, adding that there would be further operations.
Against this backdrop, the region appears to be approaching another moment of explosion.
It may be delayed, or it may erupt at any moment, particularly as Iran studies the options available to it and considers how to respond to the tightening US blockade, the strikes it is facing and the escalation in Lebanon.
In Yemen, Iran has moved towards an escalation through its allies, with the aim of strengthening control over Bab al-Mandab.
This has come alongside advances by the Yemeni government in other provinces as it seeks to tighten pressure around Sanaa and weaken the Houthis.
Iran’s moves in Yemen therefore constitute one of the most important tests of the Mecca security arrangement between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey.
Dealing with the situation in Yemen will require renewed activation of the international coalition established by Saudi Arabia to protect navigation through Bab al-Mandab and the Red Sea.
Israel is likely to watch from the sidelines initially and wait for an opportunity to impose itself as a central player there, whether through security and intelligence cooperation or through direct military power.
But that would come at a high political price: first through a security agreement with Saudi Arabia, and then through a political agreement, peace deal or normalisation.
Israel as the region's policeman
What Israel wants is clear: to become the “policeman of the region” and the effective successor to US predominance from the Gulf to the Arab Levant.
Israel is presenting itself as a state capable of guaranteeing the security of regional governments and protecting them, on the basis that such protection requires alliance with Israel and acceptance of its conditions.
Israel also wants to demonstrate that the Mecca arrangement, or any other security or defence agreement, cannot provide Saudi Arabia or other regional states with an alternative source of military strength.
Turkey and Pakistan did not intervene militarily in support of Saudi Arabia in the past, have not done so now and may not do so in the future.
Israel, which is increasingly fighting over strategic routes, corridors and crossings, is also unlikely to accept a Turkish military presence around Bab al-Mandab or Turkish intervention in a campaign against the Houthis.
Israel is seeking to widen the war across the region.
It wants to show that it alone is capable of confronting Iran and its allies, and through that confrontation impose itself as an essential party in any regional equation involving the Arab Levant, the Gulf or the Eastern Mediterranean.
This is what Israel has been working towards for years.
It has built partnerships and strategic alignments around the Eastern Mediterranean, particularly with Cyprus and Greece, while also seeking to connect these arrangements to the Gulf.
The same logic is visible in the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor, or IMEC, which links India to Europe through the Gulf and the Eastern Mediterranean.
Israel wants Saudi Arabia and Egypt to become part of this wider strategic architecture, while gradually drawing Lebanon and Syria into it as well.

articles.title: EU gives final green light to 6 billion euros in defense aid for Ukraine, Patriot missiles purchase
articles.body:
EU gives final green light to 6 billion euros in defense aid for Ukraine, Patriot missiles purchase
BRUSSELS, Belgium — The European Commission approved a 6.1 billion euros ($7.1 billion) tranche of defense aid for Ukraine on Sept. 11, along with several requests for Ukraine to source weapons from outside the bloc, namely Patriot missiles.
The approval allows Ukraine to use funds from the EU's 90-billion-euro ($104-billion) support loan to purchase U.S.-made PAC-3 Patriot interceptors, one of the few weapons capable of intercepting Russian ballistic missiles.
This, however, does not mean an immediate delivery of the missiles. There is a global shortage of Patriot interceptors, while Ukraine is bracing for a new wave of Russian strikes against its energy grid in winter.
EU member states voiced support for the new defense tranche and the Patriot purchase earlier this week, but the steps still needed final approval from the European Commission.
EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius confirmed at a press conference in Brussels on Sept. 11 that the EU's executive arm has signed off on the measures.
With the latest package, the EU has approved all of the 28.3 billion euros ($32.9 billion) earmarked for Ukraine's defense under the support loan this year.
So far, 8.4 billion euros ($9.7 billion) of that defense money has been disbursed, a process that can only occur once Ukraine provides receipts for cross-checking. Kubilius said another 4.7 billion euros ($5.5 billion) is now being processed.
In April, EU countries approved the 90 billion euro support loan for Ukraine, intended to cover two-thirds of Kyiv's defense and budgetary needs in 2026 and 2027, to be delivered in tranches.
The loan also includes requirements to buy weapons from the EU and Ukraine. Any item where more than 35% of the value of its components comes from third countries requires explicit approval.
Kubilius mentioned that five such derogations had been granted: three for Ukrainian companies to source drone components, and two for U.S components, including the PAC-3 missile interceptors.
Justifying the decision to grant the exemptions, Kubilius said: "Ukraine's military edge depends on the rapid availability of critical products in the required quantities and within very short time frames."
The commissioner did not explain which countries would benefit from the exemption for drone components, but an earlier such exemption, made in April, allowed Kyiv to source components from China.

articles.title: In Gaza, we’ve seen horror unfold with global powers’ support. Is that a blueprint for horror elsewhere? | Ahdaf Soueif
articles.body:
Last week, Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel’s minister of national security, put out an AI-generated video that showed a conveyor belt of overweight Palestinian prisoners – dreaming of food and education – entering one of his prisons; he pops the dream bubbles above their heads and they come out emaciated and crying. Ben-Gvir is building an execution site for Palestinian prisoners with spectator booths, and he recently showed up at Damon prison in northern Israel and taunted female prisoners who complained about the poor conditions. He is digging a moat around a new high-security jail and planning to introduce crocodiles to patrol it. In all this, he has the approval of Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, while the law that he championed mandating the death penalty for Palestinians deemed terrorists by military courts and convicted for lethal attacks is built on public support.
Sometime around 2017, many Palestinians and their supporters in the global media felt a change. Articles about Palestine no longer drew the hate mail we’d been accustomed to and events in support of Palestinian rights were hardly heckled. It seemed that people were less and less convinced by the image long cultivated by Israel and its supporters – the bearer of “western values” in the Middle East, the home to the “most moral army in the world”, a country acting only in self-defence – while it regularly assaulted Gaza and continued to expand its illegal settlements in the West Bank.
It had been a widely held tenet that if enough people in the democratic western world knew the reality of what Israel was doing to the Palestinians, they would pressure their governments, and Israel would be made to observe the norms of international law. Eventually, a reality would be born in which Jews, Muslims and Christians would live as equals within some political system that would be as good – and as flawed – as others. South Africa was always cited as the example, where rising international pressure over the decades was decisive.
But what looked like the winning of the moral, rational argument was offset by an acceleration of the processes of occupation, an increase in the frequency and blatancy of settler attacks in the West Bank, and of Israel Defense Forces (IDF) attacks on Gaza. The past three years have been the logical development of this. In the aftermath of the 7 October 2023 attacks, Israel escalated its killing, maiming and displacement of the Palestinians to the level of certifiable genocide. The defence minister, Israel Katz, says he is committed to the ethnic cleansing of Gaza, while a West Bank settler proudly tells the BBC that one Jewish life is worth 10 million Palestinian lives. Social media is awash with Israelis – from pundits on TV news debates to IDF soldiers – stating and performing the outrages necessary to achieve the objective of a Palestinian-free Palestine.
And while people across the world now know the truth of what is happening in Palestine and repeatedly and full-heartedly reject it, many democracies across the west continue to send arms and provide intelligence to Israel – even in a time of genocide. The US president’s Board of Peace makes a mockery of Palestinians, while hundreds of Israeli trucks clear the rubble from Gaza – and, with it, evidence of war crimes. The US attacks international institutions, such as the international criminal court, that seek to offer some semblance of justice for Palestinians. And to repress the constant protests of hundreds of thousands of their citizens, western democracies compromise their justice systems, attack their educational institutions and undermine their own democratic freedoms. Some have belatedly announced sanctions limited to Israeli settlements – illegal settlements that have should have been sanctioned years ago.
In 2014, I served on the jury of the Russell Tribunal on Palestine. In the preface to the report, which came after Israel’s third war on Gaza in six years, I wrote: “If not genocide, then genocide is not far behind.” Today I wonder if the genocide is not also a trailer for something more to come.
If the genocide was not a surprise, neither is the fact that the old colonial masters have no particular aversion to it. In a line of continuity with their own history, western countries have for decades partnered with Israel on weapons production and intelligence and surveillance technology. The west has sought Israeli advice and training in counter-terrorism, interrogation and civilian population-control techniques. A selling point for Israeli weapons has always been that they have been tried and tested.
And now, as Israel’s genocide is livestreamed, the establishment watches, enables, protects and helps tidy up. We may be watching a research and development exercise, a blueprint, a template, an example being created. We are already in a world where – it has been argued – some populations are surplus to requirements. Some of them live in areas that are a property developer’s dream.
This war is not only about Palestinians and Israelis, but about ideologies of supremacy and domination that threaten the people of the world, its civil societies and what is left of its international organisations. For the moment, it is the Palestinians who are on the frontline, the Palestinians who are being killed and maimed and tortured and displaced. But the Palestinians are also standing between all of us and a world remade in Israel’s image.
- 
  Ahdaf Soueif is the author of Mezzaterra: Fragments from the Common Ground
- 
  Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here.

articles.title: Building Brics: PM Modi-Putin talks, a Thirukkural gift and Xi's big return - key points
articles.body:
With the 18th Brics Summit under way in New Delhi, key developments have already emerged from the high-level engagements. Prime Minister Narendra Modi held talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, gifting him a Russian translation of the Thirukkural, while Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met PM Modi. Chinese President Xi Jinping is also due to arrive on Saturday for the summit and bilateral talks.India is hosting the September 12-13 summit under its 2026 chairship theme, “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability”. The expanded Brics grouping, which now has 11 members, is expected to focus on development, trade, technology, sustainability and strengthening cooperation among emerging economies and the Global South.
PM Modi-Putin talks, Thirukkural gift & carpooling
Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin held bilateral talks, with trade, industrial cooperation, civil nuclear energy and other areas of strategic partnership being prominent in the discussions ahead of the 18th Brics Summit.They reviewed progress in bilateral cooperation across political, economic, defence, energy, space, skill mobility and people-to-people ties. They welcomed Russia’s INNOPROM India exhibition, held for the first time in India, and stressed its role in expanding trade and industrial cooperation, according to an MEA statement.
The leaders also visited the exhibition and interacted with participants.The two leaders also discussed India-Russia engagement in Brics under India’s 2026 chairship, along with key regional and global issues, including the conflicts in West Asia and the Black Sea region and their impact on maritime trade and the safety of Indian seafarers. PM Modi reiterated that dialogue and diplomacy were the way forward in resolving conflicts and said India was ready to assist in peace efforts."They also exchanged views on issues of mutual interest in the regional and global sphere, including conflicts in West Asia and the Black Sea region. PM reiterated that dialogue and diplomacy remains the way forward in resolving conflicts and India stands ready to assist in peace efforts," MEA said in a statement.Moreover, Putin invited PM Modi to visit Russia for the 24th India-Russia annual summit, and Modi accepted the invitation, the MEA said.During the meeting, PM Modi gifted Putin a Russian translation of the Thirukkural, the classical Tamil work attributed to poet-saint Thiruvalluvar. The 1,330 couplets deal with virtue, wealth and statecraft, and love. Modi said the translation would carry Thiruvalluvar’s “eternal wisdom” across languages and borders.
"Presented President Putin with a Russian translation of the Thirukkural, which carries the eternal wisdom of the great Thiruvalluvar across languages and borders," PM Modi said in a post on X.After the bilateral meeting, PM Modi and Putin shared a car as they travelled to an exhibition at Bharat Mandapam.
PM Modi, Pezeshkian hold bilateral talks
PM Modi and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian held a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of Brics Summit. The meeting followed their participation in the Brics Business Forum, where the two leaders, along with Russian President Putin and South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, discussed ways to deepen cooperation in trade, investment, innovation and global development.The talks came against the backdrop of Pezeshkian’s call at the forum for Brics countries to move from “potential cooperation to operational” cooperation. He said the grouping’s strength would be better realised by building stronger networks of trade, investment and joint financing among member countries.Pezeshkian also flagged geopolitical uncertainty, supply-chain disruptions and the increasing use of economic instruments as a means of political pressure.Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian arrived in New Delhi for the 18th Brics Summit. The MEA said India and Iran, as Brics partners, are working towards “shared progress and prosperity”.
Xi’s visit, PM Modi talks and Beijing’s message on managing differences
Chinese President Xi Jinping will arrive in New Delhi on Saturday for the Brics Summit and a bilateral meeting with PM Modi, his first visit to India in nearly seven years. Beijing said the two countries should view ties from a strategic and long-term perspective, strengthen communication, enhance cooperation and properly handle their differences.
The PM Modi-Xi meeting comes as India and China work to stabilise ties following the 2020 Eastern Ladakh standoff. The two sides have held talks on the boundary issue and agreed to advance discussions on an “Early and Substantial Harvest” of boundary delimitation and border management. Xi’s visit is expected to offer fresh indications of the future direction of bilateral relations.
Aastha Jha is a writer at The Times of India, covering politics. She also writes on business, global affairs, social issues, with a focus on policy, governance and their impact on everyday lives. Her work brings together reportage and analysis, tracking developments in India and abroad while examining the broader social and economic currents shaping public discourse.

articles.title: F-16s That Defended Capital on 9/11 Preserved for History
articles.body:
Three F-16s that flew in defense of Washington, D.C., on Sept. 11, 2001, will be retired and preserved as museum artifacts.
The three planes all flew on 9/11: two were among the first three jets to scramble in defense of the capital and the third escorted Air Force One as it returned to Washington later in the day.
On Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist groups hijacked four U.S. airliners, with two striking the twin World Trade Center towers in New York City and the third slamming into the Pentagon near Washington, D.C. The fourth plane was the one that would eventually crash in Shanksville, Pa.
This week, on the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, the National Guard Bureau confirmed that the three planes would be saved:
- Tail number 85-1438, flown by now-Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine, will go to the National Museum of the U.S. Air Force in Dayton, Ohio. His plane was the third to scramble on 9/11.
- Tail number 85-1461, flown by now-retired Lt. Gen. Marc Sasseville, will become a static display at Joint Base Andrews. He was the first to scramble, but this was the jet he flew as escort for Air Force One at the end of the day.
- Tail number 86-0255, flown by Heather Penney, now director of research at AFA’s Mitchell Institute of Aerospace Studies, will go to the American Heritage Museum in Hudson, Mass. Penney’s was the second plane to scramble, flying with Sasseville.
Saving the Vipers
Members of the wing began research more than a year ago to figure what had happened to the jets flown on that fateful day, tracking down old paperwork to figure out who signed out which aircraft and then to discover where those tails were today.
Working with the National Guard Association of the United States, a nonprofit association that advocates for the Guard, they reached out to the Air Force, the Air National Guard, the White House, and others, offering ideas for preserving the historic aircraft under the National Museum of the United States Air Force Heritage Program.
Among the D.C. National Guard F-16s flown on 9/11, one remains in regular flying status with the Air National Guard’s 162nd Wing in Tucson, Ariz. That was the plane Caine flew, which will eventually go to the Air Force Museum.
Guard advocates learned three other planes flown on 9/11 had been converted into QF-16 Full-Scale Aerial Target drones. One—the jet Sasseville scrambled in—was destroyed at the end of its flying life in a missile test. The remaining two were headed for a similar fate when the issue of saving the planes was raised with the Air Force and others.
Jon “Ice” Eisberg, vice president at NGAUS, said once the issues were clear, the challenge was getting the attention of the right people.
“This was a team effort,” Eisberg said. “We just reached out to some of our normal contacts. We went to the National Security Council. We went to Office of Public Liaison in the White House. We went to the Pentagon, and we alerted some folks up on Capitol Hill to this issue.”
The challenge in saving the planes was that QF-16s are a limited resource. The conversions are expensive, about $5 million apiece. The last of 127 conversions was delivered to the Air Force by contractor Boeing in April 2025, according to Air & Space Forces Magazine’s 2026 USAF & USSF Almanac.
QF-16 drones are used for targeting, and once their available flying hours are used up, they can be used in destructive live ordnance tests. One program that would benefit from such tests is the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile, which the Air Force is developing to extend the range of air-to-air combat capabilities beyond visual range.
Still, saving the planes was a priority, and the Air Force came up with a solution: Run down the clock on the QF-16s available flying time, and when their flying hours were all used up, transfer the planes for preservation.
The 9/11 Mission
In a National Guard Bureau video created for the 25th anniversary, Caine recounted his 9/11 experience. “I was running our flying program” that day, Caine recalled. When he saw the second plane hit the World Trade Center on TV, “it was clear that the United States was at war.”
Caine, a major and the wing’s weapons officer at the time, called for live weapons to be readied on the flightline, but getting weapons ready takes time. Soon after, the White House called, he said, “telling us to get airborne.”
Joining Sasseville, a major and the wing’s operations director, and two junior pilots, Penney and Brandon “Igor” Rasmussen, Caine said the group formulated “a hasty, quickly constructed gameplan.”
The clock was ticking as they waited for official authority to launch, and once they had that, weapons were still not ready. Sasseville, who would eventually rise to become Vice Chief of the National Guard Bureau, told Penney as they headed to their plane that they would have to ram the airliner.
“We had an entire wing of support behind us, getting things moving that day, reacting to that terrible attack,” he said. “The White House communicated with us because we were one of the few units in a position to actually do something. … We took off as soon as we could.”
Penney, a young lieutenant and the daughter of an experienced fighter pilot, has wondered why she got the nod that day. “I like to think it was because I was a good pilot,” she said in a recent conversation. “But I think it was because I was single. It was just me and a dog.”
Everyone was operating on adrenaline, Sassevile said. “No one asked any questions.”
Once on the flightline, they dispensed with the routine pilot’s precheck, climbing directly into their planes, trusting their maintainers to have gotten everything ready. Penney had never scrambled an aircraft before—or even trained to.
They took off without clear rules of engagement—these were arranged once they were airborne—and headed out in search of what would later become known as Flight 93, which crashed in a field in Shanksville, Pa., after the passengers stormed the cockpit to stop the terrorists inside.
In fact, they had already done so when Sasseville and Penney took off, but no one knew that at the time.
“We understood what the threat was,” Penney said, recalling their flight up the Potomac River to the northwest of Andrews. “We were looking for a rogue airliner, flying low. We knew they had turned off their transponders.”
Without missiles or bullets—the F-16 has a gun, but they were loaded only with training rounds—the objective target would have to come down with brute force.
“Our only choice,” Penney said, “was going to be to ram the airliner.”
But first they’d have to find it. Unsure of its location or even what vector it was taking to the capital, they headed up the Potomac, then circled back to defend the city. The plan, Sasseville told Penney, was that he would aim his jet at the cockpit and the terrorists, and Penney would take aim at the tail.
The Federal Aviation Administration had ordered all planes in U.S. airspacer to land, and it gradually became clear that Flight 93 had crashed short of the terrorists’ intended target.
Returning to Andrews, Penney recalled looking down at a base that had come alive, its parking lots full, and a line of cars backed up waiting to get on base. “Guardsman came to their units without needing orders, without waiting for paperwork,” she said. They got planes ready, set up cots in the operations area, brought in food. The Guardsman would fly air combat patrols over Washington for the next 90 days straight, and they were already on duty—before they’d ever received orders or even a call.
“They just told their employers, ‘You know, boss, my nation’s calling,’ and they went.”
Now their planes will endure as a reminder of that day and the clear sense of duty those Airmen displayed when the United States came under attack.

articles.title: Race for Xi-Modi meeting at Brics summit
articles.body:
Beijing and New Delhi are arranging for a bilateral meeting between President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a Foreign Ministry spokeswoman said in Beijing on Friday, as Xi is set to travel to India to attend a Brics summit this weekend.
A meeting would mark the third consecutive year in which Xi and Modi meet, following their talks in Kazan and Tianjin, said Mao Ning at a regular news briefing.
She said China stands ready to work with India to follow the strategic guidance of the two leaders, view bilateral relations from a strategic and long-term perspective, strengthen communication, expand cooperation and properly handle differences, so as to be good-neighbourly friends and partners helping each other succeed. 
Xi will attend the 11-member Brics summit, address the event and have in-depth exchanges with leaders on the current international situation, she said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin arrived in New Delhi on Friday and was followed hours later by his Iranian counterpart, Masoud Pezeshkian, for a summit set to be dominated by wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, as well as economic challenges.
Putin and Pezeshkian were due to hold talks with Modi.
For Xi, it will be his first visit to India since 2019 and marks the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the neighbours that has seen flights, visas and high-level contacts gradually being restored.
Brics, created in 2009, now includes Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates – three countries with sharply differing positions on the war launched by the United States and Israel in February.
"The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the Brics summit," said Harsh V Pant of India's Observer Research Foundation. "What was seen until last year as an achievement – the expansion of Brics – today looks like a big constraint on Brics." 
"The war in Iran will provide a stern test of the [expanded] group's cohesion," said Shilan Shah of Capital Economics, noting the failure of the Brics foreign ministers to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May.
The summit is being held on Saturday and Sunday at the capital's Bharat Mandapam convention centre amid heightened security measures.
   
Around 15,000 police personnel and 200 companies of paramilitary forces have been deployed, India's state-run broadcaster All India Radio quoted Manish Kumar Agrawal, special commissioner of police of the protective security division, as saying.
Traffic on key roads may be temporarily halted or diverted, and government and private schools have been shut. (Agencies)
Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: 25 years after 9/11: Did Osama bin Laden really win?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
25 years after 9/11: Did Osama bin Laden really win?
A quarter-century tends to sharpen questions that once sounded indecent to ask out loud. On the eve of the 25th anniversary of 11 September 2001, one of them refuses to go away: did Osama bin Laden win?
The instinctive answer is no. Bin Laden is dead. Al-Qaeda's core was hunted into irrelevance years before a US Navy SEAL team found him hiding, isolated and largely powerless, in a walled compound in Abbottabad, Pakistan. No caliphate rose from the ashes of the Arab autocracies he despised. When the region's people finally did rise, in 2011, they carried no black banners and quoted no jihadist scripture. They wanted bread, dignity and a vote - not a war with Rome.
And yet, a quarter-century out, with US troops gone from Kabul in humiliation and the region's old American-built order in open collapse, the honest answer is more uncomfortable than the instinctive one. It requires separating two projects that have been carelessly conflated for 25 years: bin Laden's theological ambition, and his strategic method. The first failed absolutely. The second worked - not as he designed it, but as an act of asymmetric provocation succeeds: by luring a far stronger adversary into destroying itself.
A miscalculation
Nothing has done more to correct the record on bin Laden's own thinking than Nelly Lahoud's forensic reading of the roughly 6,000 Arabic-language documents recovered from his compound. Her account of the archive demolishes a myth popular on both the jihadist and the neoconservative side: that bin Laden foresaw, and welcomed, a long American entanglement in Muslim lands. He didn't. His calculation was almost the opposite, and considerably cruder.
Bin Laden had watched Washington abandon Beirut after the 1983 barracks bombing, and flee Mogadishu after the 1993 firefight. He concluded, wrongly, that the American public had no stomach for casualties, and that one spectacular strike would do to Washington what a decade of Vietnam had done: force a humiliated retreat from the Muslim world. Strip away the US security umbrella, he reasoned, and the "apostate" Arab regimes propped up by it would collapse on their own, clearing the way for al-Qaeda to lead the masses into a restored caliphate.
It was, in the language of his own circle, a plan to strike the head of the snake rather than its tail. It was also a catastrophic misreading of American politics. Rather than withdraw, Washington rallied behind an open-ended global war. Al-Qaeda's core, by its own internal correspondence, spent the following decade not building a movement but simply surviving - hunted by drones, its own security committee called a calamity, cut off from the regional franchises that hijacked its brand for sectarian wars it privately regarded as disastrous for its image.
The organisation was reduced to watching the Arab Spring unfold on satellite television with a mixture of excitement and dread.
Bin Laden's own daughter, according to the documents, worried openly that a new generation might conclude that political change was possible without jihad. She was right. It was.
Judged on its own terms, bin Laden's project was a rout. He did not mobilise the Ummah. His own franchises did not obey him. He died in hiding, isolated even from the organisation that bore his name. This part of the story is genuinely worth putting to rest.
The trap sprung anyway
But grand strategy is not measured only by whether the plan worked as drafted. It is measured by what an adversary's reaction costs. And on that score, the story Andrew Bacevich tells in America's War for the Greater Middle East is not one of jihadist failure. It is one of imperial self-harm.
Convinced of its own indispensability, Washington treated 9/11 as a licence to remake the Islamic world by force, launching an open-ended "war on terror" that eventually touched some 85 countries. By the accounting of Brown University's Costs of War project, the bill has run past $6 trillion - closer to $8 trillion counting veterans' care - and has cost close to a million lives, including thousands of American service members.
The invasion of Iraq did not produce a client democracy. It produced a sectarian civil war, the rise of the Islamic State group, and a decisive strategic gift to Iran. Two decades spent chasing a stateless enemy through the mountains of the Hindu Kush were two decades China spent consolidating power in Asia largely undisturbed.
None of that was written into bin Laden's plan. He did not predict a multipolar 2026 any more than he predicted his own decade in hiding. But he understood something his adversary did not: a wounded superpower certain of its own righteousness can be goaded into wounding itself far more badly than any non-state actor ever could.
An order that cannot be rebuilt
This is usually where the anniversary essay stops, with irony and a shrug. It shouldn't. Because the structure 9/11 set in motion did not just cost blood and treasure - it broke the political architecture that made American primacy in the Middle East possible in the first place.
Marc Lynch has called this structure the "American Middle East": the post-1991 order built on Washington's protection of Israel, its access to Gulf oil, and its sponsorship of a network of compliant, heavily militarised Arab autocracies. As Lynch argues in Foreign Affairs, that order is now finished - and the recent war with Iran was only its final casualty, not its first.
Steven Cook's diagnosis in The End of Ambition supplies the mechanism. Throughout the Cold War, he argues, Washington succeeded precisely because its Middle East goals were modest and preventive: keep oil flowing, keep the Soviets out, keep Israel secure. Only after 1991, drunk on unipolar confidence, did the foreign policy establishment swap prevention for transformation - and transformation, in the Middle East, is where American power keeps going to die.
The invasion of Iraq was, in Cook's own reading, Washington's Suez moment: the self-inflicted blow that broke the back of its regional order, much as the 1956 Suez crisis broke Britain's and France's.
The bookends of that unravelling arrived a generation apart: the fall of Kabul to the Taliban in 2021, and the Saudi-Iran normalisation two years later, brokered not in Washington but in Beijing, with the United States pointedly absent. Riyadh, Abu Dhabi and Cairo no longer behave as client states. They hedge, openly, between Washington, Beijing and Moscow, having concluded, correctly, that American protection is no longer unconditional and American attention no longer reliable.
Add to this the moral cost. Unconditional US backing for Israel's campaign in Gaza finished off whatever remained of Washington's claim to defend a rules-based order, in full view of a generation across the Global South that will not forget what it watched happen, with American fingerprints on it.
Two ledgers, one verdict
So did he win? Only if the two ledgers are kept scrupulously separate.
On the ledger of political theology, bin Laden's account is bankrupt. No caliphate. No mobilised Ummah. A movement that outlived him mainly as a brand hijacked by local warlords for massacres he privately deplored. The region's people rejected his vision the moment they had a real choice, in favour of something more modest and more human: a job, a vote, an end to the torture chamber.
On the ledger of systemic consequence, the verdict runs the opposite way. Bin Laden did not need to build anything. He needed only to provoke a superpower certain of its own virtue into a two-decade campaign of overreach that would drain its treasury, fracture its domestic politics, distract it from its real strategic competitors, and ultimately dissolve the very regional order his 19 hijackers set out to attack. He got exactly that - more than he could have imagined from a cave in Tora Bora.
None of this vindicates him. But a quarter-century on, as Washington confronts a Middle East it can no longer arrange, referee or rebuild, the uncomfortable truth is that the man who lost the argument over what the region should become nonetheless helped determine, more than any other single actor, who no longer gets to decide.
Hesham Gaafar is a researcher specialising in Islamic thought and movements and conflict resolution. He served as editor-in-chief of the Arabic section of IslamOnline.net portal from 2000 to 2010. He co-founded the Regional Center for Mediation and Dialogue and serves as a consultant to a number of international institutions in the field of conflict resolution.
Have questions or comments? Email us at: editorial-english@newarab.com
