articles.title: Pentagon’s top weapons buyer says Congress must act on munitions
articles.body:
Pentagon’s top weapons buyer says Congress must act on munitions
A top Pentagon official said lawmakers must “step up and deliver” on the Trump administration’s US$1.5 trillion (S$1.9 trillion) funding request if the military is to replenish its stockpiles of key air defence interceptors and deep-strike weapons that have seen heavy use in the Iran war.
“We have the contracts in place, we have the acquisition reform in place,” Michael Duffey, the undersecretary of defense for acquisition and sustainment, said on Sept 11 on Bloomberg Television’s Balance of Power. “We need that funding to deliver for the warfighter.”
Duffey would not speculate on the risk that Congress could decline to finance the Pentagon’s priorities through a party-line budget manoeuvre known as reconciliation.
Regardless of the funding mechanism employed, he said the full US$1.5 trillion is crucial to achieving US President Donald Trump’s objectives.
“It will be incumbent on us to work with Congress over the next couple of months to ensure that we get that full funding for our programme,” Duffey said.
He added that empowering the Pentagon to enter into seven-year production contracts with defence contractors has “incentivised industry to invest their own money” to increase production rates for key munitions.
Asked about the Defense Department’s priorities, he said “we’re focused on the critical munitions that are so essential for our competitive advantage and that are sought after worldwide – weapons like the Patriot, the Tomahawk, the Thaad interceptor, the Standard Missile”.
The administration has announced framework agreements with prime contractors and suppliers of core components for high-end munitions as part of an effort to expand production dramatically in the coming years.
“These investments and these ramp rates will allow us to replenish much faster – expended munitions and also ensuring that we’re building out capacity for the next generation,” Duffey said. BLOOMBERG

articles.title: UAE might be the best way to solve S-400 saga: US congressman
articles.body:
A senior U.S. congressman has suggested that transferring Russian-made S-400 air defense systems to the United Arab Emirates could be the ideal solution to the ongoing rift between Türkiye and the United States, potentially allowing Ankara to reenter the F-35 fighter jet program.
“We have discussed this matter extensively. The core issue here is how this can be implemented. As you know, negotiations were held with the UAE. This might be the best solution,” U.S. Congressman Darrel Issa told the daily Hürriyet in an interview in Ankara on Sept. 10.
Issa paid a visit to Ankara, where he was hosted by President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan. He also attended the 250th anniversary reception of the U.S. at the Ankara Embassy along with U.S. Ambassador to Türkiye Tom Barrack.
Türkiye and the United States have long been negotiating the former’s return to the F-35 joint fighter program and the removal of all remaining sanctions stemming from its 2019 purchase and deployment of Russian S-400 air defense systems.
In July, U.S. President Donald Trump promised to lift the sanctions imposed on Türkiye under the Countering America’s Adversaries Through Sanctions Act (CAATSA), but that requires Türkiye to give up possession of the S-400s.
Issa recalled talks between Türkiye-U.S. and the UAE for the re-export of the air defense systems to the latter.
On sanctions, Issa recalled the promises voiced by Trump, saying “A decision has already been made from the President down to the lowest level; there are no sanctions against Türkiye.”
On Türkiye’s return to the F-35 program or sales of these jet fighters to Türkiye, the congressman underlined that there is a huge backlog of orders.
“Right now, in my opinion, the highest priority needs to be the modernization of the F-16s. The modernization of existing aircraft is a high priority for both Türkiye and the U.S.,” he stated.
Türkiye has agreed to buy 40 brand-new F-16 fighter jets from the U.S., but negotiations continue over pricing. It dropped the initial request for 79 modernization kits from the package and decided to assign Turkish Aerospace Industries (TUSAŞ) to upgrade the existing F-16 fleet.

articles.title: Key Russian ally mulls military mobilization
articles.body:
Key Russian ally mulls military mobilization
Belarus will bolster its military combat readiness and could even announce “mobilization” to test it, President Alexander Lukashenko has said.
The Belarusian leader made the remarks on Friday when he toured the Obuz-Lesnovsky military training grounds near the city of Baranovichi in the west of the country. During his visit, Lukashenko met top military officials and inspected communications and control systems. The president said that he was set to continue vetting the country’s forces, revealing that an artillery brigade and signal troops are currently undergoing extensive inspections.
“I’ve already put it in plain terms: the army needs a shake-up – the time has come. The entire army. We will vet everyone. Right up to the point of mobilization,” Lukashenko told reporters.
The vetting process is set to be as close to real war conditions as possible, he added. “We are preparing for war so that it does not happen,” the Belarusian leader stated.
Speaking to senior military officials, the president reiterated that Minsk was not seeking to attack anyone but only to bolster its defenses. “We have no intention of attacking anyone; we are pragmatists. We understand that attacking anyone – say, one of our neighbors – would be tantamount to suicide. We cannot win a conflict against the ‘monsters’ – the states situated along our borders,” he said.
While it was not immediately clear which countries exactly Lukashenko described as “monsters,” most of the Belarusian neighbors’ militaries greatly surpass its capabilities. Minsk maintains a modestly sized military of less than 50,000 active-duty servicemen, against some 1.5 million troops in Belarus’ key ally, Russia. Ukraine, which has been locked in a conflict with Russia for over four years, is believed to have around 900,000 active-duty personnel.
Other neighbors of Belarus, Poland, Lithuania, and Latvia are NATO member states. While the two Baltic nations have tiny militaries, Warsaw has been actively building up its force recently. Poland has some 220,000 active-duty troops and continues to expand the force as well as rearm it with modern weaponry. Numbers-wise, the country’s military has become the third-largest within the NATO bloc, surpassed only by the US and Türkiye.

articles.title: Ukraine's Fire Point confirms attack on Ozon in Russia's Saratov and reports Flamingo strike in Volgograd
articles.body:
Ukraine's Fire Point confirms attack on Ozon in Russia's Saratov and reports Flamingo strike in Volgograd
Ukraine's defence forces struck an Ozon warehouse complex in the Russian city of Saratov and the chemical plant Volgogradpromproekt on the night of 10-11 September.
Source: Fire Point; Andrei Bocharov, Governor of Russia's Volgograd Oblast
Quote from Fire Point: "Overnight, Ukraine's defence forces destroyed another Ozon warehouse complex using FP-1 drones – this time in Saratov. The area of the destroyed warehouse was 85,000 sq m. The complex was designed to store more than 30 million items of goods."
Details: It was also reported that FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles struck the Volgogradpromproekt plant in Volgograd overnight.
"Direct missile hits on the target were recorded, resulting in a fire… Ukrainian sanctions, as always, proved to be the most effective," Fire Point stated.
On the morning of 11 September, Volgograd Oblast Governor Andrei Bocharov reported a missile attack on the region, saying that "debris was recorded falling on the territory of an industrial facility in the south of Volgograd".
"Emergency services are working and dealing with the consequences. Emergency services and the municipality have been instructed to assess the damage, deal with the consequences and prepare temporary accommodation facilities," Bocharov stated.
For reference: Volgogradpromproekt LLC is under US sanctions for working with the Russian military-industrial complex. The company produces ferrocene-containing combustion catalysts and develops chemical production technologies.
Background: On the night of 10-11 September, drones struck the Saratov oil refinery in Russia. In addition to the refinery, a fire broke out at an Ozon logistics centre.

articles.title: Zelensky’s chief of staff suspect in new graft probe – RT source
articles.body:
Zelensky’s chief of staff suspect in new graft probe – RT source
Vladimir Zelensky’s chief of staff Kirill Budanov is being investigated by Western-backed anti-corruption detectives over possible crimes committed during his tenure as head of Ukraine’s military intelligence agency (HUR), a source familiar with the matter has told RT.
Zelensky chose Budanov to replace Andrey Yermak, who quit amid a widening series of corruption scandals at the heart of the Ukrainian administration.
The National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) has launched a new probe into Budanov over possible wrongdoing during his tenure in the intelligence agency HUR, which he headed from 2020 to 2026.
Last month, Ukrainian media linked Budanov to a money laundering scandal involving his now-fired deputy in Zelensky’s office, Irina Mudraya. NABU accused her of orchestrating a scheme to use bags of cash to pay bail for former Energy Minister German Galushchenko, who is a suspect in a separate graft case involving Zelensky’s inner circle.
According to sources cited by Ukrainskaya Pravda, Budanov ordered Mudraya to help Galushchenko secure his release from pre-trial detention, likely at Zelensky’s direction.
In surveillance tapes published by NABU, Mudraya said she was acting on behalf of her superiors without naming anyone. The outlet suggested, based on the context of the conversation, that she was likely referring to Budanov when she quoted an official as saying that “corruption needs to be systematized and controlled” and not combated.
Asked by Hromadske about the allegation, Budanov said: “Let the court sort out whose names are mentioned and where.”
HUR came under media scrutiny earlier this month after its personnel engaged in firefights in Kiev with troops from the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU). The altercation stemmed from a custody dispute over a member of a neo-Nazi-led militia force, which the military intelligence incorporated under Budanov’s leadership.
Last week, Ruslan Kravchenko, a Zelensky appointee, tendered his resignation as prosecutor general after NABU accused his chief cybercrime investigator of extracting payments from scam-call centers on behalf of his superior.
Zelensky previously tried and failed to place the Western-backed agency under the control of the Prosecutor General’s Office.

articles.title: Why is the Kremlin staging Russia’s most boring election ever?
articles.body:
Hello and welcome to Vlast! This time, we focus on the Kremlin’s strategy for next week’s parliamentary elections.
We also analyze why the Kremlin is forcing companies to fund air defense; a 100,000-strong Orthodox religious procession in Moscow; and the closure of the Goethe-Institut in Russia amid deteriorating relations with Berlin.
⏳ This newsletter contains 1,826 words and will take about 10 minutes to read.
Why parliamentary elections resemble presidential elections
Russia’s parliamentary elections next week look set to be the most uneventful in the country’s modern history. Candidates are not campaigning, the major political parties are silent, and there is no criticism of the authorities. The only visible politician is President Vladimir Putin. Notably, the most prominent news story in recent weeks in state-owned media has been speculation about whether a concert by rapper Kanye West will take place in St. Petersburg.
Of course, in Russia’s closely controlled public politics, a lack of drama is no accident. It’s deliberate. The Kremlin believes that suppressing voter turnout by minimizing coverage and campaigning is the best way to increase support for the ruling United Russia party. Particularly given that the war in Ukraine means there is no cash for populist pre-election handouts.
It’s possible that candidates may become more visible in the final week of campaigning (the vote takes place over three days from September 18), but this will not alter the dynamic. After the authorities last month barred the liberal, anti-war Yabloko party from participating, there has been no debate or controversy. Politics has disappeared from the airwaves.
Many candidates do not attend pre-election debates, with empty studios becoming a social media meme. It’s obvious that none of the parties taking part in the elections are trying to attract attention: they do not criticize the authorities, and refrain from discussing topical issues. Televised campaign ads tend to be cheap, make heavy use of AI, and be devoid of substance. None of the parties that are—at least on paper—competing against United Russia have funded their candidates in single-mandate districts.
At the same time, United Russia, which traditionally absorbs public anger directed at the authorities, is pretending it does not exist. The main public figures representing the party in these elections—Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin, war correspondent Yevgeny Poddubny, Children’s Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova, and Ukraine war veteran Vladislav Golovin—have each given one interview to state-owned TASS. That essentially marks the extent of United Russia’s campaign.
Instead, the only political figure visible to voters in recent weeks has been Putin. The result is that parliamentary elections have begun to look a lot like presidential elections—again, a deliberate Kremlin strategy.
On state-owned television, Putin has been doing most of the campaigning for United Russia. Putin has always been involved in boosting support for United Russia, and he “shares” his approval rating with the party. But the absence of United Russia and its candidates in these elections have made his involvement particularly glaring.
In his campaigning, Putin appears to have been aiming to reassure people on key issues. Last week, he twice dismissed the possibility of another imminent round of mobilization. He also said the government would not be confiscating the bank deposits of ordinary people—another major worry for Russians. Data published by Kremlin polling organization FOM on Thursday showed that general anxiety levels have fallen almost 10 percentage points from a multi-year high at the end of July, perhaps as a result of Putin’s interventions.

articles.title: Ukrainian FP-5 Flamingo Missiles Strike Sanctioned Russian Defense Enterprise in Volgograd
articles.body:
- Category

Ukrainian FP-5 Flamingo Missiles Strike Sanctioned Russian Defense Enterprise in Volgograd
Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck the Volgogradpromproekt enterprise in Russia’s Volgograd overnight on September 11 using FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles, according to the compamy’s statement.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The missiles hit the targeted facility, triggering a fire at the site.
Volgogradpromproekt is under US sanctions over its involvement with Russia’s military-industrial complex. The company produces ferrocene-based combustion catalysts and develops technologies for manufacturing chemical substances.
The strike came amid reports of explosions and fires in Volgograd overnight, as the city was targeted in a missile and drone attack.
Volgograd region Governor Andrei Bocharov said that missile debris fell on the grounds of an industrial facility in the southern part of the city following the attack. He also reported damage to an apartment building in Volgograd’s Krasnoarmeysky district.
The attack on Volgograd coincided with Ukrainian strikes on other targets inside Russia. Overnight on September 11, Ukrainian strike drones also targeted Saratov, sparking fires at a local oil refinery and an Ozon logistics center, according to the Exilenova+ OSINT project.
Footage and photographs shared by local residents showed large fires and thick columns of smoke rising from both sites following the attack.
Ukrainian defense manufacturer Fire Point confirmed that its FP-1 long-range drones carried out the strike on the Ozon facility.

articles.title: Gateway or outpost? Inside Israel's growing footprint in Cyprus
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Gateway or outpost? Inside Israel's growing footprint in Cyprus
On the southern coast of Cyprus, the signs of a growing Israeli presence are becoming harder to miss.
There are new housing developments marketed to Israeli buyers, large parcels of land changing hands, political posters, and a network of schools, synagogues, kosher businesses, and other institutions serving a community that is no longer made up solely of tourists and second-home owners.
The result is an increasingly visible Israeli footprint on an island that has long relied on foreign capital to drive its property market.
Yet the scale and concentration of some projects have prompted a debate on the island: is this simply another wave of foreign investment, or is something more permanent taking shape?
A new wave of foreign investment
Cyprus’s economy has long depended on third-state investment, with successive schemes – including the controversial “golden passports” and golden visas – designed to attract capital, particularly into property.
Historically dominated by the United Kingdom and Russia, capital has more recently come from Lebanon, Ukraine, and Israel.
The golden visa scheme enables non-European Union (EU) nationals to obtain residency by investing €300,000 in property or a company, raising concerns over transparency and regulation.
Direct investment vis-à-vis Israel stood at around €3.5 billion in stock in 2025, with €308 million in transactions, according to preliminary data from the Central Bank of Cyprus.
Recent Israeli investments have involved large land purchases and projects combining housing developments with resorts and gated communities. In 2023, liberal Israeli newspaper Haaretz wondered whether Cyprus was becoming the “second Israel?”
Israel's growing exodus
The trend coincides with rising Israeli emigration. Since 2023, political tensions surrounding judicial reforms proposed by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's far-right coalition government, followed by the Gaza war, have fuelled mounting insecurity and pessimism about the country’s future.
“The justice reform from January 2023 was the first turning point. Many lost hope in the future of Israel. October 2023 confirmed this trend, and many decided to move,” Michael Harari, Israel’s former ambassador in Cyprus, told The New Arab.
Between 2023 and 2025, 270,000 citizens left Israel, a recent study based on data from the Israel Central Bureau of Statistics (CBS) found, highlighting particularly substantial emigration among highly educated and economically strong groups.
In Cyprus, this movement has translated into both relocation and investment – helping turn what was once largely a tourism and property relationship into a more visible presence.
Cyprus as a haven
In this troubled landscape, removed from regional convulsions, Cyprus has become “Israel’s favourite island escape” – less than an hour away by plane, relatively affordable and safe.
“Cyprus offers the closest escape,” Louisa Varaclas, director of the Israel Office within the Cyprus Tourism Ministry, told The New Arab.
Israel was Cyprus’s second-largest tourism market in 2025, accounting for 13% of all arrivals, or 600,000 visitors. The Israeli Embassy estimates that around 15,000 to 20,000 Israelis currently live in Cyprus, compared with 6,500 in 2018, although the exact number is difficult to determine because many hold European Union (EU) passports.
Geographical proximity, political ties, a favourable tax regime, business opportunities, and a sense of security have helped make the island attractive for residence and investment.
“Cyprus is a security partner,” Roee Kibrik, Director of Research from the Israeli Institute for Regional Foreign Policies (Mitvim), told The New Arab. For Israel’s strategic logic, he argues, the island can almost be understood as an extension of Israel’s security space - while the partnership also serves Cyprus’s security interests.
“Given that political and economic relations between Israel and Cyprus deepen, there will also be growing Israeli interest in tourism, residence, and investment in Cyprus,” Zenonas Tziarras, a lecturer in the Department of Turkish and Middle Eastern Studies from the University of Cyprus, told The New Arab.
Cyprus also offers a “gateway” to the European Union (EU), its market, its electricity and gas infrastructures and sea routes, but also its institutional structures and political channels, Kibrik argues.
From property to communities
The growing Israeli presence is particularly visible in coastal areas around Larnaca, Limassol, and Paphos, where Israelis have purchased property and marketed dedicated housing complexes. Jewish institutions, kosher businesses, and Hebrew-language services have expanded alongside them.
“Some definitely left Israel. Some others live in Cyprus while continuing to work in Israel, while others are moving part of their assets or establishing companies in Cyprus,” Kibrik says.
This trend has also fueled concerns over housing affordability. Property prices rose by 11.7% in Larnaca and 10.7% in Limassol between 2025 and 2026, with the Central Bank of Cyprus attributing part of the inflation to stronger demand from third-country investors, alongside construction and labour costs.
Harari admits there are tensions. “This migration is a natural process and contributes largely to the local economy. But of course, for a small place as Cyprus, these numbers are substantial, and you can also understand concerns from local populations because there is influence on property prices.”
The island’s role as a refuge during crises has further deepened these connections. In October 2023, 5,000 Israelis landed in Cyprus. During the Israel-Iran conflict in June 2025, 15,000 Israelis were stranded after airspace closure.
Chabad centres provided accommodation, food, and emergency assistance, illustrating how a network initially serving religious and tourist needs has also become part of the infrastructure supporting a growing Israeli community.
Chabad, a global Hasidic Jewish movement, operates around 4,000 centres in 100 countries. Publicly apolitical, recent investigations have documented support from parts of the movement for Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power), the far-right party led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
In Cyprus, Chabad operates six centres, alongside a synagogue, kindergarten, mikvah, kosher certification agency, a cemetery, and summer programmes. Its founder and Cyprus’s chief rabbi, Zeev Raskin, also promotes the development of resorts and tourist complexes designed to comply with Jewish law.
Gated communities and contested projects
Several projects have sparked controversy over planning and environmental regulation, the role of national and local authorities, and the longer-term character of this presence.
In Latchi, a large hotel complex completed the final stages of construction while licensing issues remained unresolved. In Polemidia, a €50 million Jewish school designed for up to 1,500 students has generated concerns over traffic and planning, while the municipality had not been involved in the process.
Its slated director, Rabbi Yehoshua Smukler, has described the project as the future “cornerstone” of Cyprus’s Jewish community.
In Trozena and Gerovasa, Hungarian-Israeli businessman Uriel Kertesz has proposed redeveloping abandoned villages into an “ecotourism” project combining homes, vineyards, a wellness centre and restored ruins. The project has faced environmental scrutiny, as the area falls within the Natura network of protected natural areas.
In Zygi, a 60,000-square-metre luxury development is marketed as a gated complex of residences serving the Jewish community. When announced in 2024 by property entrepreneur Daniel Morris Goldberg and Rabbi Ziv Raskin, the project was promoted as a “kosher slice” of Cyprus.
“Do we have closed communities, rather than absorbing individuals into the local culture?” Kibrik asks, pointing to an emerging debate over housing, culture, and the transformation of some areas.
The speed and concentration of Israeli investments distinguish them from the longer-established Russian presence, notes Nasia Hadjigeorgiou, Assistant Professor in Transitional Justice and Human Rights from the University of Central Lancashire - Cyprus.
“Russians have had a very long-standing presence on the island, which developed gradually, whereas Israelis have been much more sudden and economically aggressive, with entire areas being purchased. Russians are primarily based in Limassol and live within the city, whereas some Israelis have begun constructing gated communities, separating themselves within exclusive areas," Hadjigeorgiou tells The New Arab.
"There is also an oversensitivity here because of what is happening in Israel and Palestine and the history of Israelis settling on land, accompanied by violence and displacement, while the local history of occupation vis-à-vis Türkiye adds another layer.”
Theodosis Pipis, a doctoral candidate in History from the University of Leiden, puts the question more bluntly.
“Given these projects and the high concentration of land purchases happening swiftly in coastal and port cities, could Cyprus be falling under the auspices of some form of permanent or semi-permanent Israeli expansionism?”
Growing influence and public outrage
In July 2026, campaign posters for Gadi Eisenkot, former Israeli army chief-of-staff and candidate in Israel’s elections, popped up along highways around Larnaca airport, generating an unusual debate over Israel’s growing influence in Cyprus.
This event echoed wider concerns. “Israeli buyers are purchasing significant land parcels and strategic economic assets. This cannot but sound the alarm for us,” Stefanos Stefanou, a spokesperson for the Progressive Party of Working People (AKEL), warned in June 2025.
And this trend has become a significant issue across the political spectrum, from the election posters to the redevelopment of abandoned villages.
“It’s a topic most circles on the island discuss - no matter though you are from the left, the far-right, the centre, we can all see the growing Israeli presence on the island,” Pipis tells The New Arab.
Growing economic connections also involve powerful business interests. Cypriot-Israeli real estate businessman Yakir Gabay, whose fortune is estimated at around $4 billion, has become a prominent figure in Cyprus.
He is involved in an €856 million investment project around Limassol and recently purchased a 950,000-square-metre plot from the Bank of Cyprus for €28 million.
In February 2026, he also joined the executive committee of the 'Board of Peace'. He visits Israel frequently, operates behind the scenes, and has close personal and business ties to Jared Kushner and, as early as November 2023, reportedly submitted a reconstruction plan for Palestine.
Cyprus, alongside Greece, has recently become an essential part of Israel’s strategic environment. The relationship spans defence, military cooperation and energy, and has developed into a deeper strategic partnership.
Since June 2017, the Israeli military has regularly conducted exercises on the island, including air force, naval, and ground forces units, and intelligence and evacuation drills. The exercises have included simulations relevant to operations in southern Lebanon, making Cyprus a uniquely accessible training environment for Israel’s military.
“Of course, the deepening strategic relationship between both states has made Cyprus an attractive place to Israeli citizens, as a place to invest and live. Both come together,” Harari says.
Sylvain Henry is a writer based in Samos, Greece, and a master's graduate in sociology and political philosophy. He recently worked with the Cyprus Refugee Council
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: Ukraine shows its drones in Canada as Ottawa pledges a third of its future output
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney attended a presentation of Ukrainian drones, Ukrainian-Canadian developments, and defense-component manufacturers in Calgary on 10 September, the Ukrainian presidential readout said.
The event followed the signing of documents on defense and security cooperation, which Kyiv calls the first step toward a Drone Deal on the American continent. That deal would take cooperation beyond individual Ukrainian-Canadian production projects toward a broader industrial model pairing Ukrainian technology with Canadian manufacturing capacity.
The systems shown included the Vampire 4S, a heavy multirotor that drops munitions at night and that Russian troops call Baba Yaga, and SkyFall's P1-SUN interceptor, designed to bring down Shahed-type drones and priced at about $1,000 at this year's World Defence Show. The lineup also included the Shrike FPV drone and the Hor reconnaissance UAV. Companies also presented projects involving drones, ground robotics, and secure communications.
The systems and joint projects
The presentation featured Himera radio sets alongside the four drone systems. Zelenskyy and Carney were also shown the remote operation of the Ratel ground robotic complex and uncrewed maritime systems from UFORCE and Scorpena.
Airlogix plans to produce the Hor reconnaissance UAV with Canada's Sentinel. Ai Drones UA and Bombardier Recreational Products (BRP) showed a prototype ground robotic complex, while Himera and Quantropi presented secure communications solutions. The announcements at the event covered future cooperation between GTH and General Dynamics Mission Systems–Canada, JK Land Vehicles and General Dynamics Land Systems, and a training program between SkyFall and Calian.
The readout said that 21 Canadian companies took part and that they already integrate their components into Ukrainian systems.
Canada's drone problem
Canada's armed forces hold 2,000 drones today and will need millions, Carney said in Calgary. A new national drone marketplace is meant to build the capacity for those millions inside two years, with Ukrainian firms teaching Canadian ones while Canadian manufacturing and AI expertise flows back the other way.
A third of all the drones Canada builds will go to Ukraine's defense, Carney pledged. The presidential readout puts the share at 30% of the drones the joint program is to produce.

articles.title: Escaping the AI safety nightmare: What can governments do?
articles.body:
India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi takes a group photo with AI company leaders including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei at the AI Impact Summit in New Delhi on February 19, 2026. | Ludovic Marin/AFP via Getty Images
A dramatic resignation from AI company Anthropic this week where a researcher accused it and OpenAI of “gambling with our lives,” threw fuel onto the fire around AI safety.
As governments from California to the U.K. scramble for a political response to the issue of whether AI can be made safe, three experts told POLITICO that to make real progress, laboratories, governments and international bodies must first get on the same page about testing.
The steady flow of revelations that AI labs failed to contain models they were testing, allowing them out into the world where they lied, hacked and coordinated with each other, has heightened urgency to address core questions of how governments or other bodies can or should guarantee that AI is being developed and deployed safely.
Advertisement
Lawmakers, campaign groups and developers alike are calling for new laws and international treaties on AI. “It’s a wake-up call to the United States Congress, to parliaments all over the world, that we’ve got to do something immediately to stop the uncontrolled growth of AI,” U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders told BBC’s Newsnight program Thursday.
The experts POLITICO spoke to want to see an overhaul of the existing approaches championed by developers, testing AI agents en masse rather than one at a time, and for the industry to submit itself to more old-school auditing like the nuclear sector.
Getting the basics right
This year’s heightened AI anxieties started when OpenAI admitted that during internal testing, its own AI agents autonomously gained access to the internet and had hacked fellow AI company Hugging Face, where they thought they would find the answers to the assignments they’d been set.
OpenAI wasn’t the only one: copycat confessions from Anthropic and Meta AI drove home the breadth of the problem, and even the U.K.’s taxpayer-funded AI Security Institute admitted to errors in evaluating Anthropic and OpenAI agents that saw near misses with agents targeting real people and organizations.
Developers and testers alike say they’re working to avoid the mistakes of the past, for example making sure models can't access the internet and deploying data monitoring to detect unexpected activity by the AI being tested.
Another relatively simple concept would be requiring AI companies to report safety incidents, whether or not during testing.
Advertisement
A case in point is that OpenAI agents hacked a German website back in May to use it as a messaging board, Reuters reported last week. OpenAI had not publicly announced the incident and responded to the Reuters reporting on X saying: “We and the larger AI community do not yet have a clear standard for how to report misalignment that shows up during training, evaluation, and deployment.”
“[Reporting] timelines are going to need to be dramatically shortened [for incidents], and so we need much better continuous monitoring capabilities,” said Imogen Stead, AI policy manager at London-based think tank the Centre for Long-Term Resilience, adding that the data will be needed in real time “and that will be true for governments and for labs.”
Speaking at a London event for U.K. lawmakers arranged by campaign group ControlAI on Monday, computer scientist Stuart Russell said that the most concerning aspect of the Hugging Face incident for him was that “by running a thousand agents communicating with each other, they were able to generate behaviors that no one agent could do by itself,” referring to investigations showing the incident was far more severe than OpenAI first acknowledged.
“But [in] the evaluations, standard testing is done with a single AI system, not with a thousand,” he told lawmakers, so now the industry must anticipate the possibility of many agents all collaborating at once.
Out of alignment
Beyond avoiding any obvious mistakes in testing, there are issues in the culture of AI testing that are more deeply embedded.
The concept of the alignment of AI models or agents — i.e. making sure AI systems do what they're told by human users and don’t go off-piste — has been one of the cornerstones for AI safety in the industry’s eyes.
Advertisement
AI companies like OpenAI champion alignment as the best way to make AI safe. In last week’s release of new model GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI called it “our most aligned model … more likely to operate within the boundaries set by the user and implied by its environment.”
Others view alignment as one of the main obstacles to AI safety, seeing it more as a Band-Aid that gives the semblance that models are being made safe.
“The wider problem is that alignment has become a stand-in for all of AI safety,” said Andrew Strait, former head of societal resilience at the U.K.’s AI Security Institute.
Boyan Milanov, senior research scientist at the AI Now Institute, said alignment will “never be reliable enough to replace proper safety.”
The investigations into the Hugging Face incident showed AI agents were aligned with their own objectives, not those of their human creators. Former OpenAI researcher and whistleblower Daniel Kokotajlo told the London ControlAI event that the incident was an “example of misalignment: in no way, shape, or form were these AIs trained or instructed to do this sort of thing.”
The sector seems stuck on alignment. AI researcher Jacob Coxon, the researcher who relit the AI safety debate this week with his resignation from Anthropic, also said that “attempting to speedrun alignment should require extraordinary confidence that there are no better trajectories available.”
Advertisement
Alignment is “significantly insufficient when we talk about agents interacting with each other and in potentially adversarial environments like the open web,” said Strait. The focus on alignment has also led to the sector “drastically under-resourcing” other aspects of safety, said Strait.
He said his concern is that the industry is racing to deploy agents “while treating the infrastructure needed to contain their behavior as something we can catch up on later.”
“The people whose websites, businesses and public services those agents interact with have not agreed to be part of that experiment,” said Strait.
Old but gold
An old-fashioned approach to safety standards is an alternative to the industry’s preference for alignment. Calls for AI to defer to existing safety engineering practices from sectors such as nuclear safety, civil aviation or medical devices stretch back years.
In these other sectors, there is the concept that an overall system will include fail safes to ensure that if one element of the system fails, either something else kicks in or the system shuts down.
The problem with AI is that it’s still highly unpredictable. “It can fail in very weird ways. There are a lot of attacks against AI that don't fit traditional frameworks,” said Milanov, and so any safety engineering approaches should “evolve to take AI into account.”
Advertisement
There is a fundamental issue here, said Russell, speaking alongside OpenAI whistleblower Kokotajlo at the ControlAI event, that even AI’s creators don’t really understand it. Developers “tell us that we, the human race, cannot protect ourselves with such rules because they, the developers, do not know how to comply with them. Obviously, this is a fallacy,” said Russell.
Milanov pointed to another issue with how models are built. AI developers train their models to resist answering questions on topics such as chemical, biological and nuclear risk, he said, whereas the “real solution” is controlling the data that models are trained on so the models don’t know how to give instructions to build a biological weapon.
Regulation, regulation, regulation
Pushback is needed against AI labs creating their own safety standards, said Milanov, as OpenAI has again called for this week. Instead, new regulation should “force them to adhere to existing standards that we already have now,” he said.
There is some regulation in the works at the U.S. state level. California Governor Gavin Newsom signed two bills on AI safety testing Wednesday. Anthropic had already backed the bills, but OpenAI added its support just before Newsom gave his approval.
The bills mark a small step for formalizing testing: they create a registry and ethical rules for external auditors and ways to check the credentials of organizations touting for testing work.
Outside of the U.S., the EU has an AI Act in force that means companies must work to combat “systemic risks.” The U.K. government abandoned its initial plans for an overarching AI bill last year, but some U.K. lawmakers are taking that fight back up. This week one British MP introduced a bill to prohibit the development of artificial superintelligence, another wrote to the U.N. and OECD begging them to do more at the global level.
Companies like OpenAI and Anthropic’s public willingness to back new regulation could be heartening, although Strait noted “the test is whether they accept independent scrutiny, enforceable obligations and decisions that go against their commercial interests.”
“We should not keep releasing systems with unresolved, serious safety failures and asking society to absorb the consequences,” Strait said. “Safety testing needs to give the public a basis for trusting these products, and regulators the evidence and authority to act when that trust is not warranted.”

articles.title: How 9/11 Helped Shape Our Politics Today
articles.body:
From the moment they occurred, the terror attacks of Sept. 11, 2001 were seen as inaugurating a new age of asymmetric violence and warfare. President George W. Bush described the war on terror that followed as a generational conflict.
Yet, for all the transformations it produced, Al-Qaeda and Islamic militancy more broadly have, in my view, receded within a decade. Not so much because it was defeated on the battlefield but because it was unable to gain much support among Muslims. When popular uprisings swept the Arab world in the early 2010s, protesters in Tunisia, Egypt, Syria, Bahrain, and elsewhere in the region took to the streets not in the name of Islam, but democracy. The Arab Spring, more than any military victory, signaled the decline of militancy. Al Qaeda faced its greatest defeat at Tahrir Square.
Islamic militancy flourished principally on the battlefields of war on terror, in countries such as Afghanistan and Iraq, a trajectory epitomized by the emergence of the Islamic State from within the American prison system in Iraq. While Islamic militancy still survives in pockets of weak or fractured states, elsewhere it has petered out into the province of petty criminals or psychologically disturbed individuals. What, then, does its brief and brutal career mean for world history?
The End of the Cold War
The dramatic arrival of Al-Qaeda and Islamic militancy in the global public sphere in the early 2000s did not mark the beginning of a new chapter of global history. Perhaps that confrontation between Al-Qaeda and America signaled a historical ending: the true conclusion of the Cold War. By the fall of 2001, the Soviet Union and the bipolar world had been dead for a decade.
The Cold War survived in the institutions and practices it had created: NATO, the United Nations and its conventions, international courts and the multilateral institutions established to knit together a divided world through systems of deterrence, development and compromise born of the fear of an atomic holocaust. For a while, these institutions appeared capable of operating without their founding cause, but that hope proved illusory. In the 1990s, wars swept across the Balkans, the Caucasus, the Middle East and Africa. Al-Qaeda arose at the confluence of post-Cold War globalization and unipolar violence.
With its emergence at the turn of the millennium, Al-Qaeda, I argue, brought the Cold War to a definitive close by overturning its central presuppositions. The war on terror rendered the familiar categories of the Cold War—the balance of power, deterrence, great-power rivalry, and hegemony—increasingly obsolete. Fought in civilian spaces against nonstate actors dispersed around the globe, the war on terror also ended up destroying most of the Cold War’s remaining ideological states in the Middle East, including the socialist republics of Iraq, Libya, and Syria.
Al-Qaeda's emergence also marked the end of Islamism, which was itself a Cold War movement dedicated to revolution and the creation of ideological states. Islamism’s only durable strongholds, Iran and Afghanistan, came to embody its takeover by clerical establishments of the kind it had once sought to displace.
The war on terror also weakened the liberal state, another creature of the Cold War, whose animating purpose had been to pose capitalist liberty against Communist dictatorship. Osama bin Laden used to claim that Westerners thought their interventions in the Middle East would remake the region’s states in the images of their own, but instead it was the Americans and Europeans who came to resemble their despotic and corrupt clients in the region.
One of the goals of Al-Qaeda’s campaign of terror was to precisely achieve that by showing how even violence falling short of a conventional war and posing no genuine existential threat was sufficient in provoking Western democracies to dismantle the civil liberties of their own citizens, exposing their claims to freedom as hypocritical. As the war on terror dragged on, Al-Qaeda’s leaders portrayed the anti-terror laws and the increasingly militarized conduct of the U.S. and its allies not as signs of resolve and strength but as displays of weakness and proof of the shallowness of Western liberalism. Bin Laden might have been disappointed by Al-Qaeda’s inability to mobilize enough Muslims around the world to overthrow their dictatorships, but the U.S. and its European allies, which sustained those authoritarian regimes, sadly behaved much as he had predicted.
A sacrificial, if not nihilistic, movement whose iconic figure was the suicide bomber, Al-Qaeda had little interest in conquest and government. One of its major objectives was to provoke Western states into attacking their own democracies, in a kind of auto-immune response to terrorism, in which the effort to defend the political body corroded it from within. In that particular sense, bin Laden was perversely successful in dragging America and its allies into expensive wars and weakening their liberal norms as they chose widespread use of emergency powers, surveillance, indefinite detention, torture, and rendition. The war also brought suspicion of Muslims, hostility toward immigration, civilizational rhetoric, and border militarization from the political margins to the center of Western public discourse.
America’s preoccupation with the war on terror did squander its unipolar decade. It wasn’t a coincidence that the rise of China—and the China shock—came a few years after the Great Recession of 2008 and a decade after the 9/11 attacks. The cultural and political landscape of Europe and America today—characterized by polarization, populism, and a pervasive distrust of institutions—can be understood, at least in part, as the legacy of the response to the 9/11 attacks by Al-Qaeda. By this measure, my assertion would be that bin Laden won the war on terror much as he had predicted he would.
What sustained the liberal order
The rise of populism and far-right politics in America and Europe has generated great laments for the corrosion of a golden age of liberalism and progress following the victory of the Allied powers against fascism in World War II. The flowering of postwar liberal democracy owed less to the defeat of fascism than to the Cold War, when the existence of a socialist alternative compelled Europe and North America to emphasize social protections, greater equality, and meaningful political rights.
Thus, the crisis of liberal democracy after 9/11 might be better understood not simply as a blowback from the war on terror, but as an aftershock of socialism’s collapse. After the collapse of the Soviet bloc, that pressure disappeared. Though liberal institutions survived formally, the social and economic settlement that sustained them had begun to erode.
During World War II and in its immediate aftermath, the Allies were hardly exemplars of liberal standards. Several allied powers were colonial empires engaged in the violent suppression of nationalist movements in Asia and Africa even as they fought fascism. Nor can any account of Allied conduct ignore the firebombing of German cities or the atomic destruction of Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
Although the war in Europe and the Pacific dominates debates about Allied misconduct, the colonial character of World War II may tell us more about the origins of our present moment. Colonial armies fought in every theater and constituted some of the forces deployed during the war. At least a million soldiers fighting in the British and French armies against fascism were Muslims. Civilians in territories like India, though far from the principal battlefields, also suffered immensely during the war. The Bengal famine, in which some three million people, Hindus and Muslims, starved to death, was, as many have argued, caused in part by wartime disruptions to grain supplies and by imperial policy.
Europe didn’t only take men and material from the colonies for the Great War, but also a repertoire of its illiberal practices in the colonies. The Nazis drew upon precedents established in colonial wars waged by European powers. The Allies, in turn, brought home methods of coercion that had previously been largely confined to their empires. Among them was the revival of medieval doctrines of just war, which subordinated contractual obligations to unilateral claims of moral authority—doctrines that resurfaced during the war on terror to justify pre-emptive attacks and torture.
World War II should be understood not simply as liberalism’s triumph over tyranny but also as a source—and continuation—of Western illiberalism, much like what came to the surface after 9/11. It was the Cold War that provided the real foundation of mid-century liberalism. One might even argue that the post-9/11order, from which today’s far-right movements partly emerged, has its roots in World War II’s struggle for global hegemony, a contest suspended for the duration of the Cold War.
The war on terror represented a failed effort to impose a unipolar order on the world, one that could no longer rely on the economic instrumentality of globalization alone. And its failure also discredited the globalization associated with free trade and mass migration. In its place arose far-right movements in Western Europe and North America dedicated to dividing the world into racial and cultural blocs, divisions often defended in the language of the struggle against terrorism and Islam.
In America, this political vision harks back to the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine; in Europe, it reaches further, to the myth of a culturally homogeneous Christian continent. In both cases, the animating force is not social conservatism alone but hostility toward immigrants, and toward Muslims in particular. Its deeper history may therefore lie in decolonization, which transformed immigration into a defining political reality distinct from the colonial systems of slavery, indenture and managed labor migration that preceded it.
Asian and African decolonization not only overlapped with the Cold War but was, in many important ways, made possible by it. As the rival superpowers courted newly independent countries, they helped secure what sovereignty many of those states possessed. Yet decolonization, no less than the Cold War, also made possible the European Economic Community and, eventually, the European Union. Europe emerged from World War II with most of its colonial possessions more or less intact. It was only decolonization that allowed the continent to cohere into a new kind of economic and political unit.
The long aftermath of decolonization
Immigration has a double history in America, proceeding from two waves of decolonization: the 19th century independence of Latin American countries and that of Asian and African nations in the 20th century. American anti-immigrant politics consequently differs from the European version, remaining more closely bound to the Monroe Doctrine and its vision of hemispheric control.
Europe may possess the older political history, but its encounter with immigration is more recent, starting with labor migration to help with European reconstruction after World War II and expanding again in the wake of the Cold War. The end of the Cold War weakened the sovereignty of many postcolonial states, producing new waves of migration as those countries faced economic pressure or were drawn into conflict. It also reduced European countries from strategic partners in the Cold War to increasingly dependent allies—a relationship laid bare by the war on terror, which expanded American power while disproportionately rewarding American companies.
The end of the Cold War, made visible through 9/11 and its aftermath, has also transformed Europe’s understanding of its past. While World War II is still invoked, especially by liberals, it no longer occupies its former place as the 20th century’s defining event and the founding moment of the international order now coming apart.
The ascendance of immigration—and, with it, race and culture—as the central political concern on both sides of the Atlantic suggests that decolonization has displaced the war in the historical imagination. Narratives about the struggles against fascism or Communism still shape Western identities, but political debate is increasingly dominated by fears of what might be called “reverse colonization.”
Europe’s unwillingness or inability to reckon with colonialism may explain its strange, even pathological identification with the anxieties of its former subjects. The fear of foreign settlement, demographic change, and cultural swamping all echo the language once used in colonized societies of Asia and Africa, where the Christian West was regarded as precisely such a threat. This switching of places is apparent in portrayals of Islam as both an alien and more virile force than Western liberalism, a force whose supposed cohesion and will to dominate must be countered by weapons of solidarity and domination.
European politics has thus increasingly begun to appropriate the defensive posture of the peoples Europe once ruled. Perverse though this identification may be, it reveals the extent to which decolonization—itself part of the Cold War’s history— has become the century’s central historical drama. This switching of places is especially true of Islam seen as an alien but also more virile force than Western liberalism, one whose power thus needs to be countered by its own weapons of solidarity and domination.
For all the spectacle of its asymmetric attacks, Al Qaeda—and Islamist militancy more broadly—never had more than some tens of thousands of committed supporters worldwide. These movements did not emerge from some hermetically sealed Islamic history. They belonged to global events and narratives, which gave them what influence they possessed. The disproportion between their small numbers and enormous consequences cannot be explained primarily by technology, mass media or even the war on terror. It arose from the institutional and political vulnerabilities exposed by the Cold War’s belated conclusion.
We now live amid the detritus of the end of the Cold War and are able to recognize decolonization as the crucial event of the 20th century. Its legacy animates both movements seeking greater inclusion and campaigns promising to restore a national unity defined in racial or cultural terms. More than three decades after the Soviet Union’s collapse, we still live in the wake of the Cold War, an aftermath that first revealed its force in the attacks of Sept. 11, 2001 on New York and Washington, D.C.

articles.title: UK lawmakers urge Burnham to back ban on superintelligent AI after chilling warnings
articles.body:
More than 70 MPs and peers have urged Andy Burnham to back a ban on the creation of artificial superintelligence (ASI) and lead an international movement to stop the technology after a week of warnings from experts of a 10% chance it could kill all humans.
Fifteen former government ministers, along with the former head of the civil service Robin Butler, senior Labour MPs including John McDonnell and leading Conservatives, Liberal Democrat and Scottish National party MPs have written to the prime minister. They urged him to throw the government’s weight behind a bill, tabled in the Commons on Tuesday, that would prohibit ASI – an as-yet-nonexistent AI that would outcompete human capabilities in most domains.
They have escalated their campaign to Downing Street after concerning statements from current and former AI insiders. Evan Hubinger, a senior employee at Anthropic, said he believed there was a greater than 10% chance the technology could wipe out humanity, and Jacob Coxon, a 28-year-old researcher at Anthropic, who previously worked at OpenAI, quit on Tuesday with a warning that went viral, claiming “neither company was acting responsibly”, they were “gambling with our lives” and were locked in a race for AI supremacy.
Alex Sobel, the Labour MP behind the bill, said he and other signatories – ranging from the children’s TV presenter Floella Benjamin to the former Conservative environment minister Zac Goldsmith and former Northern Ireland first minister Arlene Foster – want Burnham to foster “a clear framework where superintelligent AI cannot be created”. He added: “AI companies have made it clear that they will develop agents without constraint. They’re trying to develop superintelligence, while openly admitting there is a significant risk of human extinction.”
The bill mirrors legislation banning ASI promoted in Washington DC by Bernie Sanders, who this week said: “You’ve got to be a moron not to say slow it down.” It is backed by the Nobel prize-winning nuclear proliferation campaigner Beatrice Fihn and the leading Berkeley AI professor Stuart Russell, as well as Control AI, a transatlantic lobby group funded by the billionaire Skype co-founder and self-described “anti-extinctionist” Jaan Tallinn.
A ban on ASI in the UK, but not in the US or China where the frontier models are being created, risks having little impact. But the parliamentarians’ bill aims to pave the way to an international agreement. They call on Burnham to use next year’s UK presidency of the G20 to create “a coalition of the willing to tackle this national and international security threat”.
A government spokesperson said: “While we do not consider the measures proposed in the bill to be the right approach, we are exploring whether additional targeted interventions may be needed in future to address the most significant AI-related national security risks.”
Others have played down the risk, saying that ASI remains only theoretical and that guardrails could work to prevent the worst outcomes. Experts warn that these could include catastrophic cyber-attacks, novel biohazards and AIs in control of autonomous weaponry. This week’s wave of concern follows a spate of more minor but still worrying incidents involving unexpected misbehaviour by AI agents under training by OpenAI and Anthropic in which they broke out of training environments, secretly conspired and hacked into other systems.
Elon Musk, who runs xAI as part of his SpaceX empire, suggested without evidence that this week’s warnings of catastrophic risk were part of a “psyop” that “has been prepared for a long time”. The world’s richest man gave a different read on the state of AI, claiming: “AI+robots will more than double the global economy in less than 10 years.”
Anthropic revealed another incident of a rogue AI this week and said criminals, state-sponsored groups, spyware vendors, scientists and propagandists had attempted to use its AI models to design missiles and bombs, create deadly pathogens and surveil dissidents. At its main rival, OpenAI, Paul Christiano, an AI adviser to the US government, joined the lab’s non-profit foundation and immediately warned the company was not on track to reduce the risk of “catastrophic” loss of control to an acceptable level.

articles.title: Canada sanctions eight Russians over deported Ukrainian children as only about 2,500 of more than 20,000 have come home
articles.body:
Canada has sanctioned eight people over Russia's deportation of Ukrainian children and their indoctrination and militarization, Ukrinform reported on 11 September. It is the second Canadian package this year built around the removal of children from occupied areas. The measure surfaced during Ukraine's presidential visit to Canada, at a moment when Kyiv's own register counts far more children taken than brought home.
Eight names, and what Ottawa says they did
Canada's foreign ministry says all eight took part, now or earlier, in unlawfully deporting and transferring Ukrainian children, and in subjecting them to indoctrination and militarization. The department published the eight names without setting out the posts they hold. Its own register dates the listing's entry into force to 4 September.
The listing is an administrative measure, not a criminal charge. In most cases, people in Canada and Canadians abroad may not deal in a listed person's property or provide them financial services. Breaking those rules is a criminal offense, investigated by the border agency and the federal police.
Canada pledges more than $1 billion for Ukraine’s critical air defense as Russia intensifies missile and drone attacks
Canada's Ukraine-related listings cover more than 3,500 individuals and entities across its Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, and Moldova regulations. Its separate ship list reached 731 vessels in June, listed for shadow-fleet work moving sanctioned Russian oil, gas, and arms. The previous expansion, in August, hit a manufacturer of armored vehicles.
Thousands of children taken, about 2,000 home
Russia has deported or displaced 20,651 Ukrainian children since February 2022, and Ukraine has brought just over 2,000 of them home through the Bring Kids Back UA initiative. Officials believe the real figure is far higher.
Russian authorities have moved groups of Ukrainian teenagers through military-patriotic camps, occupation schools, and youth movements in occupied areas and inside Russia, and Ukraine has named the people running that work.

								Russia weaponizes Ukrainian children in occupied territories. Ukraine singles out those responsible

articles.title: “Its task is not cargo. Its task is people”: After Russian FPV drone hit their house, K-2 brigade sent ground robot to carry casualties out
articles.body:
A Ukrainian ground robot that usually hauls ammunition and supplies to the front carried a different load out of it this time: wounded civilians. The 20th "K-2" Unmanned Systems Brigade sent the unmanned vehicle to evacuate people hurt when a Russian FPV drone struck their house, and its soldiers walked the entire route to shield them from more drones.
On a front where Russian FPV drones hunt anything that moves, Ukraine has handed its ground robots the jobs that get soldiers killed: hauling ammunition, clearing mines, and dragging out the wounded. Its units ran more than 100,000 such robot missions in the first eight months of 2026, and Zelenskyy has pushed to contract at least 50,000 more of the machines.
The robot carries people, not cargo
An FPV drone hit the civilian house and left casualties who had to be moved out of the danger zone, K-2 explained, and an ordinary evacuation would have been too risky, so the unit used an unmanned ground vehicle instead.
"Its task is not cargo. Its task is people," the brigade said.
Soldiers guard the whole route
The robot did not go alone. As the footage shows, K-2 soldiers escorted the vehicle along its entire path so they could protect the wounded from Russian drones if the machine came under attack.
That risk is real: Ukraine's evacuation robots have themselves become targets, with Russian forces striking anything that moves on a front where the drone kill zone can stretch a dozen kilometers back from the line.
Near Kupiansk, a robot that once ran a dozen missions now survives three or four before it is destroyed, according to a robot-unit commander.
Earlier, Tetiana Chornovov, the commander of a platoon of anti-tank guided missile systems, said that Ukraine still didn't have a proper system for getting its wounded off the battlefield. Chornovol believes that creating separate staffed evacuation units within brigades is the most necessary reform now, each with an autonomous team and special transport.
